◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before building anything, you need to know what tool does what. Power BI is a family of products, not just one app. The PL-300 exam tests knowing which tool to reach for in which scenario.

The Power BI family

ProductPurposeAudience
Power BI DesktopBuild reports, model data, write DAXReport authors (free)
Power BI ServicePublish, share, refresh, RLS, scheduleAll users (cloud)
Power BI MobileConsume reports on phone/tabletConsumers on the go
Power BI Report ServerOn-premises hostingOrganizations needing on-prem
Power BI EmbeddedEmbed in custom apps via AzureApp developers (ISV)
Power BI Report BuilderPaginated reports (.rdl format)Print-style detail reports

The five-step BI workflow

1. CONNECT — Get Data from sources (databases, files, APIs)
2. TRANSFORM — Clean/shape with Power Query (M language)
3. MODEL — Define relationships, calculated columns, measures (DAX)
4. VISUALIZE — Build report pages with visuals
5. SHARE — Publish to Service, distribute via apps / Teams / email

The same flow whether your data is 1,000 rows or 100M.
Each step has its own toolset and best practices.

Power BI Desktop interface

Three primary views (left sidebar icons):

REPORT view (default)
 - Drag visuals, build pages
 - Fields pane (right): tables and measures
 - Visualizations pane: visual types + field wells
 - Filters pane: filters at visual/page/report level

DATA view
 - Inspect underlying data row-by-row
 - Add calculated columns
 - Categorize fields (e.g., set as Geo type)

MODEL view
 - See and edit relationships between tables
 - Set cardinality and direction
 - Group tables, hide fields

Ribbon tabs:
 Home, Insert, Modeling, View, Help, External tools

Bottom tabs:
 Pages of the report (rename, hide, duplicate)

Common data sources

CategoryExamples
FilesExcel, CSV, JSON, XML, PDF, Parquet
DatabasesSQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake, BigQuery
Cloud servicesAzure SQL, Synapse, Databricks, Dataverse
SaaSSalesforce, Dynamics 365, ServiceNow, Google Analytics
SharePoint / OneDriveLists, folders of files
Web / APIWeb pages, REST endpoints, OData
Power PlatformDataflows, Datamarts, Datasets

Connection modes

When connecting, Power BI offers up to three modes:

IMPORT
 Default; loads data into the .pbix in memory (compressed columnar)
 - Fast queries
 - Requires refresh
 - Size limits: 1 GB (Pro), 100 GB (Premium per User), 400 GB (Premium per Capacity)
 - Full DAX functionality

DIRECTQUERY
 Sends queries directly to source on demand
 - No refresh needed
 - Live data
 - Slower queries; some DAX functions unavailable
 - Source must support it (SQL DBs, Spark, etc.)

LIVE CONNECTION
 Special case: connect to existing Power BI dataset / Analysis Services model
 - No local model
 - All modeling happens at source
 - Used to build reports on shared semantic models

COMPOSITE MODEL
 Mix Import and DirectQuery in one report
 - Some tables imported (dimensions)
 - Some tables DirectQuery (large fact)
 - Most flexible but most complex

File types

ExtensionContents
.pbixPower BI report file: model + visuals + data
.pbitTemplate: model + visuals, no data (for distribution)
.pbidsData source: just connection info, no model
.rdlPaginated report (built in Report Builder)
.json (theme)Theme definition for styling

The Microsoft Fabric umbrella

As of 2024+, Power BI is part of Microsoft Fabric

Fabric capacities (F SKUs) replace Premium capacity (P SKUs) for new purchases
Fabric workloads (alongside Power BI):
 - Data Engineering (Spark notebooks, Lakehouses)
 - Data Science (ML pipelines, AutoML)
 - Real-Time Analytics (KQL databases, Eventstreams)
 - Data Factory (Pipelines, Dataflows Gen2)
 - Data Warehouse (T-SQL warehouse)
 - OneLake (unified data lake under everything)

Power BI items still exist:
 - Reports, datasets, dashboards, dataflows, datamarts
 - Now sit alongside Lakehouses, Warehouses, Notebooks in workspaces

For PL-300 today: focus is still Power BI; Fabric awareness helps.

Roles in a typical BI team

RoleResponsibility
Data engineerSource systems, dataflows, datamart
Data modelerStar schema, measures, DAX
Report author (PL-300 focus)Build visuals, layout, interactivity
AdminWorkspaces, capacities, governance
ConsumerView reports, ask questions
Data stewardEndorsement, data quality, lineage

Common ecosystem mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing dashboards (Service) with reports (Desktop)
  2. Choosing DirectQuery when Import would be faster — DQ only when you need live data or can't fit it in memory
  3. Building paginated reports in Desktop — that's what Report Builder is for
  4. Storing .pbix files in random places — use OneDrive / SharePoint or Git for version control
  5. Mixing Pro and Premium plans confusingly — clarify before committing
  6. Skipping the "Connect → Transform → Model → Visualize → Share" workflow
  7. Treating Power BI Embedded as Premium — they're different (Embedded is Azure-billed for ISVs)
  8. Forgetting Power BI is part of Fabric now — capacities may be F SKUs
★ ON THE EXAM

"Where do reports get built?" → Power BI Desktop.

"Where do dashboards get built?" → Power BI Service.

"Where are paginated reports built?" → Power BI Report Builder.

"On-premises Power BI hosting?" → Power BI Report Server.

"Embed in custom apps?" → Power BI Embedded (Azure).

".pbix vs .pbit?" → pbix = report; pbit = template (no data).

"Connection modes?" → Import, DirectQuery, Live, Composite.

"Modeling languages?" → M (Power Query) for transformation; DAX for measures.

"BI workflow?" → Connect → Transform → Model → Visualize → Share.

"Fabric F SKUs?" → New unified capacity covering Power BI + other Fabric workloads.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power BI is a family: Desktop (build), Service (share), Mobile (view), Report Server (on-prem), Embedded (apps), Report Builder (paginated)
  • Workflow: Connect → Transform → Model → Visualize → Share
  • Three Desktop views: Report (build visuals), Data (inspect rows), Model (relationships)
  • Wide range of data sources: files, databases, cloud, SaaS, web/API, Power Platform
  • Connection modes: Import (fast, refresh), DirectQuery (live, slower), Live (shared semantic model), Composite (mixed)
  • .pbix is the standard report file; .pbit is a template without data
  • M language for transformations in Power Query; DAX for measures and calculations
  • Premium capacities are now Fabric F SKUs (newer purchases)
  • Choose tool by audience: Desktop for authors, Service for collaboration, Mobile for consumers
  • Each role in a BI team has different responsibilities — report author is PL-300's focus

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every Power BI project starts with Get Data. Choosing the right connector and connection mode determines refresh strategy, performance, and what's possible downstream. The PL-300 exam tests connecting to common sources, choosing modes, and handling credentials.

The Get Data button

Home tab → Get Data

Two ways to access:
 - Get data dropdown (Most common) — shortcuts to recent sources
 - Get data → More... — full connector list (200+)

Categories in the connector dialog:
 All / File / Database / Power Platform / Azure / Online Services / Other

Each connector has:
 - Authentication options
 - Optional advanced parameters
 - Specific connection string format

Excel as a source

Home → Excel workbook → browse to file

Navigator dialog appears:
 Lists sheets and named tables
 Select what to load:
 ☑ Multiple selection enabled
 Preview pane shows data

Best practices:
 - Use Excel TABLES (Ctrl+T) — much cleaner than sheets
 - Tables have explicit column headers and ranges
 - Avoid merged cells, blank rows, formatting-as-data

After Load:
 Each chosen sheet/table becomes a Power BI table
 Power BI infers data types but verify them

CSV / Text files

Home → Text/CSV → browse

Settings to configure:
 File origin (encoding):
 65001 (UTF-8) — most common
 1252 (Western European)
 Other encodings for international data

 Delimiter:
 Comma (CSV)
 Tab (TSV)
 Semicolon, Space, Custom

 Data type detection:
 Based on first 200 rows (default)
 Based on entire dataset
 Don't detect (recommended if you'll set types yourself)

Click Load (direct) or Transform Data (cleanup first)
Transform Data opens Power Query Editor — recommended for production

Folders — multiple files combined

Get Data → Folder
 Choose folder path; all files inside become rows in a metadata table

 Click "Combine & Transform" (button in preview)
 Power BI auto-detects file structure
 Creates a function that loads each file the same way
 Stacks results from all files into one table

Use cases:
 - Monthly CSV exports (one file per month)
 - Web log dumps
 - Multi-region exports

If new files appear in the folder → next refresh picks them up
Perfect for repeating ingest patterns

Caveats:
 - All files must have similar schema
 - Filename can be retained as a column (useful for traceability)

SQL Server / database connections

Get Data → SQL Server database

Required:
 Server: e.g., "myserver.database.windows.net" or "sql01\PROD"
 Database: name (optional; can pick from list after auth)

Optional:
 Command timeout
 Custom SQL statement: prefilters in the source (recommended for big tables)
 Include relationship columns
 Navigate using full hierarchy

Connection mode choice:
 Import — load into Power BI memory
 DirectQuery — query on demand

Authentication:
 Windows (current user / specific user)
 Database (SQL login)
 Microsoft account (Azure AD)
 Service principal (for automation)
 Key (for some Azure services)

Privacy level:
 Public, Organizational, Private
 Controls cross-source query folding

Web pages and APIs

Get Data → Web

Two modes:
 Basic — paste URL; Power BI scans page for HTML tables
 Advanced — URL parts, custom headers, request body

For REST APIs:
 Get Data → Web → Advanced
 - URL: https://api.example.com/v1/sales
 - HTTP headers:
 Authorization: Bearer xxxxx
 Accept: application/json

 Power BI parses JSON, exposes as records
 Use Power Query to expand nested structures

Authentication:
 Anonymous (public APIs)
 Basic (username/password)
 Web API (key in URL or header)
 Organizational (Azure AD)

For long-running ingest:
 Use a dataflow instead of a report
 Schedule the dataflow refresh
 Reports consume cleaned dataflow output

SharePoint / OneDrive sources

Excel/CSV in SharePoint:
 Get Data → SharePoint folder
 Enter site URL (not file URL)
 Navigate to file in browser

OneDrive for Business files:
 Right-click in OneDrive → Copy direct link
 Power BI: Get Data → Web → paste link
 - Refreshes automatically in Service (no gateway needed!)
 - Excellent for files updated regularly by humans

SharePoint Lists:
 Get Data → SharePoint Online list
 Loads list as a table
 Note: be cautious with large lists (10K+ items get slow)

Privacy levels

When Power BI combines data from MULTIPLE sources, it considers privacy:

Public:
 Information available to anyone (currency rates from a public API)
 Can be combined freely

Organizational:
 Internal company data
 Can be combined with other Organizational data

Private:
 Sensitive data (HR, salary, customer PII)
 Cannot be combined with other sources

Why this matters:
 Power BI uses query folding to push joins to the source
 If sources have incompatible privacy levels, folding stops
 Performance and security implications

Configure: File → Options and settings → Data source settings
Or: per-connection during the Get Data flow

Credential management

Power BI stores credentials per data source

In Desktop:
 File → Options and settings → Data source settings
 - Edit permissions (change auth method)
 - Clear permissions (force re-auth)
 - Edit privacy levels

In Service (after publishing):
 Workspace → Dataset → Settings → Data source credentials
 Re-enter credentials if dataset can't refresh

Service users may need to re-enter credentials when:
 - Password changes
 - Token expires
 - Account locked
 - Service principal rotated

Choosing the right connector — quick guide

NeedBest connector
Excel from local diskExcel workbook
Excel from OneDrive (live refresh)Web (with OneDrive direct link)
Multiple files of same shapeFolder
SQL Server / on-prem DBSQL Server database (gateway needed)
Azure SQL / SnowflakeNative cloud connector (no gateway)
REST APIWeb (Advanced)
SharePoint listSharePoint Online list
Salesforce / Dynamics 365Native CRM connector
Power BI dataset (shared model)Power BI datasets (Live)

Common Get Data mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Loading entire SQL tables when WHERE clause would do — pre-filter at source
  2. Skipping the Transform Data step — loads raw bad data into model
  3. Wrong encoding on CSV — UTF-8 mojibake (Ã©, â€™)
  4. Importing 50M rows when DirectQuery is needed — file size explodes
  5. Wrong privacy levels — query folding stops; slower performance
  6. Local file path with on-prem files — won't refresh in Service without gateway
  7. Hardcoded credentials in M code — never; use Manage Credentials
  8. Web connector against authenticated APIs without proper auth flow
  9. Loading all sheets in an Excel file when only one is needed
  10. Folder source with mixed schemas — combine fails or produces garbage
★ ON THE EXAM

"Get Data button?" → Home tab → Get Data → choose source type.

"Multiple CSVs same shape?" → Folder connector.

"Cloud Excel with auto-refresh?" → Web connector with OneDrive direct link.

"On-prem SQL?" → SQL Server database connector; gateway required.

"Connection modes?" → Import, DirectQuery, Live, Composite.

"REST API?" → Web (Advanced) with headers and JSON parsing.

"Encoding for non-English CSV?" → UTF-8 (65001).

"SharePoint list?" → SharePoint Online list connector.

"Privacy levels?" → Public, Organizational, Private — affects cross-source folding.

"Edit credentials in Desktop?" → File → Options → Data source settings.

"Edit credentials in Service?" → Dataset → Settings → Data source credentials.

"Use Excel TABLES, not sheets?" → Cleaner; explicit headers; resilient to row changes.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Get Data → choose source category and connector
  • Power BI has 200+ connectors covering files, databases, cloud, APIs, SaaS
  • Excel: prefer named tables (Ctrl+T) over raw sheets
  • CSV: choose correct encoding (UTF-8 most common) and delimiter
  • Folder connector combines many files with the same schema
  • SQL Server / on-prem databases require an On-Premises Data Gateway for refresh in Service
  • Cloud sources (Azure SQL, Snowflake, OneDrive for Business links) don't need a gateway
  • Web connector handles REST APIs (Advanced mode with headers)
  • Connection modes: Import (default; in memory), DirectQuery (live), Live (shared semantic model), Composite (mix)
  • Authentication options vary by source: Windows, database, Microsoft account, service principal, key, anonymous
  • Privacy levels (Public/Organizational/Private) affect cross-source query folding
  • Credentials managed in Desktop (Options → Data source settings) and Service (dataset settings)
  • Use SharePoint folder/list connectors for content stored in Microsoft 365
  • Pre-filter at source (custom SQL, query parameters) to avoid loading millions of unused rows
  • Click "Transform Data" instead of "Load" to clean before modeling

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power Query Editor (PQE) is where data cleaning lives in Power BI. Every transformation generates a step in M code, recorded in the Applied Steps pane. The PL-300 exam tests common transformations, the Applied Steps pane, and recognizing M syntax.

Opening Power Query Editor

Three ways:
 1. Home tab → Transform data
 2. From Get Data dialog → Transform Data button
 3. From an existing table → right-click → Edit query

PQE opens in a separate window with:
 - Queries pane (left): list of all queries / tables
 - Preview pane (center): top ~1000 rows
 - Query Settings pane (right):
 - Properties: query name, description
 - Applied Steps: list of transformations

Ribbon tabs:
 Home, Transform, Add Column, View, Tools, Help

Applied Steps — the transformation history

Every transformation adds a step to Applied Steps:
 Source
 Promoted Headers
 Changed Type
 Filtered Rows
 Renamed Columns
 ...

Click any step → preview shows table AT THAT POINT
Useful for debugging: where did this column disappear?

Right-click a step:
 Rename — give meaningful names (not "Renamed Columns1")
 Delete — remove step (cascades if downstream depends on it)
 Delete until end — delete this and all after
 Insert step after — manual M code
 View native query — see SQL that PQ generates (if folding)

Click "fx" in formula bar:
 Shows the M code for the current step
 Edit directly for fine control

Common transformations from the ribbon

Removing rows/columns

Home tab:
 Choose Columns / Remove Columns — keep / remove specific columns
 Keep Rows: Top N / Bottom N / Range / Duplicates / Errors
 Remove Rows: Top N / Bottom N / Alternate / Duplicates / Blank / Errors

Right-click column header for shortcuts:
 Remove
 Remove Other Columns (keep only this one)
 Duplicate Column

Filtering

Click filter arrow on column header:
 - Type-specific filters (Text Filters, Number Filters, Date Filters)
 - Search box for value selection
 - Top 1000 distinct values shown

Common filters:
 Text: Contains, Begins With, Equals
 Number: Equals, Greater Than, Less Than, Between
 Date: In the previous N days, This year, Custom range
 Null: equals null / not null

Filters create a "Filtered Rows" step
Visible in formula bar:
 = Table.SelectRows(#"Previous Step", each [Status] = "Active")

Splitting columns

Home → Split Column

By delimiter:
 - Choose delimiter (comma, semicolon, custom)
 - Split at: each occurrence / left-most / right-most
 - "FirstName LastName" → split by space → two columns

By number of characters:
 - Fixed width fields
 - Once / Repeatedly

By positions:
 - Specify column position numbers

By transition:
 - Lowercase to Uppercase (camelCase splitting)
 - Letter to Digit, Digit to Letter

Merging columns

Select multiple columns (Ctrl-click headers) → Transform → Merge Columns

Choose:
 - Separator (none, space, comma, tab, custom)
 - New column name

= Table.AddColumn(
 #"Previous Step",
 "Full Name",
 each [First] & " " & [Last]
 )

Example: combine [Street] + [City] + [State] into [Address]

Replacing values

Right-click cell → Replace Values
 Value to find / value to replace
 ☑ Match entire cell content
 ☑ Use special characters (\t, \r, \n)

Or in M:
 = Table.ReplaceValue(#"Source", "N/A", null, Replacer.ReplaceValue, {"Region"})

Common use cases:
 Replace "N/A" with null
 Replace inconsistent spellings ("NYC" → "New York City")
 Strip prefixes / suffixes

Data types

Click the type icon (e.g., ABC, 123) on column header → choose type:
 Text, Whole Number, Decimal Number, Date, Date/Time, Date/Time/Timezone,
 Duration, True/False, Binary, Any

Best practices:
 - Set types EXPLICITLY (don't trust auto-detection)
 - Use most specific type (Date if no time component → not DateTime)
 - Set types early — affects downstream transformations
 - Watch for errors after type change (Errors column appears if cells fail)

Locale considerations:
 Right-click → Change Type → Using Locale
 e.g., parse dates in dd/MM/yyyy format vs MM/dd/yyyy
 Critical for international data

Add Column tab

Custom Column — write M expression for a new column
 = if [Score] >= 80 then "Pass" else "Fail"

Conditional Column — GUI for if/then/else (multiple conditions)

Index Column — adds a sequential index (from 0 or 1)

Column from Examples — type a few examples; Power BI infers the pattern
 Excellent for parsing complex strings

Duplicate Column — copies an existing column

Standard / Statistics / Text / Date / Time / Duration columns:
 Standard: Add (sum), Multiply, Modulo, etc.
 Statistics: Average, Median, Standard Deviation
 Text: Trim, Clean, Length, Case, Prefix, Suffix
 Date: Year, Month, Day, Quarter, Day Name, Age
 Time: Hour, Minute, Second

Group By

Home → Group By (or Transform → Group By)

Basic:
 Group By: Region
 New column name: Total Sales
 Operation: Sum
 Column: Sales

Result: one row per Region with summed Sales

Advanced grouping:
 Multiple group columns
 Multiple aggregations (sum, count, average, max, min, all rows)
 "All Rows" — returns nested tables for each group

Use cases:
 - Aggregate transactions into customer summaries
 - Count distinct values per category
 - Build dimension tables from facts

Append vs Merge

OperationWhat it doesSQL equivalent
AppendStacks tables verticallyUNION ALL
MergeJoins tables horizontally by keyJOIN
 
Append Queries:
 Home → Append Queries → choose tables
 - Two tables: stack them
 - Three or more: append multiple

Columns matched by NAME (not position)
 - Same column names: data combined
 - Different column names: nulls appear

Merge Queries:
 Home → Merge Queries → choose right table
 Click matching column in each table (highlight key)
 Join type:
 Left outer (default; like SQL left join)
 Right outer
 Inner
 Full outer
 Left anti (rows in left NOT in right)
 Right anti (rows in right NOT in left)

After merge: new column appears with nested table
 Click expand arrow → choose which right-table columns to include

Pivot and Unpivot

Unpivot Columns (most common direction):
 Wide table → Long (tidy) table
 Select category columns → Transform → Unpivot Columns
 Result: each value becomes a row with Attribute, Value columns

 e.g.:
 Year Jan Feb Mar
 2024 100 200 150

 Unpivot Jan/Feb/Mar →
 Year Month Sales
 2024 Jan 100
 2024 Feb 200
 2024 Mar 150

Pivot Column:
 Long → Wide (rare; usually go the other direction)
 Select a column → Pivot Column → choose values column

Most analytics work needs LONG format
 - Easier to group and aggregate
 - Easier to filter
 - Plays better with date intelligence

Query references and parameters

Reference a query:
 Right-click → Reference
 New query starts from the output of the referenced one
 Changes upstream propagate downstream

Duplicate (different concept):
 Right-click → Duplicate
 Creates a fresh copy of all the steps
 Independent of the original

Parameters:
 Home → Manage Parameters → New Parameter
 - Define name, type, default value, allowed values
 - Use in source connection or in custom column expressions

Common uses:
 - Server name (so report can switch between Dev/Prod)
 - File path
 - Date range (start date, end date)
 - Region filter

Close & Apply

Home → Close & Apply
 Closes PQE
 Applies all queries to the model
 Loads / refreshes table data

Close & Apply uses two variants:
 Apply — apply changes (reload data)
 Close — close without applying (discard changes)

While PQE is open, no other Power BI work possible
Changes don't take effect until Apply

Worked example — common workflow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Clean a messy CSV
// Raw CSV:
// ID Name Email Phone Amount Date
// 1 ALICE smith alice@example.com (555) 123-4567 $1,234.50 01/15/2024
// 2 BOB JONES bob@EXAMPLE.com 555.987.6543 $2,500.00 02/20/2024
// 3 carol@example.com N/A not a date

// Workflow in Power Query Editor:

// 1. Load CSV
// 2. Promote first row to headers (if needed)
// 3. Remove empty rows (Home → Remove Rows → Remove Blank Rows)
// 4. Filter ID is not null (right-click ID column → Filter)
// 5. Replace "N/A" with null in Amount column
// 6. Clean Amount: remove "$" and "," then change type to Decimal
// Transform → Replace Values: "$" → ""; "," → ""
// Click type icon → Decimal Number
// 7. Title-case Name: select column → Transform → Format → Capitalize Each Word
// 8. Lowercase Email: Format → lowercase

// Add Column → Custom Column:
// Text.Remove([Phone], {"(", ")", " ", ".", "-"})
// 10. Date type: change with locale en-US (MM/dd/yyyy)
// Errors column will flag "not a date"
// Handle errors: Replace Errors → null (Transform → Replace Errors)
// 11. Set explicit data types on all columns
// 12. Rename columns to BI-friendly names (e.g., "Amount" → "Order Amount")
// 13. Close & Apply

// Applied Steps list:
// Source
// Promoted Headers
// Removed Blank Rows
// Filtered Rows (ID not null)
// Replaced N/A with null
// Replaced $
// Replaced ,
// Changed Type (Amount → Decimal)
// Capitalized Name
// Lowercased Email
// Added Phone Clean
// Changed Type Date (locale)
// Replaced Errors

Common PQE mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Not renaming Applied Steps — "Renamed Columns3" tells you nothing in a year
  2. Type changes before filtering — errors on filtered-out rows still count
  3. Reorder columns by drag instead of explicit step — fragile
  4. Missing the Refresh button while in PQE — preview goes stale
  5. Loading every column when only a few are needed — bloats model
  6. Confusing Reference and Duplicate — Reference shares upstream; Duplicate is independent
  7. Forgetting locale for international dates — DD/MM/YYYY parsed as MM/DD/YYYY
  8. Pivoting when unpivoting was intended — long-to-wide is rarely useful for analytics
  9. Skipping data type assignment — auto-detection misses edge cases
  10. Doing transformations in DAX that should be in Power Query — slower model
★ ON THE EXAM

"Open Power Query Editor?" → Home → Transform data.

"Each transformation creates?" → A step in Applied Steps list.

"M language used where?" → Inside Power Query Editor for transformations.

"Combine tables vertically?" → Append Queries.

"Combine tables horizontally?" → Merge Queries (specify join type).

"Six join types?" → Left outer, Right outer, Inner, Full outer, Left anti, Right anti.

"Wide to long?" → Unpivot Columns.

"Long to wide?" → Pivot Column.

"Parameter use case?" → Switch sources between Dev/Prod, configurable values.

"Reference vs Duplicate?" → Reference shares upstream changes; Duplicate is independent.

"Apply changes?" → Home → Close & Apply.

"View the M code?" → View → Advanced Editor.

"Change to locale-aware date?" → Right-click → Change Type → Using Locale.

"Aggregate before loading?" → Group By in PQE.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power Query Editor (PQE) is where data cleaning happens — opened from Home → Transform data
  • Every transformation adds a step to Applied Steps — rename for clarity
  • Click any step to see the table at that point — great for debugging
  • Common transformations: filter, sort, split, merge, replace, type, group by
  • Set explicit data types early — don't trust auto-detection
  • Use locale-aware date parsing for international data (Change Type → Using Locale)
  • Append Queries combines tables vertically (UNION ALL)
  • Merge Queries combines horizontally (JOIN) with six join types
  • Unpivot wide tables to long format — easier for analytics
  • Group By aggregates rows; supports multiple group columns and aggregations
  • Reference creates a query that depends on another; Duplicate is independent
  • Parameters let queries take inputs (e.g., server name, date range)
  • Close & Apply applies all queries to the model
  • Do transformations in Power Query, not DAX — better performance and clarity
  • Column from Examples auto-infers transformation logic from a few examples

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The data model determines what's possible in your reports. Get the model right and DAX measures are simple, performance is good, and users can self-serve. Get it wrong and you'll fight the tool forever. The PL-300 exam tests star schema, relationship cardinality, and direction.

The star schema — Power BI's preferred shape

STAR SCHEMA
ONE central fact table surrounded by dimension tables.

Fact table: numeric measurements (Sales, Orders, Events)
  Many rows; narrow columns
  Foreign keys to dimensions

Dimension tables: descriptive context (Customer, Product, Date, Region)
  Fewer rows; more columns
  Primary key referenced by fact

Relationships flow FROM dimension TO fact (one-to-many). 
Visualized in Model view:

 [Customer] [Product]
 \ /
 \ /
 [Sales fact table]
 / \
 / \
 [Date] [Region]

Why star schema:
 - Vertipaq engine optimized for it
 - DAX is simpler (filter context flows along clean paths)
 - Easier for users to understand
 - Easier to extend (add new dimensions without restructuring)

Snowflake schema (avoid in Power BI)

Snowflake = dimensions normalized into multiple tables

 [Country] ← [State] ← [City] ← [Customer] → [Sales]

vs star (denormalized):
 [Customer] (with Country, State, City as columns) → [Sales]

Snowflake problems for Power BI:
 - More relationships = more query work
 - Slicing on Country requires joining multiple tables
 - DAX measures become trickier
 - Performance degrades

Fix in Power Query:
 Merge child dimension into parent
 Flatten: Customer with Country, State, City columns
 Single Customer dimension joins to fact

Cardinality — the relationship type

CardinalityMeaningUse case
One-to-many (1:*)One row in dim → many in factStandard star schema relationship
Many-to-one (*:1)Same as above, reversed direction in diagramStandard star schema (alternate phrasing)
One-to-one (1:1)Each row matches exactly one rowSplitting dimension columns; rare
Many-to-many (*:*)Both sides have duplicates of the join keyUse bridge table; or M2M relationship type

Direction — single vs bidirectional

Single direction (recommended default):
 Filter flows ONE way: dim → fact
 [Customer] → [Sales]
 Filtering Customer to "Alice" filters Sales to Alice's rows
 Filtering Sales does NOT filter Customer

Bidirectional:
 Filter flows BOTH ways
 Useful when: many-to-many bridges, special filter propagation needs
 Risks:
 - Performance degradation
 - Ambiguous filter paths
 - Slower CALCULATE evaluations

Best practice:
 Single direction by default
 Bidirectional only when you have a specific need
 Document why each bidirectional exists

Creating relationships

Auto-detect:
 When loading data, Power BI tries to detect relationships from column names
 Often catches matching keys (customer_id <-> customer_id)

Manual creation:
 Model view → drag from one column to another
 Or: Home → Manage relationships → New

Properties:
 - From table / column
 - To table / column
 - Cardinality (typically auto-detected)
 - Direction (Single / Both)
 - Make this relationship active
 - Assume referential integrity (for DirectQuery; enables inner joins)
 - Apply security filter in both directions

Active vs inactive relationships:
 Only ONE active relationship between two tables at a time
 Inactive ones exist but don't auto-filter
 Activate inactive via USERELATIONSHIP() in DAX

Role-playing dimensions

When the same dimension is used multiple ways in a fact:
 Sales has Order_Date AND Ship_Date AND Due_Date
 All reference the Date dimension

Two approaches:

OPTION 1: Multiple inactive relationships + USERELATIONSHIP
 Create three relationships from Date to Sales (one per date field)
 Mark only one as active (e.g., Order_Date)
 Other two are inactive

 In measures:
 Sales by Order Date = SUM(Sales[Amount]) // uses active relationship
 Sales by Ship Date =
 CALCULATE(
 SUM(Sales[Amount]),
 USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[Ship_Date], Date[Date])
 )

OPTION 2: Multiple Date tables (renamed)
 Date_Order, Date_Ship, Date_Due — separate copies in model
 Each has its own active relationship
 Easier for users (no DAX trick needed)
 More memory used (three date tables)

Date tables — the foundation of time intelligence

Power BI needs a proper Date table for time intelligence functions

Best practices:
 - Contiguous dates from min to max in fact table (no gaps)
 - Marked as Date table: Modeling → Mark as date table → pick the date column
 - Disable Auto date/time: File → Options → Data Load → Auto date/time off
 (otherwise hidden tiny date tables explode model size)

Creating a Date table:

OPTION 1: CALENDAR() / CALENDARAUTO() in DAX
 Date = CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2030,12,31))
 Date = CALENDARAUTO() // auto-spans your data

 Then add columns:
 Year = YEAR([Date])
 Month = MONTH([Date])
 Quarter = "Q" & QUARTER([Date])
 MonthName = FORMAT([Date], "MMMM")
 WeekDay = WEEKDAY([Date])
 IsWeekend = WEEKDAY([Date], 2) > 5

OPTION 2: Power Query M
 Use List.Dates and Table.FromRecords
 Date = List.Dates(#date(2020,1,1), 365*10, #duration(1,0,0,0))

OPTION 3: Import from SQL / Excel
 Pre-built date table file (common in enterprise)

Set Sort by column:
 MonthName sorted by MonthNumber
 Otherwise alphabetical order shows April → August → December

Calculated columns vs measures

AspectCalculated ColumnMeasure
ComputedAt refresh (per row)At query time (per filter context)
StoredIn the modelNo (computed on demand)
MemoryUses RAM for every rowMinimal memory
Use forRow attribute (Category, Bucket)Aggregation (Total, Average)
ExampleBucket = IF([Sales] > 1000, "High", "Low")Total = SUM(Sales[Amount])

Preference: do row-level work in Power Query (more efficient) — reserve calculated columns for things that need DAX context.

Hiding fields from report view

In Model view or Fields pane:
 Right-click a column or table → Hide in report view

Reasons to hide:
 - Foreign key columns (don't drag those into visuals)
 - Internal helper columns
 - Surrogate keys

Hidden ≠ removed; still usable in DAX
Just doesn't clutter the Fields pane for end users

Common modeling mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Snowflake instead of star — denormalize for Power BI
  2. Bidirectional relationships everywhere — performance killer
  3. No proper Date table — time intelligence functions fail or auto-bloat
  4. Auto date/time enabled — hidden mini date tables per date column
  5. Calculated columns for things that should be measures
  6. Multiple active relationships between two tables — not allowed; only one active
  7. Foreign key columns visible in Fields pane — users drag them by mistake
  8. Many-to-many without bridge table — ambiguous filters
  9. Forgetting Sort by column on Month Name — alphabetical order in charts
  10. Inconsistent grain in fact table — mixing transaction and summary rows
★ ON THE EXAM

"Preferred schema for Power BI?" → Star schema.

"Fact table?" → Numeric measurements with foreign keys to dimensions.

"Dimension table?" → Descriptive attributes; primary key referenced by fact.

"Cardinality types?" → 1:1, 1:*, *:1, *:*.

"Direction default?" → Single (from dim to fact).

"When bidirectional?" → Many-to-many bridge tables; specific filter propagation needs.

"Same Date used multiple ways?" → Role-playing dim: inactive relationships + USERELATIONSHIP, or duplicate the dim.

"Mark as date table?" → Modeling → Mark as date table; required for time intelligence.

"Auto date/time?" → Disable; bloats model with hidden tables.

"Calculated column vs measure?" → Column = stored per row; measure = computed per query.

"Hide foreign keys?" → Right-click → Hide in report view.

"Month name alphabetical order?" → Set Sort by column = Month Number.

"CALENDARAUTO?" → Generates date table covering data's date range.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Star schema is the preferred shape: fact table in center, dimensions around
  • Denormalize snowflake dimensions into single tables for Power BI
  • Fact tables hold measurements; dimensions hold descriptive context
  • Cardinality: 1:1, 1:*, *:1, *:* — standard star uses 1:* / *:1
  • Use single-direction relationships by default; bidirectional only when needed
  • One active relationship between two tables at a time; others can exist as inactive
  • USERELATIONSHIP() activates inactive relationships in DAX for role-playing dimensions
  • Always include a proper Date table covering your fact's date range
  • Mark date tables explicitly: Modeling → Mark as date table
  • Disable Auto date/time to avoid hidden bloat
  • Calculated columns stored per row; measures computed at query time
  • Prefer measures for aggregations; only use calculated columns for row attributes
  • Do row-level transformations in Power Query, not calculated columns when possible
  • Hide foreign-key columns from report view
  • Use Sort by column for fields with non-alphabetical order (e.g., Month Name sorted by Month Number)

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language for measures, calculated columns, and calculated tables in Power BI. Every non-trivial report has DAX. The PL-300 exam tests basic functions, filter context, CALCULATE, and time intelligence.

DAX vs M — which language for what

DAXM (Power Query)
Aggregations, measures, calculated columns / tablesData shaping at load time
Evaluated at query timeEvaluated at refresh time
Used inside the data modelUsed inside Power Query Editor
Excel-like syntaxFunctional, more like SQL/JavaScript

Creating measures

Three ways:
 1. Right-click table in Fields pane → New measure
 2. Home tab → New measure
 3. In formula bar after selecting a measure: type expression

Syntax:
 Measure Name = expression

Example:
 Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

DAX is case-insensitive for keywords but case-sensitive for table/column references.
Always use quoted column reference format: TableName[ColumnName]
For measures: just use the measure name (no table prefix needed, but allowed)

Basic aggregations

SUM(column) — total
AVERAGE(column) — mean
MIN(column) — minimum
MAX(column) — maximum
COUNT(column) — count of non-blank rows
COUNTA(column) — count including text values
COUNTROWS(table) — count of rows in a table
DISTINCTCOUNT(column) — count of distinct values

X-versions (iterators, see below):
SUMX(table, expression)
AVERAGEX(table, expression)
MAXX, MINX, COUNTX, etc.

Examples:
 Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
 Average Order = AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])
 Customer Count = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
 Order Count = COUNTROWS(Sales)

Iterators — the X functions

SUMX iterates row by row and sums results
 SUMX(table, expression)

When to use:
 - Expression involves multiple columns
 - Need per-row calculation before aggregating

Example:
 Sales[Amount] * Sales[Quantity] doesn't exist as a column
 but SUMX(Sales, Sales[Amount] * Sales[Quantity]) computes per-row and sums

Common iterators:
 SUMX — sum of per-row expression
 AVERAGEX — average of per-row expression
 MAXX — max
 MINX — min
 COUNTX — count
 RANKX — rank
 CONCATENATEX — string concat across rows

Performance:
 Iterators can be slow — every row evaluated
 Use scalar aggregations when possible

CALCULATE — the core DAX function

CALCULATE
Modify filter context, then evaluate an expression.

CALCULATE(expression, filter1, filter2, ...)

Each filter ARGUMENT replaces or augments the current filter context.
This is the foundation of advanced DAX. 
Example 1: explicit filter
 Sales East = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Region] = "East")
 Returns total sales filtered to East, regardless of slicer context

Example 2: remove filter
 All Region Sales =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], REMOVEFILTERS(Sales[Region]))
 Ignore any Region filter; show grand total

Example 3: change filter direction
 Prev Year Sales =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))

Example 4: multiple filters
 Active Customers = CALCULATE(
 DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID]),
 Sales[Status] = "Active",
 Sales[Year] = 2024
 )

The most important DAX function — master CALCULATE first.

Filter context vs row context

FILTER CONTEXT
 Set by visuals, slicers, filters
 Affects which rows are visible to an aggregation
 Measures evaluated in current filter context

ROW CONTEXT
 Set when iterating rows (calculated columns, X functions)
 Refers to "the current row"
 Calculated columns are evaluated in row context by default

Example:
 Calculated column on Sales table:
 Margin = Sales[Revenue] - Sales[Cost]
 Each row's margin uses ITS revenue and cost (row context)

Measure:
 Total Margin = SUM(Sales[Margin])
 Or:
 Total Margin = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Revenue] - Sales[Cost])
 Evaluated under filter context

Common DAX functions by category

LOGICAL
 IF(condition, true_value, false_value)
 SWITCH(expression, value1, result1, ..., default)
 AND(a, b), OR(a, b), NOT(a)
 IFERROR(value, fallback)

TEXT
 CONCATENATE(s1, s2) or s1 & s2
 LEFT(s, n), RIGHT(s, n), MID(s, start, n)
 UPPER(s), LOWER(s), PROPER(s)
 LEN(s), TRIM(s)
 FORMAT(value, "format_string")

DATE
 TODAY(), NOW()
 YEAR(d), MONTH(d), DAY(d)
 WEEKDAY(d), WEEKNUM(d)
 EOMONTH(d, months_offset)
 DATEDIFF(start, end, unit)

FILTER / TABLE
 FILTER(table, condition) returns filtered table
 ALL(table) remove all filters from table
 ALLEXCEPT(table, col) remove filters except specified
 KEEPFILTERS(filter) preserve existing filters when adding new
 RELATED(table[col]) lookup related column (one-to-many)

INFO / METADATA
 ISBLANK(value), ISERROR(value)
 HASONEVALUE(column)
 SELECTEDVALUE(column) gets the value when filtered to one

Time intelligence functions

All require a marked Date table

Year-over-year:
 Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))
 Sales YoY = [Total Sales] - [Sales LY]
 Sales YoY % = DIVIDE([Sales YoY], [Sales LY])

Year-to-date:
 Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], Date[Date])
 Sales QTD = TOTALQTD([Total Sales], Date[Date])
 Sales MTD = TOTALMTD([Total Sales], Date[Date])

Period offsets:
 PREVIOUSYEAR(Date[Date])
 PREVIOUSQUARTER, PREVIOUSMONTH, PREVIOUSDAY
 NEXTYEAR, NEXTQUARTER, etc.

Custom ranges:
 DATESBETWEEN(Date[Date], start, end)
 DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], end_date, n, MONTH) // last N months

Comparison patterns:
 Sales YoY Growth =
 VAR Current = [Total Sales]
 VAR LastYear = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))
 RETURN DIVIDE(Current - LastYear, LastYear)

Variables — VAR / RETURN

Use VAR to break complex measures into steps

Without variables:
 Profit Margin =
 DIVIDE(
 SUM(Sales[Amount]) - SUM(Sales[Cost]),
 SUM(Sales[Amount])
 )

With variables:
 Profit Margin =
 VAR Revenue = SUM(Sales[Amount])
 VAR Cost = SUM(Sales[Cost])
 VAR Profit = Revenue - Cost
 RETURN DIVIDE(Profit, Revenue)

Benefits:
 - Readable
 - Variables computed ONCE (performance)
 - Easier debugging (each var holds an intermediate result)
 - Self-documenting

Always use VAR / RETURN for multi-step measures.

DIVIDE — safer than /

DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, [alternate_result])

Pros over /:
 - Handles division by zero (returns alternate or BLANK)
 - More performant in some cases

Examples:
 Bad: Margin Pct = ([Sales] - [Cost]) / [Sales]
 // Errors out if Sales is 0

 Good: Margin Pct = DIVIDE([Sales] - [Cost], [Sales])
 // Returns BLANK if Sales is 0

 Good: Conversion Rate = DIVIDE([Conversions], [Visitors], 0)
 // Returns 0 if Visitors is 0

Always prefer DIVIDE over /.

Common DAX patterns

Running total:
 Running Total =
 CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 FILTER(ALL(Date), Date[Date] <= MAX(Date[Date]))
 )

Top N filter in a measure:
 Sales Top 10 Products =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales],
 TOPN(10, ALL(Product), [Total Sales])
 )

Percentage of total:
 Pct of Total =
 DIVIDE([Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales))
 )

Conditional aggregation:
 Big Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Amount] > 1000)

Ratio measures:
 Avg Order Size = DIVIDE([Total Sales], DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[OrderID]))

Worked example — sales dashboard measures

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build foundational measures
// === Foundational ===
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
Order Count = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[OrderID])
Customer Count = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])

// === Averages ===
Average Order Value = DIVIDE([Total Sales], [Order Count])
Sales per Customer = DIVIDE([Total Sales], [Customer Count])

// === Time intelligence ===
Sales Last Year =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))

Sales YoY = [Total Sales] - [Sales Last Year]

Sales YoY % =
 DIVIDE([Sales YoY], [Sales Last Year])

Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], Date[Date])

// === Conditional ===
High-Value Sales =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Amount] > 1000)

Active Sales =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Status] = "Active")

// === Variables example ===
Profit Margin =
 VAR Revenue = [Total Sales]
 VAR Cost = SUM(Sales[Cost])
 VAR Profit = Revenue - Cost
 RETURN DIVIDE(Profit, Revenue)

// === Top N pattern ===
Sales Top 5 Customers =
 CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 TOPN(5, ALL(Customer), [Total Sales], DESC)
 )

Common DAX mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Using / instead of DIVIDE — division-by-zero errors
  2. SUM in measure when SUMX needed — multi-column products break
  3. Forgetting to mark Date table — time intelligence fails
  4. Hardcoded year filters — measures break next year
  5. RELATED in measures — only works in row context (calculated columns); use LOOKUPVALUE in measures
  6. Calculated columns where measures fit — bloats model
  7. FILTER inside CALCULATE for column filters — slow; use simple Filter[col] = value syntax
  8. Not using VAR for repeated subexpressions — computed multiple times
  9. ALLSELECTED vs ALL confusion — different scope of filter removal
  10. Bidirectional filtering hacks instead of explicit DAX — performance issues
★ ON THE EXAM

"Aggregation function for sum?" → SUM.

"Sum of per-row product?" → SUMX(table, [col1] * [col2]).

"Most important DAX function?" → CALCULATE.

"Change filter context?" → CALCULATE with filter arguments.

"Remove a filter?" → REMOVEFILTERS(column) inside CALCULATE.

"Year over year?" → SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]).

"YTD?" → TOTALYTD(measure, Date[Date]).

"Safe division?" → DIVIDE(num, den, alt).

"Lookup in related table?" → RELATED in row context; LOOKUPVALUE in measure.

"VAR / RETURN purpose?" → Break complex measures into named steps; computed once.

"Filter context?" → What rows are visible to aggregation; set by visuals/slicers.

"Row context?" → Refers to current row; set in iterators / calc columns.

"SELECTEDVALUE?" → Returns value when filter narrows to one; useful for dynamic labels.

"DAX language?" → Data Analysis Expressions.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • DAX is the formula language for measures, calculated columns, and calculated tables
  • Measures: aggregations computed at query time; minimal memory
  • Calculated columns: stored per row; row context
  • Aggregation functions: SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN, MAX, DISTINCTCOUNT
  • X-iterators (SUMX, AVERAGEX) compute per-row expressions before aggregating
  • CALCULATE is the most important function — modifies filter context, then evaluates
  • Filter context: what rows are visible (from slicers, filters, visuals)
  • Row context: refers to current row (in iterators and calculated columns)
  • Use DIVIDE instead of / to safely handle division by zero
  • RELATED works in row context; LOOKUPVALUE works in measures
  • Time intelligence requires a marked Date table
  • Key time functions: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, TOTALYTD, PREVIOUSMONTH, DATEADD
  • Variables (VAR / RETURN) make complex measures readable and performant
  • REMOVEFILTERS removes filters from columns or tables
  • Prefer measures over calculated columns when possible (smaller, more flexible)

Two Power Query facts: Close & Apply saves your transformations and LOADS the data into the Power BI model. And query folding pushes transformations BACK to the source database — the server does the heavy work, not your laptop; folding breaks when steps can’t translate to SQL. In short: Close & Apply applies your steps and loads the model; folding delegates work upstream — each transformation step the editor records gets pushed to the source database whenever it can translate. Close & Apply neither cancels nor discards your work, and it does more than refreshes — it saves the changes and loads the data.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The difference between basic and advanced DAX is mastery of filter context — how CALCULATE, ALL, ALLSELECTED, KEEPFILTERS, and FILTER interact. These functions unlock complex business logic. The PL-300 exam tests recognizing the right combination for advanced patterns.

Filter context — the foundation

FILTER CONTEXT
Every measure evaluates in some filter context — the set of column filter values currently active.

Sources of filter context:
  1. Slicers on the page
  2. Filters pane (visual / page / report level)
  3. Visual's own field wells (each row of a matrix has implicit filter)
  4. CALCULATE arguments within the measure itself
  5. Other relationships automatically propagated through model

ALL — remove all filters from a table or column

ALL(table_or_column)

Use cases:
 Pct of total:
 Pct of Total =
 DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales))
 )
 Denominator = grand total, regardless of current filter

 Ignore a specific filter:
 Sales Ignoring Region =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(Sales[Region]))
 Even if a Region slicer is active, this measure ignores it

ALL on a table: removes filters from all columns of the table
ALL on a column: removes filters from just that column
ALL on multiple columns: ALL(Table[Col1], Table[Col2], ...)

ALLEXCEPT — keep specified filters, remove the rest

ALLEXCEPT(table, col1, col2, ...)

Use case: % of category total
 Pct of Region Total =
 DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(Sales, Sales[Region]))
 )

 Numerator: sales for current Product + Region (e.g., Widget in East)
 Denominator: total sales for the region (all products in East)
 Ratio: each product's share within its region

ALLEXCEPT keeps the specified column filters; removes everything else
Powerful for nested aggregations

ALLSELECTED — respect user filters, ignore visual-local filters

ALLSELECTED removes filters added by the visual but keeps external filters
 (page-level, slicers, report filters)

Use case: row % within a slicer's selection
 Pct of Visible Total =
 DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLSELECTED(Sales))
 )

 If a slicer selects "Q3 2024 only", the denominator is Q3 2024 total
 Each row's % adds up to 100% within the visible (slicer-filtered) data

Compared to ALL:
 ALL → grand total ignoring all filters
 ALLSELECTED → total of what's currently selected via filters

Most "% of total in this view" patterns use ALLSELECTED, not ALL.

FILTER — generate a filtered table

FILTER(table, condition)

Returns: a filtered version of the table for use in another DAX expression

Examples:
 FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 1000)

Used inside CALCULATE:
 Big Sales =
 CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 FILTER(Sales, Sales[Amount] > 1000)
 )
 But for simple column filters, prefer direct syntax:
 Big Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Amount] > 1000)

When FILTER is necessary:
 - Condition references a MEASURE (not just a column value)
 - Condition involves multiple columns or complex logic

 Top Earners =
 CALCULATE(
 [Customer Count],
 FILTER(Customer, [Customer Lifetime Value] > 10000)
 )

KEEPFILTERS — preserve existing filters when adding new ones

By default, CALCULATE replaces filters on a column
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Region] = "East")
 → Forces Region to East, overriding any existing Region filter

KEEPFILTERS intersects with existing filters:
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], KEEPFILTERS(Sales[Region] = "East"))
 → If existing filter is "East or West", result narrows to "East"
 → If existing filter is "West", result is empty (intersection of "East" and "West")

Common scenario:
 Sales by Region visualization filtered to North America
 Slicer selects countries
 CALCULATE([Sales] , Sales[Year] = 2024) → ignores region filter (replaces)
 CALCULATE([Sales] , KEEPFILTERS(Sales[Year] = 2024)) → respects existing region filter

KEEPFILTERS is subtle but important for nuanced measures.

USERELATIONSHIP — activate an inactive relationship

For role-playing dimensions: same Date dim used for multiple date columns

Sales has Order_Date (active) and Ship_Date (inactive)

Default measure uses active relationship:
 Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount]) // sliced by Order_Date

Switch to inactive relationship for this measure:
 Sales by Ship Date =
 CALCULATE(
 SUM(Sales[Amount]),
 USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[Ship_Date], Date[Date])
 )
 Now sliced by Ship_Date instead of Order_Date

Only inside CALCULATE; deactivates for this query only
Lets one Date dim handle Order/Ship/Due dates without duplicating

RELATED vs LOOKUPVALUE vs RELATEDTABLE

FunctionWhen to useReturns
RELATEDIn row context (calculated columns); follow many-to-oneScalar from related dim
RELATEDTABLEIn row context; follow one-to-manyFiltered table of related rows
LOOKUPVALUEIn any context; no relationship neededScalar from lookup
 
RELATED example (calculated column in Sales):
 Customer City = RELATED(Customer[City])

RELATEDTABLE example (calculated column in Customer):
 Order Count = COUNTROWS(RELATEDTABLE(Sales))

LOOKUPVALUE example (measure or column, no relationship needed):
 USD Rate =
 LOOKUPVALUE(
 ExchangeRate[USD_Rate],
 ExchangeRate[Date], MAX(Sales[Date]),
 ExchangeRate[Currency], MAX(Sales[Currency])
 )

SELECTEDVALUE — when a column is filtered to one

SELECTEDVALUE(column, [alternate_result])

Returns the single value if exactly one is in filter context, else alternate

Use cases:
 Dynamic title:
 Selected Region Title =
 "Sales for " & SELECTEDVALUE(Region[Name], "All Regions")

 Conditional behavior:
 Bonus Pct =
 VAR Region = SELECTEDVALUE(Region[Name])
 RETURN
 SWITCH(
 Region,
 "East", 0.10,
 "West", 0.08,
 "North", 0.06,
 0.05 // default
 )

 Hide totals row:
 Sales No Total =
 IF(HASONEVALUE(Sales[Region]), [Total Sales], BLANK())
 Returns blank for the grand total row in matrix

CALCULATE filter modifiers

ModifierEffect
ALL(col)Remove filter from column
ALLEXCEPT(table, col)Remove all filters except specified column(s)
ALLSELECTED(...)Remove visual filter; keep external
REMOVEFILTERS(col)Same as ALL but used inside CALCULATE
KEEPFILTERS(filter)Intersect with existing filter (don't replace)
USERELATIONSHIP(a, b)Activate alternate relationship

Worked example — top N within category

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Top 5 products per region
// Goal: in a matrix of Region × Product, show only top 5 products per region
// (Other product rows show blank for that region)

Top 5 Sales Within Region =
 VAR CurrentProductSales = [Total Sales]
 VAR RegionSales =
 CALCULATETABLE(
 ADDCOLUMNS(
 VALUES(Product[Product]),
 "@Sales", [Total Sales]
 ),
 ALLEXCEPT(Sales, Sales[Region])
 )
 VAR Top5Threshold =
 MINX(
 TOPN(5, RegionSales, [@Sales], DESC),
 [@Sales]
 )
 RETURN
 IF(CurrentProductSales >= Top5Threshold, CurrentProductSales)

// What it does:
// 1. Get current cell's product sales
// 2. Compute sales for ALL products in current region (ALLEXCEPT)
// 3. Find threshold = 5th-highest sales in region
// 4. Show value only if current >= threshold; else blank

// Result: matrix shows top 5 products per region; others blank
// User sees the most important products without clutter

DAX Studio — external tool for performance

DAX Studio (free Microsoft tool) is essential for advanced DAX

Capabilities:
 - Execute DAX queries against your model
 - Run server timings to measure performance
 - Inspect storage engine vs formula engine time
 - Format DAX automatically
 - Query plan analysis
 - Capture DAX queries from a running report

Install: DAX Studio website
Connect via External Tools tab in Power BI Desktop
Or copy DAX from Performance Analyzer for tuning

For PL-300, just know it exists and what it does
For real-world performance tuning, it's indispensable

Common advanced DAX mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Confusing ALL with ALLSELECTED — different scope of filter removal
  2. Using FILTER for simple column comparisons — slow; use direct CALCULATE syntax
  3. Forgetting KEEPFILTERS when adding to existing filters
  4. Using RELATED in a measure — only works in row context
  5. Iterating tables when scalar aggregation suffices — SUMX where SUM works
  6. Not understanding context transition — CALCULATE in a row context creates filter context
  7. Hardcoded column counts in SELECTEDVALUE — what if filter shows zero?
  8. Forgetting alternate_result in SELECTEDVALUE — blank when not single value
  9. Time intelligence without marked Date table
  10. Using EVALUATE for everything — that's a DAX Studio query, not a measure
★ ON THE EXAM

"Remove filter from column?" → ALL or REMOVEFILTERS.

"% of grand total?" → CALCULATE([measure], ALL(Table)).

"% of slicer-visible total?" → CALCULATE([measure], ALLSELECTED(Table)).

"% within category?" → CALCULATE([measure], ALLEXCEPT(Table, Category)).

"Intersect new filter with existing?" → KEEPFILTERS(condition).

"Activate inactive relationship?" → USERELATIONSHIP() inside CALCULATE.

"Lookup without relationship?" → LOOKUPVALUE.

"Lookup with relationship (row context)?" → RELATED.

"Get child rows of current row?" → RELATEDTABLE.

"Filter condition uses a measure?" → FILTER(table, [measure] > value).

"One value or alternate?" → SELECTEDVALUE(column, alternate).

"Total row hidden in matrix?" → IF(HASONEVALUE(col), [measure], BLANK()).

"Top N rank?" → RANKX or TOPN.

"Performance tool?" → DAX Studio.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Filter context is the set of currently active filters — drives measure evaluation
  • CALCULATE modifies filter context; each filter argument adjusts it
  • ALL removes filters from a column or table; for grand totals
  • ALLEXCEPT removes all filters EXCEPT specified columns; for category totals
  • ALLSELECTED removes visual-local filters but keeps external (slicer / page); for "% within view"
  • REMOVEFILTERS is equivalent to ALL when used as a CALCULATE modifier
  • KEEPFILTERS intersects with existing filters instead of replacing
  • USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship temporarily
  • RELATED follows many-to-one in row context (calculated columns)
  • RELATEDTABLE follows one-to-many; returns a filtered table
  • LOOKUPVALUE works without a relationship and in any context
  • SELECTEDVALUE returns the single filter value or an alternate when not exactly one
  • HASONEVALUE tests whether a column is filtered to exactly one value
  • FILTER is needed when condition uses a measure; otherwise use direct CALCULATE filter syntax
  • DAX Studio is the go-to tool for performance tuning and query analysis

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Relationships determine how filters flow through the model and what aggregations make sense. The PL-300 exam tests cardinality choice, direction, ambiguity resolution, and many-to-many patterns.

Creating and managing relationships

Three ways to manage:

Model view:
 Drag from column to column visually
 Double-click line → Edit dialog
 Delete by selecting line + Delete key

Manage relationships dialog:
 Home → Manage relationships
 Tabular list of all relationships
 Create / Edit / Delete / Auto-detect

Right-click in Fields pane:
 Right-click a column → Create relationship → choose target

Relationship dialog fields:
 - From table / column
 - To table / column
 - Cardinality
 - Direction (Single / Both)
 - ☑ Make this relationship active
 - ☑ Assume referential integrity (DirectQuery)
 - ☑ Apply security filter in both directions (RLS interaction)

The "1" side and the "Many" side

In a 1:many relationship:
 The "1" side has unique values in the join column
 Customer[CustomerID]: each row is unique
 The "many" side can repeat the join column
 Sales[CustomerID]: each customer appears in many sales

Power BI auto-detects which side is which based on unique-ness
 If both sides are unique → 1:1
 If both have duplicates → flagged as Many-to-Many

You can override the auto-detection in Edit relationship dialog
 But misclassifying causes incorrect aggregations

Filter propagation

Filter flows from 1 to Many by default:
 [Customer] (1) → [Sales] (many)
 Filter Customer → Sales rows narrow accordingly

In a STAR schema:
 Each dimension filters fact independently
 Date filter → fact filtered
 Product filter → fact filtered
 Both filters combine (AND) on fact

This is why star schema is ideal: filters from many dimensions converge cleanly on one fact

Snowflake forces chained propagation:
 Country → State → Customer → Sales
 Filter Country → reaches Sales through 3 hops; slower

Active vs inactive relationships

Only ONE active relationship between any two tables at a time

Why: avoids ambiguity. If Date is connected to Sales through both Order Date
 AND Ship Date, Power BI needs to know which one to use by default.

Visual representation:
 Active relationship: solid line
 Inactive relationship: dotted line

Switch the active one via USERELATIONSHIP in DAX (covered in ch2/s3)

Creating inactive relationships:
 Edit relationship → uncheck "Make this relationship active"
 Or: in Manage relationships dialog, uncheck Active checkbox

Use cases:
 - Role-playing dimensions (same Date dim for multiple date columns)
 - Snowflake hops you DON'T want active

Cardinality types in depth

One-to-many (typical)

[Customer] (1) ───→ [Sales] (*)

Customer.CustomerID is unique in Customer
Customer.CustomerID can repeat in Sales

This is the standard star schema relationship
Filter flows: Customer → Sales

One-to-one

[Customer] (1) ───→ (1) [Customer_Details]

Both sides unique on the join column
Effectively splits one logical table into two physical ones

When this happens:
 - Splitting a wide table for partial loading
 - Privacy boundary (sensitive columns in separate table with RLS)
 - Different refresh schedules

Filter flows both directions automatically (since both are 1)

Avoid unless there's a clear reason — usually merge instead

Many-to-many — the tricky one

[Customer] (*) ←→ (*) [Account]

Both sides have duplicates on the join column
Power BI supports m:m relationships directly (introduced in 2018)
 No bridge table required (but still common)

Use cases:
 - Customers and Accounts (one customer can have many accounts; one account can have many owners)
 - Students and Classes (many-to-many via enrollment)
 - Products and Suppliers

Direct M:M caveats:
 - Bidirectional filter by default
 - Filter propagation can be ambiguous
 - Performance degrades with large tables
 - Hard to add measures correctly

Bridge table pattern (often safer):

 [Customer] (1) → [Customer_Account_Bridge] ← (1) [Account]
 
 Bridge has unique CustomerID + AccountID pairs
 Two 1:many relationships through bridge
 Cleaner filter logic

Bidirectional filtering — when and why

Single direction (default):
 Customer (1) → Sales (*)
 Filter on Customer filters Sales
 Filter on Sales does NOT filter Customer

Bidirectional:
 Customer (1) ↔ Sales (*)
 Filter flows BOTH directions
 Filter on Sales now also filters Customer

When to use bidirectional:
 - Many-to-many via bridge tables (propagate filter through bridge)
 - Show "customers who bought something" not "all customers" in slicer
 - Specific measure logic requiring upward filter flow

When NOT to use:
 - Default star schema (single direction works fine)
 - Many tables (creates ambiguous paths)
 - Performance-critical reports

Risks:
 - Ambiguity: Power BI can't auto-determine which path to use
 - Performance: extra filter evaluation
 - Counterintuitive measures: filtering Customer might exclude some, surprising users

Best practice: single direction by default; bidirectional only when explicitly needed.

Ambiguous filter paths

When multiple paths exist between two tables, Power BI must pick one

Example:
 [Date] → [Sales] (active)
 [Date] → [Customer] → [Sales] (inactive, via Customer.SignupDate)

If both were active, ambiguity arises:
 Filter Date → Sales directly?
 Or Date → Customer → Sales?

Power BI's solution:
 Only one active relationship at a time
 Inactive ones present but don't auto-propagate

If you need both paths:
 - Activate via USERELATIONSHIP per measure
 - Or duplicate the dimension table (one for each role)

The error "ambiguous filter path" usually means:
 You've enabled bidirectional on a relationship that creates two active paths
 Fix by setting one back to single direction

Referential integrity assumption (DirectQuery)

In DirectQuery: ☑ "Assume referential integrity" option

What it does:
 Tells Power BI: every foreign key in fact MUST exist in dimension
 Enables Power BI to use INNER joins instead of LEFT OUTER

Why:
 INNER joins are faster than OUTER joins
 Most enterprise data warehouses do enforce RI

When to use:
 - Source DB has explicit foreign key constraints
 - You're sure every fact row has matching dimension row

When NOT to use:
 - Data quality is poor (orphan fact rows exist)
 - Will cause rows to silently disappear from results

Verify before enabling:
 In source DB, run COUNT and JOIN tests to confirm 100% match rate

Common relationship mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Many-to-many that should be one-to-many — extra duplicates in "1" side; check uniqueness
  2. Bidirectional everywhere — slow, ambiguous, hard to debug
  3. Multiple active relationships between two tables — Power BI prevents this; rethink design
  4. Forgetting to mark inactive relationships as inactive — Power BI auto-picks one to deactivate
  5. Snowflake when star would work — denormalize for Power BI
  6. No relationship where one should exist — manual lookups via DAX are slow and brittle
  7. Wrong cardinality direction in setup dialog — Power BI usually auto-detects but verify
  8. Enabling referential integrity assumption on dirty data — rows disappear silently
  9. Inactive relationship used in default DAX — silently uses the active one; results wrong
  10. Bridge tables without proper unique combinations — m:m relationships break
★ ON THE EXAM

"Active relationship?" → Solid line; default filter propagation.

"Inactive relationship?" → Dotted line; activate via USERELATIONSHIP.

"Default direction?" → Single (filter flows from 1 side to many side).

"When bidirectional?" → Many-to-many bridge tables; specific filter propagation needs.

"Many-to-many direct support?" → Yes (since 2018); but bridge table often safer.

"Multiple paths between tables?" → Only one path can be active; others inactive.

"Date dim with multiple date columns?" → Role-playing dim: inactive relationships + USERELATIONSHIP, or duplicate the dim.

"Referential integrity assumption?" → DirectQuery; enables inner join; only if data is clean.

"Cardinality 1:1?" → Both sides unique; usually merge tables instead.

"Bridge table?" → Junction table with unique pairs; converts M:M to two 1:M.

"Filter direction in M:M?" → Bidirectional by default; needed to propagate through bridge.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Manage relationships via Model view, Manage relationships dialog, or right-click in Fields pane
  • The "1" side has unique values in the join column; the "many" side has duplicates
  • Standard star schema relationship: 1:* with single direction (dim → fact)
  • Only one ACTIVE relationship between two tables at a time
  • Inactive relationships exist but don't auto-propagate; activate via USERELATIONSHIP in DAX
  • Bidirectional filtering propagates filters both ways — use sparingly
  • Many-to-many supported directly in Power BI; bridge tables often safer
  • Bridge table pattern: two 1:many relationships through a junction with unique pairs
  • Ambiguous filter paths occur when multiple active routes exist between tables
  • Referential integrity assumption (DirectQuery): enables faster INNER joins; only with clean data
  • One-to-one relationships rare; usually merge the tables instead
  • Avoid snowflake schemas; denormalize for better Power BI performance
  • For role-playing dimensions: inactive relationships + USERELATIONSHIP, or duplicate the dim
  • Verify cardinality auto-detection — sometimes it's wrong
  • Single-direction relationships are the default; only override with clear reason

Data modeling is 30-35% of the PL-300 exam — the single largest topic. The star schema is the foundation: get this right and DAX, performance, and visuals all become straightforward. Get it wrong and everything else fights you. Microsoft expects you to recognize star vs snowflake, identify fact/dimension tables, and know when to flatten or normalize.

The star schema

STAR SCHEMA DEFINITION
A data model with ONE central fact table (numerical, transactional data) surrounded by multiple dimension tables (descriptive attributes).

Looks like a star when drawn — fact in the middle, dimensions radiating outward.

Why Microsoft loves it: optimized for the VertiPaq engine that powers Power BI. Star schemas are FAST to query because relationships are simple (one fact → many dimensions, no chains). 
 DimDate
 |
DimProduct ─── FactSales ─── DimCustomer
 |
 DimStore

FactSales (the FACT table):
 OrderID | DateKey | ProductKey | CustomerKey | StoreKey | Quantity | Revenue
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 1001 | 20250115 | P-42 | C-301 | S-7 | 2 | $99.98

DimProduct (a DIMENSION table):
 ProductKey | ProductName | Category | SubCategory | UnitPrice
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 P-42 | Wireless Mouse | Electronics | Accessories | $49.99

Fact vs dimension tables

AspectFact tableDimension table
ContainsMeasurements, metrics, transactionsDescriptive attributes (who, what, when, where)
RowsMillions / billions (large)Hundreds / thousands (small)
KeysMany foreign keys (one per dimension)One primary key (the surrogate)
ColumnsFew, mostly numbersMany, mix of text + numbers
ExamplesSales, Orders, Visits, CallsCustomer, Product, Date, Geography, Employee
Use in visualsValues (Sum/Count/Avg)Axes, slicers, filters, legends
★ MEMORY TRICK — F vs D

Fact = facts about what happened: Sales of $500, an order of 3 units, a transaction at 9:47am. Numbers + events.

Dimension = describes context: which customer bought (Alice), what product (Mouse), when (Jan 15). Words + lookups.

If you put it on the Y-axis of a chart, it's usually a fact. If it's a slicer or X-axis category, it's usually a dimension.

Star vs snowflake

STAR SCHEMA (flat dimensions — PREFERRED for Power BI):

 DimDate
 |
 FactSales ──── DimProduct
 | (Category, SubCategory in one table)
 DimCustomer

SNOWFLAKE SCHEMA (normalized — AVOID in Power BI):

 DimDate
 |
 DimSubCategory ── DimProduct ──── FactSales ──── DimCustomer
 | |
 DimCategory DimCountry
 |
 DimRegion

The snowflake has MORE tables and MORE relationships — slower and harder to use.
PL-300 EXAM RULE
When the exam asks "what is the best model for Power BI?" the answer is almost always star schema.

When given a snowflake model with multiple linked dimensions, the recommended action is usually to merge those tables into a single flat dimension using Power Query.

Surrogate keys vs natural keys

// NATURAL KEY — meaningful business identifier
DimProduct:
 ProductCode: "MICE-2024-WIR-001" ← natural key (from the business)
 ProductName: "Wireless Mouse"
 Category: "Electronics"

// SURROGATE KEY — meaningless integer added by the data warehouse
DimProduct:
 ProductKey: 42 ← surrogate key (just a number)
 ProductCode: "MICE-2024-WIR-001" ← keep the natural key too
 ProductName: "Wireless Mouse"
★ WHY SURROGATE KEYS

Performance: integers are MUCH faster to join than strings (the VertiPaq engine compresses integers brilliantly).

Stability: if the business renames a product code, the surrogate key doesn't change — your historical relationships still work.

Slowly changing dimensions: surrogate keys let you track versions of a dimension (e.g., a customer moves to a new region).

The Date dimension — special case

MANDATORY FOR TIME INTELLIGENCE
Power BI's time intelligence DAX functions (TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, etc.) REQUIRE a proper Date dimension table.

Properties of a valid Date table:
  Contains CONTINUOUS dates (no gaps)
  Covers full years from earliest to latest data
  Marked as Date table: Modeling → Mark as date table
  Has a column of unique Date data type values
  Has Year, Quarter, Month, MonthName, Day attributes for slicing 
// Create with DAX (Modeling → New table):
DimDate =
ADDCOLUMNS(
 CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31)),
 "Year", YEAR([Date]),
 "Quarter", "Q" & FORMAT([Date], "Q"),
 "Month", MONTH([Date]),
 "MonthName", FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
 "MonthShort", FORMAT([Date], "MMM"),
 "DayOfWeek", FORMAT([Date], "dddd"),
 "WeekNumber", WEEKNUM([Date]),
 "YearMonth", FORMAT([Date], "YYYY-MM")
)

// Alternative: Power Query M
let
 Start = #date(2020, 1, 1),
 End = #date(2026, 12, 31),
 Days = Duration.Days(End - Start) + 1,
 DateList = List.Dates(Start, Days, #duration(1, 0, 0, 0))
in
 Table.FromList(DateList, Splitter.SplitByNothing(), {"Date"})

Granularity — getting it right

GRANULARITY = LEVEL OF DETAIL
Every fact row represents an event at a specific level of detail.

Examples:
  Order grain: one row per order (the order total)
  Order line grain: one row per line item (each product in the order)
  Daily grain: aggregated to daily totals
  Hourly grain: aggregated to hourly buckets

Choose the FINEST grain you'll ever need to analyze. Aggregating up later is easy; un-aggregating impossible.

Worked example — building a star schema

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales analysis model

You receive these source tables:

// Source: a single denormalized CSV with everything mixed
SalesTransactions.csv:
 OrderID | OrderDate | CustomerName | CustomerCity | CustomerCountry
 | ProductName | Category | UnitPrice | Quantity | SalesAmount

You should split this into a star:

// FACT TABLE
FactSales (keep only keys + measures):
 SaleKey | DateKey | CustomerKey | ProductKey | Quantity | SalesAmount

// DIMENSIONS
DimDate:
 DateKey | Date | Year | Quarter | Month | MonthName

DimCustomer:
 CustomerKey | CustomerName | City | Country

DimProduct:
 ProductKey | ProductName | Category | UnitPrice

Each dimension's primary key (CustomerKey, ProductKey, DateKey) links to a foreign key column of the same name in FactSales. This is the "star" pattern Power BI is optimized for.

Common modeling mistakes

⚠ AVOID THESE — ALL TESTED ON PL-300

Single flat table: everything in one CSV. Power Query loads it; queries are slow; can't drill cleanly.

Snowflake instead of star: linking SubCategory → Category → Product. Should be flattened.

Bi-directional relationships everywhere: causes ambiguous paths and slow queries. Use only when needed (e.g., many-to-many).

Date as text: "Jan 2025" stored as a string instead of a proper Date. Breaks time intelligence.

Using calculated columns for time intelligence: use a Date dimension instead.

No Date dimension: trying to use the OrderDate column from the fact table directly. Works for simple cases, fails for "year over year" and similar.

★ ON THE PL-300

"What is a star schema?" → ONE fact table, MANY dimension tables, all flat.

"Star vs snowflake?" → Star is preferred (faster, simpler).

"What's a fact table?" → contains measures (numbers to aggregate); has foreign keys to dimensions.

"What's a dimension table?" → descriptive attributes for grouping/filtering; has a primary key.

"How to fix a snowflake?" → merge child dimension tables into parent (Power Query Merge).

"Time intelligence requires?" → marked Date table with continuous dates.

"Best granularity?" → finest you'll ever need to analyze.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Star schema = 1 fact table + many flat dimension tables — Power BI's preferred structure
  • Fact tables hold measurements (numbers); dimension tables hold descriptive attributes
  • Fact tables are large (millions of rows); dimensions are small (thousands)
  • Avoid snowflakes — flatten them with Power Query Merge
  • Use surrogate keys (integers) for relationships, not natural keys (strings) — faster + more stable
  • A Date dimension is MANDATORY for time intelligence — must be continuous and marked
  • Choose the finest grain you'll need — aggregating up is easy, splitting down isn't
  • Data modeling = 30-35% of the PL-300 exam — single highest-weighted topic
