◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Relationships are how Power BI joins your tables at query time. Get cardinality and filter direction right and your visuals work flawlessly; get them wrong and you'll see ambiguous filter behavior, blank values, or wrong totals. PL-300 always has 3-5 questions on relationships — particularly identifying cardinality and resolving "ambiguous filter path" errors.

What is a relationship?

RELATIONSHIP DEFINITION
A relationship connects two tables by matching a column in one to a column in the other. When you slice a visual by a column from one table, the relationship propagates that filter to the other table.

Set up via: Model view → drag column from one table onto matching column in another table. Or: Manage relationships dialog.

One side: the column with unique values (the dimension's primary key)
Many side: the column where values can repeat (the fact's foreign key)

Cardinality types

CardinalityMeansExampleUse
1:Many (1:*)One row in A, many in BDimCustomer → FactSales95% of relationships — DEFAULT
Many:1 (*:1)Same as above, reversedFactSales → DimCustomerDirection depends on which table you started from
1:1 (1:1)One row in each side matchesCustomer ↔ CustomerProfileRare — usually means you should merge tables
Many:Many (*:*)Multiple rows on both sides matchStudents ↔ Courses (via enrollments)Use bridge table OR DAX (avoid native M:M when possible)
★ HOW TO TELL THE CARDINALITY

Look at the column on the "one" side — values must be UNIQUE.

If DimCustomer.CustomerKey has duplicates, Power BI will refuse to make it the "one" side.

Quick check: in Data view, click the column and look at the bottom bar — it shows row count and distinct count. If they're equal, the column is unique.

Filter direction

CROSS-FILTER DIRECTION
Determines which way filters flow across the relationship.

Single (→): filter flows from the "one" side to the "many" side only. DEFAULT and PREFERRED.
Both (⇄): filter flows both ways. Sometimes needed for many:many, but slows queries and can cause ambiguous paths.

Example: DimCustomer 1→* FactSales
  Single: slicing by customer filters sales (YES); slicing by sale filters customer (NO)
  Both: both directions work 
// Visual showing the icons in Power BI's Model view:

DimCustomer ─── 1 ──→─── * ─── FactSales (Single direction: →)
DimCustomer ─── 1 ──⇄─── * ─── FactSales (Both directions: ⇄)
DimDate ─── 1 ──→─── * ─── FactSales (Single, the typical setup)

Active vs inactive relationships

MULTIPLE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN SAME TABLES
Two tables can have multiple potential relationships (e.g., FactSales has both OrderDate and ShipDate, both linking to DimDate).

Only ONE can be ACTIVE at a time (shown as solid line).
Others are INACTIVE (shown as dotted line).

Use the inactive one via USERELATIONSHIP inside a DAX measure:
SalesByShipDate = CALCULATE([Total Sales], USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDate], DimDate[Date])) 
// Setup: FactSales has OrderDate (active) and ShipDate (inactive) → DimDate

FactSales:
 OrderID | OrderDate (active rel)| ShipDate (inactive rel)| Amount

// Default behavior — uses OrderDate
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])
// Slicing by Year shows sales by ORDER year

// Switch to ShipDate when needed
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]),
 USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDate], DimDate[Date])
)

Ambiguous filter paths

⚠ THE AMBIGUOUS PATH ERROR

When Power BI sees two different paths to filter a table, it doesn't know which to use → throws an error or shows wrong totals.

Example: Both DimProduct and DimRegion connect to FactSales (good). But then someone adds a many:many between DimProduct and DimRegion (the same product is sold in multiple regions). Now filtering by Region has two paths: Region→Product→Sales AND Region→Sales directly. Ambiguous!

Fix: deactivate one of the relationships, or merge tables, or use a bridge table.

Bridge tables for many:many

// Wrong: many:many directly
DimStudent ←──── *:* ────→ DimCourse
// Power BI handles this but slowly, and filter behavior can be unexpected

// Right: bridge table
DimStudent ─── 1:* ───→ FactEnrollment ←─── *:1 ─── DimCourse

// FactEnrollment is the bridge:
// StudentKey | CourseKey | EnrollmentDate | Grade
// Each row = one student enrolled in one course.
// Many students per course, many courses per student — bridged by the enrollment fact.

Referential integrity

REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY
Every foreign key in the fact table has a matching primary key in the dimension table. NO orphaned rows.

When you have integrity, Power BI uses INNER joins (faster).
When you don't (orphan keys exist), Power BI uses LEFT OUTER joins (slower) and adds a placeholder "(Blank)" row.

Check the "Assume referential integrity" checkbox in relationship properties — but ONLY if you're certain it's true. Setting it falsely returns wrong results.

Worked example — three-table model

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Common modeling pattern
// MODEL VIEW

 DimDate DimProduct

 | DateKey * | | ProductKey * |
 | Date | | Name |
 | Year | | Category |
 | Month | | UnitPrice |
 +-----------+ +--------------+
 1 1
 | |
 * *
 FactSales
 +-------------+
 | DateKey |

 | CustomerKey | ← also FK to DimCustomer
 | Quantity |

 +-------------+

// All three relationships are 1:* with single filter direction:
// DimDate [DateKey, *] → FactSales [DateKey]
// DimProduct [ProductKey, *] → FactSales [ProductKey]
// DimCustomer [CustomerKey, *]→ FactSales [CustomerKey]

// Result: filter a visual by Year → DimDate filters FactSales → measures update.
// Filter by Category → DimProduct filters FactSales → measures update.
// All measures live in FactSales as DAX expressions.

Performance implications

PracticePerformance impact
Use single direction wherever possibleFAST
Use integer surrogate keys instead of textVertiPaq compresses better → faster
Cardinality 1:* (not *:*)Native engine path — fastest
Bi-directional everywhereSLOW — engine can't optimize joins
Many:Many directSLOWER — engine fans out join
★ ON THE PL-300

"Default cardinality?" → 1:Many (1:*).

"Default filter direction?" → Single (from one side to many side).

"Multiple relationships between same tables?" → only ONE active; use USERELATIONSHIP for others.

"Cause of ambiguous path?" → multiple ways for a filter to reach a table.

"Best for many-to-many?" → Bridge (junction) table.

"Performance hit with bi-directional?" → YES, avoid unless necessary.

"Star schema relationships?" → all 1:* from dimension to fact, single direction.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Relationships: connect tables via matching columns; filters propagate at query time
  • 4 cardinalities: 1:1, 1:*, *:1, *:* (most common: 1:* from dimension to fact)
  • Filter direction: Single (default) or Both — both is slower, use sparingly
  • "One" side column MUST be unique (Power BI enforces this)
  • Multiple relationships between same tables: only ONE active; use USERELATIONSHIP for others
  • Ambiguous path = multiple routes for filter to reach a table — must resolve
  • Many:many: use bridge tables for cleaner, faster filtering
  • Integer surrogate keys > string natural keys for performance

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

"Calculated column vs measure" is one of the most commonly missed PL-300 questions. They look similar (both use DAX), but they behave completely differently: column = computed once per row at refresh; measure = computed at query time for the filter context. Choosing wrong wastes memory or gives wrong totals.

The core distinction

CALCULATED COLUMN vs MEASURE — THE 30-SECOND VERSION
Calculated column: a new column added to a table. Computed ROW-BY-ROW at data refresh time. Stored in the model.

Measure: a formula evaluated AT QUERY TIME based on the current filter context. NOT stored — computed each time you look at a visual.

Rule of thumb:
  Need it on an axis or slicer? → Column
  Need it as an aggregation in a value? → Measure
  In doubt? → Measure (more flexible, less memory)

Side-by-side comparison

AspectCalculated columnMeasure
When computedAt DATA REFRESHAt QUERY TIME (every visual)
What it representsA value for each rowA scalar value for current filter context
Memory costStored — adds to model sizeNot stored — computed on demand
CPU costOne-time at refreshEvery time visual renders
Available in slicersYESNO
On a visual axisYESNO (only in Values area)
Context for formulaRow context (current row's values)Filter context (slicers + visual filters)
Aggregates correctlySometimes ⚠ (depends on how you slice)ALWAYS by design
Where to useCategorization, classification, attributesAll metrics, KPIs, totals

Calculated column example

// Use case: classify each customer by spending tier — useful as a slicer

// In DimCustomer table, add a new calculated column:
CustomerTier =
SWITCH(
 TRUE(),
 DimCustomer[LifetimeValue] >= 10000, "Platinum",
 DimCustomer[LifetimeValue] >= 5000, "Gold",
 DimCustomer[LifetimeValue] >= 1000, "Silver",
 "Bronze"
)

// Now each row has a tier value:
// CustomerKey | Name | LifetimeValue | CustomerTier
// 1 | Alice | 12000 | Platinum
// 2 | Bob | 800 | Bronze
// 3 | Carol | 5500 | Gold

// Drag CustomerTier into a slicer — works perfectly.
// Drag it onto X axis of a bar chart — works perfectly.

Measure example

// Use case: sum of sales, dynamic to whatever's filtered

Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[SalesAmount])

// Now this works:
// • Drop Total Sales onto a card visual → shows grand total
// • Slice by Year → shows that year's total
// • Slice by Year + Category → shows that year's total for that category
// • Build a matrix with Year on rows and Category on columns → fills every cell correctly

// The SAME measure formula produces the right answer in every context.
// It's evaluated FRESH for each cell in the visual.

The classic mistake — using column instead of measure

⚠ COMMON BUG

You want "Profit Margin" as a percentage. You write it as a calculated column:

// In FactSales, calculated column:
ProfitMargin = FactSales[Profit] / FactSales[Revenue]

This computes the margin per row. Then if you drop it in a visual as "Sum of ProfitMargin," you'll see the SUM of all the per-row margins — meaningless. Even Average gives wrong results because each row's margin is weighted equally regardless of revenue.

Fix: use a measure, which aggregates correctly:

// Measure:
Profit Margin % = DIVIDE(SUM(FactSales[Profit]), SUM(FactSales[Revenue]))

// Now: total profit ÷ total revenue, correctly weighted.
// And it re-aggregates correctly when sliced.

When DO you need a calculated column?

USE CASES FOR CALCULATED COLUMNS
1. Categorization — bucketing rows: "High" / "Medium" / "Low"
2. Slicer values — needed in filters or slicers
3. Row-level attributes — concatenated names, full addresses
4. Conditional flags — "Is this an out-of-state customer?"
5. Derived dates — Fiscal Quarter from a date (if not already in DimDate) 
// Concatenation
FullName = DimCustomer[FirstName] & " " & DimCustomer[LastName]

// Flag
IsHighValue = IF(DimCustomer[LifetimeValue] > 5000, "High Value", "Regular")

// Date derivation (when DimDate doesn't have it)
Quarter = "Q" & FORMAT(FactSales[OrderDate], "Q")

// Distance calc with two columns
DaysToShip = INT(FactSales[ShipDate] - FactSales[OrderDate])

When DO you need a measure?

USE CASES FOR MEASURES
1. Aggregations: Sum, Count, Average, Max, Min
2. Ratios and percentages: aggregate numerator ÷ aggregate denominator
3. Time intelligence: Year-over-year, Year-to-date, prior period
4. KPIs: anything you put on a card or use in a visualization
5. Conditional aggregation: "sum of sales where region = North" 
// Simple aggregations
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])
Order Count = COUNTROWS(FactSales)
Avg Order Value = AVERAGE(FactSales[Amount])

// Ratios — always with DIVIDE (handles divide-by-zero)
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])
AOV = DIVIDE([Total Sales], [Order Count])

// Conditional aggregation with CALCULATE
North Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "North")
Returning Customer Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimCustomer[IsReturning] = TRUE())

// Time intelligence
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date])
Sales Prior Year = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
YoY Growth = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales Prior Year], [Sales Prior Year])

Memory implications

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR PERFORMANCE
Calculated columns are STORED. A column with 100 million rows adds significant size to the model.

Worse: calculated columns don't compress as well as imported columns (engine has to compute them at refresh, then compress the result).

Rule: if you can do it in Power Query (during data load) or get it from the source, do it there. Use a calculated column only when neither option works.

Measures cost essentially ZERO storage. They're just formulas.

Worked example — same problem, both approaches

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales Tier ladder

Requirement: show how many customers are in each spending tier on a bar chart.

Approach 1: calculated column (CORRECT here)

// In DimCustomer:
SpendingTier =
SWITCH(
 TRUE(),
 DimCustomer[TotalSpend] >= 10000, "Platinum",
 DimCustomer[TotalSpend] >= 5000, "Gold",
 DimCustomer[TotalSpend] >= 1000, "Silver",
 "Bronze"
)

// Then build the chart:
// X-axis: SpendingTier (the calculated column)
// Y-axis: COUNTROWS(DimCustomer) — a measure
// → Works perfectly.

Approach 2: measure (DOESN'T WORK for this case)

// Can't put a measure on an axis. You'd have no way to GROUP customers by tier.

Now flip the requirement: show TOTAL REVENUE by tier.

Use the same column for the axis, but add a measure for the value:

Total Revenue = SUM(FactSales[Revenue])

// Chart:
// X-axis: DimCustomer[SpendingTier] ← column
// Y-axis: [Total Revenue] ← measure
// → Works perfectly. The measure dynamically sums revenue per tier.
★ ON THE PL-300

"Calculated column vs measure?" → column = per row at refresh; measure = aggregated at query time.

"For a slicer, use?" → calculated column (measures can't be sliced).

"For a KPI on a card, use?" → measure.

"Profit Margin shown wrong as totals?" → likely a calc column; switch to measure.

"Memory-efficient choice?" → measure (not stored).

"Best practice for aggregations?" → ALWAYS measures.

"DAX function to use when dividing in a measure?" → DIVIDE (handles /0).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Calculated column: per-row, computed at refresh, stored in model, usable on axis/slicer
  • Measure: aggregated value, computed at query time, no storage cost, only in Values area
  • Default to measures — they're more flexible and memory-efficient
  • Use calculated columns ONLY when you need the value as a category/slicer
  • Aggregations (sum, count, avg, ratios) → ALWAYS measures
  • Per-row attributes (tier, flag, full name) → calculated columns OR Power Query
  • Prefer Power Query > calculated column for large fact tables (smaller, faster)
  • Use DIVIDE for ratios to avoid division-by-zero errors

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is Power BI's formula language. Everything from "Total Sales" to "% change vs last year" is written in DAX. The PL-300 tests DAX from the very first question — knowing the syntax, the operators, and the difference between column references and table references is non-negotiable.

The DAX formula bar

Column references

Unlike C, JavaScript, or Java, DAX uses a SINGLE equals sign for comparison:

MAX(FactSales[Amount])
MIN(FactSales[Amount])
DISTINCTCOUNT(DimCustomer[CustomerKey])

// Functions can be nested:
ROUND(SUM(FactSales[Amount]), 2)
IF(SUM(FactSales[Amount]) > 1000, "High", "Low")

// Multi-line for readability (DAX is whitespace-tolerant):
Profit Margin =
DIVIDE(
 SUM(FactSales[Profit]),
 SUM(FactSales[Revenue]),
 0 -- alternate result if denominator is 0
)

Common DAX patterns

// 1. Simple aggregations
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])
Order Count = COUNTROWS(FactSales)
Customer Count = DISTINCTCOUNT(FactSales[CustomerKey])

// 2. Conditional (CASE-style)
Performance =
SWITCH(
 TRUE(),
 [Total Sales] >= 10000, "Excellent",
 [Total Sales] >= 5000, "Good",
 [Total Sales] >= 1000, "Fair",
 "Needs improvement"
)

// 3. Year-over-year change
YoY Sales =
VAR Current = [Total Sales]
VAR Previous =
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))
RETURN
 DIVIDE(Current - Previous, Previous)

// 4. Filtered aggregation
North Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "North")

Variables (VAR / RETURN)

VARIABLES — ALWAYS USE THEM
Variables store an intermediate value within a measure. Use them to:

1. Improve performance: a measure used 3 times is computed 3 times. A variable assigned once is computed once.
2. Improve readability: name the parts so the formula reads like prose.
3. Lock the context: variables capture their value when assigned — not later. 
// Without variables — Sales calculated 3 times:
Bad =
IF(
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]) > 1000,
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]) * 0.1,
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]) * 0.05
)

// With variables — Sales calculated ONCE:
Good =
VAR TotalSales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])
RETURN
 IF(
 TotalSales > 1000,
 TotalSales * 0.1,
 TotalSales * 0.05
 )

// Multiple variables — each cumulative:
Complex =
VAR Sales = [Total Sales]
VAR Cost = [Total Cost]
VAR Profit = Sales - Cost
VAR Margin = DIVIDE(Profit, Sales)
RETURN
 IF(Margin > 0.2, "High margin", "Low margin")

Comments

// Single-line C-style
-- Single-line SQL-style
/* Multi-line
 continues here */

Profit Margin =
-- Returns profit as a percentage of revenue
-- Used in the Executive Summary report
VAR Sales = [Total Sales] // grab once
VAR Cost = [Total Cost]
RETURN DIVIDE(Sales - Cost, Sales)

Naming conventions

RECOMMENDED CONVENTIONS
Measures: PascalCase or Title Case with spaces, e.g., Total Sales, Sales YTD, % of Total.
Calculated columns: PascalCase no spaces, e.g., FullName, OrderYear.
Tables: PascalCase, prefix Dim for dimensions and Fact for facts: DimCustomer, FactSales.
Hidden technical columns: prefix with underscore: _SortOrder.

Quick reference — common functions

FunctionPurpose
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAXAggregate a column
COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTROWS, DISTINCTCOUNTCount values/rows
DIVIDESafe division (handles /0)
IF, SWITCHConditional logic
CALCULATEModify filter context (most important DAX function)
FILTERReturn a filtered table
RELATED, RELATEDTABLENavigate relationships
TODAY, NOW, DATE, YEAR, MONTHDate arithmetic
BLANK, ISBLANK, COALESCEHandle missing values
★ ON THE PL-300

"Equality in DAX?" → SINGLE equals sign: [Sales] = 100.

"Column reference syntax?" → TableName[ColumnName].

"Measure reference syntax?" → [MeasureName] (no table prefix).

"Logical AND in DAX?" → && or function AND().

"Concatenation?" → & (not +).

"Safe division?" → DIVIDE(num, den, 0).

"Why use variables?" → readability + perform once vs many times.

"DAX's NULL?" → BLANK().

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Column refs use table prefix: FactSales[Amount]
  • Measure refs are bare brackets: [Total Sales]
  • Equality is SINGLE = (not ==) — comparison and assignment look identical
  • Logical: && / || / ! OR functions AND() / OR() / NOT()
  • Concatenation: & operator (not +)
  • Use VAR/RETURN for readability AND performance (compute once)
  • DIVIDE > / when there's any chance of /0
  • BLANK() is DAX's null — different from 0 or empty string
  • Comments: // -- (single-line) /* */ (multi-line)

DAX syntax basics: function arguments are separated by COMMAS — CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amt]), Region[Name] = "West") — and functions nest freely.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

You need 30-40 DAX functions to handle 90% of PL-300 exam scenarios. This section covers the must-knows: aggregations, iterators, logic, text, dates, and lookups. The exam will give you a scenario and ask which function to use — recognition is everything.

Aggregation functions

FunctionReturnsNotes
SUM(column)Total of numeric columnIgnores blanks
AVERAGE(column)Arithmetic meanIgnores blanks
MIN, MAX(column)Smallest / largest valueWorks on numbers + dates + text
COUNT(column)Count of non-blank numeric valuesNumbers only
COUNTA(column)Count of all non-blank valuesAny data type
COUNTROWS(table)Total rows in tableBest for "how many records"
DISTINCTCOUNT(column)Count of unique values"How many distinct customers"
COUNTBLANK(column)Count of blank valuesUseful for data quality

COUNT vs COUNTA vs COUNTROWS

⚠ KEY DIFFERENCES — TESTED ON PL-300
// Data:
// CustomerID | Name | Email
// 1 | Alice | alice@x.com
// 2 | Bob | (blank)
// 3 | (blank) | carol@x.com
// 4 | Dan | dan@x.com

COUNT(Customer[CustomerID]) = 4 // ID is numeric, all non-blank
COUNT(Customer[Name]) = 0 // Name is TEXT, so COUNT returns 0!
COUNTA(Customer[Name]) = 3 // 3 non-blank names
COUNTA(Customer[Email]) = 3 // 3 non-blank emails
COUNTROWS(Customer) = 4 // 4 rows total
DISTINCTCOUNT(Customer[Email]) = 3 // 3 unique emails (1 blank doesn't count)

Most common pattern: COUNTROWS for "how many records," DISTINCTCOUNT for "how many unique."

Iterator functions (X functions)

ITERATOR FUNCTIONS
Functions ending in X iterate row-by-row over a table, evaluate an expression for each row, then aggregate.

SUMX(table, expression)
AVERAGEX(table, expression)
MINX, MAXX, COUNTX

Use these when you need to compute a value PER ROW first, then aggregate. 
// SUMX example: compute revenue (which doesn't exist as a column)
// Each row has Quantity and UnitPrice — multiply them per row, then sum.

Total Revenue =
SUMX(
 FactSales, -- iterate FactSales
 FactSales[Quantity] * FactSales[UnitPrice] -- expression per row
)

// vs creating a calculated column first (wastes memory):
// Revenue = FactSales[Quantity] * FactSales[UnitPrice] ← calc column
// Total Revenue = SUM(FactSales[Revenue]) ← then sum

// SUMX is one-step and doesn't store the intermediate column.

// AVERAGEX: average order value, weighted equally
AOV = AVERAGEX(FactSales, FactSales[Quantity] * FactSales[UnitPrice])

// COUNTX: count rows matching a condition
Big Orders = COUNTX(FILTER(FactSales, FactSales[Amount] > 1000), 1)
// Or simpler:
Big Orders = COUNTROWS(FILTER(FactSales, FactSales[Amount] > 1000))

Logical functions

FunctionUse
IF(test, yes, no)Simple conditional
SWITCH(expr, val1, res1, val2, res2, ...)Multi-way (CASE-style)
SWITCH(TRUE(), cond1, res1, cond2, res2, ...)Multi-condition (if/elif/else)
AND(a, b) / OR(a, b) / NOT(a)Function-form logic
IFERROR(value, alternate)Return alternate if value errors
COALESCE(v1, v2, v3, ...)First non-blank value (Excel: IFNA)
 
// IF
Discount Flag = IF([Sales] >= 1000, "Eligible", "Not eligible")

// SWITCH (simple) — match a single expression to multiple values
DayType =
SWITCH(
 WEEKDAY(FactSales[OrderDate]),
 1, "Sunday",
 7, "Saturday",
 "Weekday" -- default
)

// SWITCH (TRUE pattern) — most flexible, used for grouping
Tier =
SWITCH(
 TRUE(),
 [Sales] >= 10000, "Platinum",
 [Sales] >= 5000, "Gold",
 [Sales] >= 1000, "Silver",
 "Bronze"
)

// COALESCE — return first non-blank
Display Name = COALESCE([Nickname], [FirstName], "Anonymous")

Math functions

FunctionReturns
ROUND(num, places)Round to decimal places (banker's: ROUNDUP / ROUNDDOWN)
CEILING(num, increment)Round up to nearest increment
FLOOR(num, increment)Round down to nearest increment
ABS(num)Absolute value
SQRT(num)Square root
POWER(num, exp)Exponentiation
DIVIDE(num, den, alt)Safe division — returns alt if /0

Text functions

// Concatenation
FullName = DimCustomer[FirstName] & " " & DimCustomer[LastName]
FullName2 = CONCATENATE(DimCustomer[FirstName], DimCustomer[LastName]) // 2-arg only
Combined = CONCATENATEX(DimCustomer, [Name], ", ") // iterator version, multiple rows

// Case
UPPER(text), LOWER(text), PROPER(text) // "PROPER CASE", "lower", "Proper"

// Find substrings
LEFT([Name], 5) // first 5 chars
RIGHT([Name], 3) // last 3 chars
MID([Name], 2, 4) // chars 2-5
LEN([Name]) // length
SEARCH("@", [Email]) // position of @ in email (1-indexed; -1 if not found... actually errors)
SEARCH("@", [Email], 1, -1) // with default -1 if not found
SUBSTITUTE([Name], "_", " ") // replace underscores with spaces
TRIM([Name]) // strip leading/trailing spaces

// Format numbers/dates as text
FORMAT([Date], "YYYY-MM-DD") // "2025-01-15"
FORMAT([Amount], "$#,##0.00") // "$1,234.56"
FORMAT([Percent], "0.0%") // "12.5%"

Date and time functions

// Constants and current date
TODAY() // current date
NOW() // current date and time
DATE(2025, 1, 15) // construct a date

// Extract parts
YEAR(date), MONTH(date), DAY(date)
QUARTER(date), WEEKNUM(date)
WEEKDAY(date, [first day]) // 1=Sunday (default) or 1=Monday
FORMAT(date, "MMM") // "Jan", "Feb", etc.

// Math on dates
DATEDIFF(start, end, "DAY") // days between (also MONTH, YEAR, etc.)
EDATE(date, months) // date N months later/earlier
EOMONTH(date, months) // end of N-months-later month

// Construct from parts
DATEVALUE("2025-01-15") // parse text date

Filter and table functions

// CALCULATE — modify filter context (covered in ch4/s4)
North Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "North")

// FILTER — return a filtered table
HighValueOrders = FILTER(FactSales, FactSales[Amount] > 1000)

// ALL — remove filters (good for ratios and rankings)
% of Total =
DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(DimProduct)) -- removes Product filter for denominator
)

// VALUES — distinct values of a column
COUNTROWS(VALUES(DimCustomer[Country])) // count of countries

// RELATED — pull a column value from a related dimension
ProductCategory = RELATED(DimProduct[Category]) // in FactSales row context

// RELATEDTABLE — pull all related rows (for one-side from many-side context)
CustomerOrderCount =
COUNTROWS(RELATEDTABLE(FactSales)) // in DimCustomer row context

// SUMMARIZE — group by columns and aggregate
SalesByCountry =
SUMMARIZE(
 FactSales,
 DimCustomer[Country],
 "Total Sales", SUM(FactSales[Amount])
)

Information functions

ISBLANK([Email]) // TRUE if blank
ISERROR(expression) // TRUE if expression errors
HASONEVALUE(DimCountry[Country]) // TRUE if exactly one value in filter context
SELECTEDVALUE(DimCountry[Country]) // The single value (or blank if multiple)
USERPRINCIPALNAME() // current user's email (for RLS)

// Pattern: show different result depending on context
Selected Country =
IF(
 HASONEVALUE(DimCountry[Country]),
 VALUES(DimCountry[Country]),
 "All countries"
)
// Or use SELECTEDVALUE which is cleaner:
Selected Country = SELECTEDVALUE(DimCountry[Country], "All countries")

The most-tested PL-300 functions

★ MEMORIZE THESE — APPEAR ON 80% OF EXAMS

Aggregations: SUM, COUNTROWS, DISTINCTCOUNT, AVERAGE

Iterators: SUMX, AVERAGEX (because of "compute then aggregate" scenarios)

Logic: IF, SWITCH (TRUE pattern), AND/OR

Filter context: CALCULATE (covered separately, most important), FILTER, ALL, ALLEXCEPT

Division: DIVIDE

Lookups: RELATED, LOOKUPVALUE

Time intelligence: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, TOTALYTD, DATEADD, DATESINPERIOD

Date: TODAY, DATE, YEAR, MONTH, FORMAT

Variables: VAR / RETURN

Worked example — Top N customers

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Top 10 customers by sales
// Common report requirement: a visual showing your top 10 customers

// METHOD 1: Visual-level filter
// Drop Customer Name on X-axis, Total Sales on Y-axis
// → Filter pane → Filter type: Top N → Show items: Top 10 by Total Sales
// → Done. No DAX needed.

// METHOD 2: DAX (if you need it programmatically)
Top 10 Customers Sales =
SUMX(
 TOPN(10, VALUES(DimCustomer[CustomerName]), [Total Sales]),
 [Total Sales]
)

// TOPN(n, table, ordering-expression, [ASC|DESC default DESC])
// returns the top N rows by ordering expression
★ ON THE PL-300

"Count distinct customers?" → DISTINCTCOUNT(FactSales[CustomerKey]).

"Number of rows?" → COUNTROWS(table).

"Avg price weighted by quantity?" → SUMX(...) / SUM(quantity) or DIVIDE.

"Multi-condition lookup like SWITCH/CASE?" → SWITCH(TRUE(), cond1, val1, ...).

"Get column from related table?" → RELATED(...) (many side to one).

"Date 30 days ago?" → TODAY() - 30.

"Safe division?" → DIVIDE(n, d, 0).

"Show selected slicer value, or 'All' if none/multiple?" → SELECTEDVALUE.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • SUM, COUNT, AVERAGE = simple aggregations on a column
  • SUMX, COUNTX, AVERAGEX = iterators: compute per-row, then aggregate
  • COUNTROWS for "how many records," DISTINCTCOUNT for "how many unique"
  • SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) is the if/elif/else pattern
  • DIVIDE is safer than / (handles divide-by-zero)
  • RELATED navigates many-to-one (from fact to dim); RELATEDTABLE one-to-many
  • SELECTEDVALUE returns the single value or a default — cleaner than HASONEVALUE+VALUES
  • FORMAT converts to text with custom format strings ($#,##0.00, MMM-YYYY, etc.)
  • DATEDIFF and EDATE for date arithmetic

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Time intelligence is THE most expected DAX topic on PL-300. Almost every real Power BI report needs "year-over-year," "year-to-date," or "vs prior period." Microsoft tests it because if you can't do time math, you can't build executive dashboards. Memorize 5-6 functions and you've covered 95% of scenarios.

The prerequisite: a proper Date table

MANDATORY SETUP
ALL time intelligence functions require:

1. A separate Date dimension table (not just the date column in your fact)
2. The table has continuous dates (no gaps, full year coverage)
3. The table is marked as a Date table: Modeling → Mark as date table → pick the Date column
4. A 1:* relationship connects DimDate[Date] to your fact's date column

Without these, time intelligence functions return wrong results or BLANK. The exam will test this. 
// Create a Date table with DAX
DimDate =
ADDCOLUMNS(
 CALENDAR(DATE(2020,1,1), DATE(2026,12,31)),
 "Year", YEAR([Date]),
 "Quarter", "Q" & FORMAT([Date], "Q"),
 "Month", MONTH([Date]),
 "MonthName", FORMAT([Date], "MMMM"),
 "MonthYear", FORMAT([Date], "MMM YYYY"),
 "WeekNum", WEEKNUM([Date]),
 "DayOfWeek", FORMAT([Date], "dddd"),
 "IsWeekend", WEEKDAY([Date], 2) >= 6
)

// Then: Modeling → Mark as date table → select [Date] column
// Then: link DimDate[Date] to FactSales[OrderDate] with 1:* relationship

The big four time intelligence functions

FunctionWhat it returnsPL-300 frequency
TOTALYTDYear-to-date sum/aggregateVERY high
SAMEPERIODLASTYEARSame dates, one year backVERY high
DATEADDShift dates forward/back by N unitsHigh
DATESINPERIODRolling N days/months/yearsHigh

TOTALYTD — year-to-date

// Syntax
TOTALYTD(expression, dates, [filter], [year_end_date])

// Basic year-to-date sales
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date])

// In a visual with Year and Month on the axis:
// Jan 2025: $100k (just Jan)
// Feb 2025: $250k (Jan + Feb)
// Mar 2025: $400k (Jan + Feb + Mar)
// ...resets at Year boundary

// With custom fiscal year ending June 30:
Sales FY-YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date], "06/30")

// Variants:
TOTALQTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date]) // quarter-to-date
TOTALMTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date]) // month-to-date

SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR — prior year

// Returns the dates shifted back exactly one year
Sales Last Year =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])
)

// In a visual:
// Mar 2025 sales: $500k ← current
// Mar 2025 last year: $420k ← same period last year (auto-shifts to Mar 2024)

// Year-over-year growth (the most common ask on PL-300):
YoY Growth % =
VAR Current = [Total Sales]
VAR Prior = [Sales Last Year]
RETURN
 DIVIDE(Current - Prior, Prior)

// Result on Mar 2025: ($500k - $420k) / $420k = 19% growth

DATEADD — flexible date shifting

// Syntax
DATEADD(dates, number_of_intervals, interval)
// interval: DAY | MONTH | QUARTER | YEAR

// Sales from 1 year ago (equivalent to SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR)
Sales 1Y Ago =
CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, YEAR))

// Sales from 30 days ago
Sales 30D Ago =
CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -30, DAY))

// Sales from one month forward (forecast comparison)
Sales Next Month =
CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], 1, MONTH))

// PARALLELPERIOD — like DATEADD but returns FULL period (e.g., entire prior month
// regardless of how many days you've selected in the current period)
Sales Prior Month Full =
CALCULATE([Total Sales], PARALLELPERIOD(DimDate[Date], -1, MONTH))
★ DATEADD vs SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR

Same result for "prior year" use case.

SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR: ONLY shifts by exactly 1 year. Cleaner syntax.

DATEADD: shift by any interval — 30 days, 2 weeks, 3 quarters, etc. More flexible.

Both honor the current filter context: in Q1 2025 they return Q1 2024.

DATESINPERIOD — rolling windows

// Syntax
DATESINPERIOD(dates, start_date, number_of_intervals, interval)

// Rolling 30-day sales (last 30 days from each point on a time axis)
Sales Rolling 30D =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]), -30, DAY)
)

// Rolling 12-month sales (very common on dashboards)
Sales Rolling 12M =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]), -12, MONTH)
)

// On a monthly chart, each point shows the SUM of the prior 12 months.
// Smooths out monthly noise and reveals trend.

Other essential time functions

FunctionReturns
DATESYTD(dates)Table of dates from Jan 1 of current year to current date
DATESQTD(dates)Dates from start of quarter to current date
DATESMTD(dates)Dates from start of month to current date
STARTOFYEAR / ENDOFYEAR(dates)First/last date of year in filter context
PREVIOUSYEAR / NEXTYEAR(dates)All dates of prior/next year
FIRSTDATE / LASTDATE(dates)First/last date in current filter
OPENINGBALANCEMONTH / CLOSINGBALANCEMONTHValue at start/end of month (for inventory-style metrics)

Common patterns — memorize these

// Pattern 1: Year-to-Date with prior year comparison
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date])
Sales YTD PY =
CALCULATE(
 [Sales YTD],
 SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])
)

// Pattern 2: Month-over-Month change
Sales MoM =
VAR Current = [Total Sales]
VAR Prior = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -1, MONTH))
RETURN DIVIDE(Current - Prior, Prior)

// Pattern 3: Cumulative running total within a year
Sales Cumulative YTD =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DATESYTD(DimDate[Date])
)

// Pattern 4: Rolling 90-day average
Sales 90D Avg =
DIVIDE(
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]), -90, DAY)),
 90
)

// Pattern 5: Fiscal year (ending Jun 30)
Sales FYTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date], "06/30")

The "Disable auto date/time" rule

⚠ PL-300 BEST PRACTICE

Power BI auto-generates a hidden Date table for every date column in your data. This:

  • Bloats the model with hidden tables (one per date column)
  • Cannot be customized for fiscal years
  • Confuses time intelligence behavior

Always disable: File → Options → Current file → Data Load → uncheck "Auto Date/Time."

Then use your own DimDate table with explicit relationships. This is a PL-300 "best practice" question.

Worked example — Year-over-year sales dashboard

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Common executive dashboard

Build these 5 measures:

// Base measure
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])

// 1. Year-to-date
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DimDate[Date])

// 2. Year-to-date for prior year
Sales YTD PY =
CALCULATE([Sales YTD], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

// 3. YoY % change
YoY Growth =
DIVIDE([Sales YTD] - [Sales YTD PY], [Sales YTD PY])

// 4. Last 30 days
Sales Last 30D =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]), -30, DAY)
)

// 5. Prior 30 days (for comparison)
Sales Prior 30D =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]) - 30, -30, DAY)
)

Drop these on cards: one shows current YTD, one shows last year's YTD, one shows the YoY % growth. Add a Line chart with [Total Sales] and [Sales YTD] for trend visualization. This pattern works for any business metric.

Troubleshooting time intelligence

⚠ COMMON ERRORS

"BLANK results": Date table isn't marked as a date table OR isn't continuous. Fix: Modeling → Mark as date table.

"Returning wrong years": Using fact table's date column instead of dimension's. Always reference DimDate[Date] in time intelligence.

"Auto Date/Time conflict": Disable Auto Date/Time in File → Options.

"YTD shows wrong fiscal year": pass the fiscal year-end date: TOTALYTD(..., "06/30").

"Same period last year is BLANK at start of dataset": Date table doesn't go back far enough. Extend CALENDAR() range.

★ ON THE PL-300

"Year-to-date?" → TOTALYTD([measure], DimDate[Date]).

"Year-over-year?" → CALCULATE([measure], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date])).

"Rolling 30 days?" → DATESINPERIOD(DimDate[Date], MAX(DimDate[Date]), -30, DAY).

"Shift dates by N months?" → DATEADD(DimDate[Date], -N, MONTH).

"Time intelligence broken?" → Mark as date table; disable Auto Date/Time; ensure continuous dates.

"Fiscal year ending June?" → TOTALYTD(..., "06/30").

"Best practice for date column?" → Always use DimDate column, never the fact's date directly.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Time intelligence REQUIRES a proper Date dimension table (continuous, marked as date)
  • The Big Four: TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, DATEADD, DATESINPERIOD
  • TOTALYTD aggregates from Jan 1 (or fiscal year start) to current date
  • SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts dates back exactly one year — for YoY comparisons
  • DATEADD shifts by any interval (DAY/MONTH/QUARTER/YEAR), positive or negative
  • DATESINPERIOD creates rolling windows (last N days/months/years)
  • Disable Auto Date/Time in Options — use your own DimDate
  • Fiscal year support: pass year-end date as last argument to TOTALYTD
  • If results come back BLANK: Date table isn't continuous or isn't marked

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

CALCULATE is the most important function in DAX. Master it and 80% of PL-300 DAX questions become trivial. Misunderstand it and you'll write measures that return wrong numbers or BLANK. Every advanced DAX pattern — KPIs, time intelligence, percentages of total, conditional aggregations — boils down to CALCULATE modifying filter context.

Filter context — the foundation

FILTER CONTEXT DEFINITION
Every cell in a Power BI visual is calculated within a specific FILTER CONTEXT — the set of filters that apply at that moment.

Filter context comes from:
  1. Slicers (e.g., "Year = 2025")
  2. Visual filters (the row/column/axis of the current visual)
  3. Page filters
  4. Report-level filters
  5. CALCULATE modifiers in DAX itself

When a measure runs, it sees ONLY the rows of the underlying tables that pass ALL active filters. 
// Example
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])

// Visual: Matrix with Year on rows, Category on columns
// Cell for (2025, "Electronics") evaluates Total Sales as:
// SUM(FactSales[Amount])
// filtered to rows where:
// DimDate[Year] = 2025
// DimProduct[Category] = "Electronics"
//
// Cell for (2024, "Books") evaluates with different filters → different result
// SAME formula, DIFFERENT filter context → DIFFERENT numbers

CALCULATE — what it actually does

CALCULATE SYNTAX
CALCULATE(expression, filter1, filter2, ...)

CALCULATE does TWO things:
1. Evaluates expression (typically an aggregation)
2. MODIFIES the filter context by applying or removing filters

Filters can:
  • Add a filter: DimCategory[Cat] = "A"
  • Remove filters: ALL(DimCategory)
  • Replace filters: any boolean column expression

The simplest example — fixed filter

// Base measure
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])

// Filtered measure — ALWAYS shows North region sales, regardless of slicer
North Sales =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DimRegion[Region] = "North"
)

// Behavior:
// • Default filter: whatever slicers + visual filters say
// • CALCULATE OVERRIDES the Region filter to "North"
// • All OTHER filters (Year, Category, etc.) still apply
//
// So if user selects Year=2025 in slicer:
// North Sales = sales for North + 2025 only

Multiple filter arguments

// Multiple filters combine with AND
High Value North =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DimRegion[Region] = "North",
 DimProduct[Category] = "Electronics",
 DimCustomer[Tier] = "Platinum"
)

// Returns: sales where region=North AND category=Electronics AND tier=Platinum

// For OR conditions, use IN or FILTER:
Premium Sales =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 DimProduct[Category] IN { "Electronics", "Premium" }
)

ALL — removing filters

ALL — IGNORE FILTERS ON A TABLE/COLUMN
ALL(table_or_column) returns a table that ignores all filters on the specified table or column.

Inside CALCULATE, this removes those filters from the calculation.

Most common use: computing a denominator that doesn't change as you slice. 
// Percent of total — the classic CALCULATE + ALL pattern
% of Total =
DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(DimProduct))
)

// Numerator: Total Sales in current filter context (e.g., specific product)
// Denominator: Total Sales ignoring DimProduct filter (the grand total)
//
// Visual showing each product's sales:
// Wireless Mouse: $50,000 → 12.5% of total
// Keyboard: $80,000 → 20.0% of total
// Monitor: $200,000 → 50.0% of total
// ...everything ÷ grand total

// Variant: ALL on the entire table — removes ALL filters from that table
% of Grand Total =
DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(FactSales))
)

ALL vs ALLEXCEPT vs ALLSELECTED

FunctionWhat it removesCommon use
ALL(table)Every filter on the tableGrand total denominator
ALL(column)Filters on that column only% of column total
ALLEXCEPT(table, col1, col2)Everything EXCEPT the specified columns% within category
ALLSELECTED(table)Filters from inside the visual, keeps slicer filters% of selected total
 
// % of total WITHIN current category
// (e.g., "this product is 30% of its category's sales")
% of Category =
DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(DimProduct, DimProduct[Category]))
)
// Keeps Category filter; removes ALL other DimProduct filters
// So denominator = total within the current Category

// % of slicer-selected total
% of Selection =
DIVIDE(
 [Total Sales],
 CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLSELECTED(DimProduct))
)
// Useful when user slices "show me only A, B, C" — denominator is A+B+C total

FILTER — when you need a table-level filter

FILTER vs simple boolean
Simple boolean (Cat = "A") works for column equality.

FILTER is needed for:
  • Filtering by an aggregation: "products with sales > 1000"
  • Multiple-column conditions
  • Iterator-style row evaluation

Syntax: FILTER(table, condition_per_row) 
// Sales from products that themselves sold over $1000
Big Product Sales =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 FILTER(
 DimProduct,
 [Total Sales] > 1000
 )
)

// FILTER iterates over each row of DimProduct, evaluates [Total Sales] for that product,
// keeps only rows where total > 1000. CALCULATE then re-evaluates using that filtered set.

// Compare to wrong attempt:
Wrong Attempt =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 [Total Sales] > 1000 -- ERROR: can't use measure on left of comparison
)

Context transition — calculated columns + CALCULATE

CONTEXT TRANSITION
When CALCULATE is invoked inside a ROW CONTEXT (e.g., a calculated column or iterator), it converts that row context into FILTER context.

This is how you can use aggregations in calculated columns.

Important PL-300 concept — appears in 1-2 questions. 
// Calculated column on FactSales — tag each row with category total
// (using context transition via CALCULATE)
CategoryTotal =
CALCULATE(
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]),
 DimProduct[Category] = RELATED(DimProduct[Category])
)

// Or more cleanly, with implicit context transition:
CategoryTotal =
VAR cat = RELATED(DimProduct[Category])
RETURN
 CALCULATE(
 SUM(FactSales[Amount]),
 FILTER(ALL(FactSales), RELATED(DimProduct[Category]) = cat)
 )

KEEPFILTERS — preserving existing filters

// Normal CALCULATE OVERRIDES existing filters on the same column:
North Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "North")
// If user has a Region slicer set to "South", North Sales STILL shows North data
// (the CALCULATE filter wins)

// KEEPFILTERS keeps the user's filter and INTERSECTS with yours:
Strict North =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 KEEPFILTERS(DimRegion[Region] = "North")
)
// If user has Region slicer set to "South", Strict North returns BLANK
// (intersection of "North" and "South" is empty)
// If user has slicer set to "North" or no filter, returns North sales

// Use KEEPFILTERS when you want your filter to be ADDITIVE, not overriding.

Putting it all together — common patterns

// PATTERN 1: Fixed-segment metric
North Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], DimRegion[Region] = "North")

// PATTERN 2: % of total
% of Total = DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALL(DimProduct)))

// PATTERN 3: % within parent category
% of Category =
DIVIDE([Total Sales], CALCULATE([Total Sales], ALLEXCEPT(DimProduct, DimProduct[Category])))

// PATTERN 4: Conditional aggregation
Online Sales = CALCULATE([Total Sales], FactSales[Channel] = "Online")

// PATTERN 5: Top N filter
Top 10 Products Sales =
SUMX(
 TOPN(10, VALUES(DimProduct[Product]), [Total Sales]),
 [Total Sales]
)

// PATTERN 6: Time intelligence (covered in s3)
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DimDate[Date]))

// PATTERN 7: Inactive relationship activation
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 USERELATIONSHIP(FactSales[ShipDate], DimDate[Date])
)

// PATTERN 8: Cumulative (running total)
Cumulative Sales =
CALCULATE(
 [Total Sales],
 FILTER(
 ALL(DimDate[Date]),
 DimDate[Date] <= MAX(DimDate[Date])
 )
)

Worked example — building a complete KPI

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales Goal Achievement

Requirements:

  • Show actual sales
  • Compare to a fixed quarterly goal of $1M
  • Show % of goal achieved
  • Color the result green if >= 100%, red if < 75%
// Base
Total Sales = SUM(FactSales[Amount])

// Quarterly goal — assume it's stored in a Goals table by quarter
Goal =
CALCULATE(
 SUM(Goals[Amount]),
 Goals[Period] = "Quarterly"
)

// % achievement
% of Goal = DIVIDE([Total Sales], [Goal])

// Status (for conditional formatting)
Goal Status =
SWITCH(
 TRUE(),
 [% of Goal] >= 1.0, "Met",
 [% of Goal] >= 0.75, "On track",
 "Behind"
)

// Goal status color (use in conditional formatting on the card)
Goal Status Color =
SWITCH(
 [Goal Status],
 "Met", "#22c55e", -- green
 "On track", "#f59e0b", -- amber
 "Behind", "#ef4444" -- red
)

Put [Total Sales], [Goal], [% of Goal] on card visuals. Use conditional formatting on the % card: "Format by → field value → Goal Status Color." Now it changes color automatically.

Common CALCULATE mistakes

⚠ COMMON ERRORS

Using a measure in a boolean filter:
CALCULATE([Total Sales], [Total Sales] > 1000) — ERROR, wrap in FILTER:
CALCULATE([Total Sales], FILTER(table, [Total Sales] > 1000))

Removing filters with simple column reference instead of ALL: doesn't work. Must use ALL/ALLEXCEPT/ALLSELECTED.

Confused about which ALL to use: ALL=remove all, ALLEXCEPT=keep some, ALLSELECTED=keep what user selected outside visual.

CALCULATE in calc column without expecting context transition: row context becomes filter context automatically, can be surprising.

Returning wrong year totals: relationship between DimDate and Fact uses wrong column, or DimDate isn't marked as date table.

★ ON THE PL-300

"Most important DAX function?" → CALCULATE.

"What does CALCULATE do?" → Evaluates an expression in a MODIFIED filter context.

"Filter context comes from?" → Slicers + visual filters + page filters + CALCULATE.

"% of total?" → DIVIDE([m], CALCULATE([m], ALL(table))).

"% within category?" → DIVIDE([m], CALCULATE([m], ALLEXCEPT(table, [Category]))).

"Filter by a measure?" → use FILTER inside CALCULATE.

"Keep filters instead of override?" → KEEPFILTERS.

"Activate inactive relationship?" → USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.

"Filter for grand total denominator?" → ALL(table or column).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Filter context = the set of filters active when a measure runs
  • CALCULATE = evaluate an expression in a MODIFIED filter context
  • CALCULATE filter args ADD, REPLACE, or REMOVE filters on columns
  • Use ALL/ALLEXCEPT/ALLSELECTED to remove filters (for ratio denominators)
  • Use FILTER when condition involves a measure or multiple columns
  • Use KEEPFILTERS to combine your filter with the user's (instead of overriding)
  • Use USERELATIONSHIP to activate an inactive relationship inside CALCULATE
  • "% of total" = DIVIDE([m], CALCULATE([m], ALL(table)))
  • "% within parent" = ALLEXCEPT — keeps parent filter, removes child filters
  • CALCULATE in calc columns triggers context transition (row → filter)
  • This is the MOST tested DAX topic on PL-300 — memorize the 8 patterns above

Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power BI ships with 30+ built-in visuals plus thousands more in the marketplace. Picking the right one is the difference between a report someone glances at and one they use to make decisions. The PL-300 exam tests recognizing which visual fits which analytical question.

The five visual categories

CategoryVisualsBest for
ComparisonBar, column, ribbon, lineRanking, change over time
CompositionPie, donut, treemap, stacked bar/areaParts of a whole
DistributionHistogram, scatter, box plotSpread of values
RelationshipScatter, bubble, correlation matrixConnection between variables
GeospatialMap, filled map, ArcGIS, shape mapLocation-based data

Bar and column charts

Stacked bar/column — composition + comparison
Clustered bar/column — multiple categories side by side
100% stacked bar — shares (each bar sums to 100%)

Bar = horizontal; better when:
 - Category names are long
 - Many categories (10+)
 - Ranking is the main message

Column = vertical; better when:
 - Time on x-axis (chronology natural left-to-right)
 - Few categories with short names
★ FIELD WELLS

Every visual has field wells where you drag fields. For bar/column:

  • Axis — the category (e.g., Region)
  • Legend — the splitting category (e.g., Year)
  • Values — the measure (e.g., Sum of Sales)
  • Small multiples — repeats the visual per category (e.g., one chart per Country)
  • Tooltips — extra info on hover

Line and area charts

Line chart — trends over time; multiple series via Legend
Area chart — emphasizes magnitude; less common
Stacked area — composition over time
100% stacked area — share over time

Combo chart — line + column on one axis (or two y-axes)
 — common: line for trend, column for volume

Ribbon chart — Power BI specialty
 — like stacked column but ribbons reorder by rank
 — shows ranking changes over time

When to use:
- Line: continuous time series; comparing trends
- Area: cumulative; emphasis on volume
- Combo: two related but different-scale measures (sales $ + units)
- Ribbon: when ranking shifts matter (top 5 products by month)

Pie, donut, and composition alternatives

Pie / Donut — for ≤ 5 slices ONLY
 — donut leaves room for KPI in center
 — avoid for ≥ 6 categories

Treemap — better than pie when:
 - Many categories (10+)
 - Hierarchical data (region → country)
 - Wide value range

Funnel — for sequential drop-off (sales pipeline, signup funnel)
 - Top: 100% input; bottom: final conversion

Waterfall — explains a change between two totals
 - Useful for variance analysis (actual vs budget)
 - Auto-categorizes increases / decreases

Decomposition tree — interactive drill-down
 - Click a category to break it down by another field
 - Great for root-cause exploration

Scatter and bubble charts

Field wells:
 X Axis — first numeric variable
 Y Axis — second numeric variable
 Size — third numeric variable (bubble size)
 Legend — categorical group (color)
 Play Axis — time field for animation (bubbles move over time)
 Details — what each dot represents (e.g., Country)

Use for:
 - Correlation between two metrics
 - Outlier identification
 - Up to 4 dimensions in one chart (x, y, size, color)
 - Animated views of change over time

Caveat: caps at ~10,000 points by default
 - Increase via Format → General → Total data points
 - Beyond ~50,000 points: aggregate or sample first

Maps

Map typeUse for
Map (bubble)Plot bubbles at locations; size = magnitude
Filled mapColor polygons (states, countries) by value (choropleth)
Shape mapCustom shapefiles (preview); for non-standard regions
ArcGIS MapsAdvanced GIS features; demographic overlays
Azure MapsCustom basemaps, heatmaps, real-time
⚠ GEOCODING REQUIRES BING

Standard Map and Filled Map send location text to Bing Maps for geocoding. To improve accuracy:

  • Use latitude/longitude when possible — no geocoding needed
  • Categorize fields as Data Category = City, State, Country, Postal Code (in Data view)
  • Pre-clean ambiguous names ("Paris, France" vs "Paris, TX")
  • Geocoding requires internet; report opens slower

Tables and matrices

Table — list of rows with columns; no aggregation by default
 — values shown as-is

Matrix — pivot-table-style; rows + columns + values
 - Rows: hierarchical (drill down)
 - Columns: optional pivot
 - Values: aggregated (sum/avg/etc.)

Differences:
 Table Matrix
 Rows flat hierarchical (drill enabled)
 Columns fixed list dynamic (one per category in field)
 Subtotals no yes (configurable)
 Total row optional always available

Common formatting:
 - Conditional formatting (color scale, data bars, icons) on Values cells
 - Sort by any column (single click for asc/desc)
 - Step in row hierarchy / step out
 - Show on rows (compact vs tabular layout)

KPI and card visuals

Card — single number, prominent display
 - Field wells: just Fields (one measure)
 - Common: total sales, count of customers

Multi-row card — multiple measures stacked

KPI — single number with TARGET comparison
 - Indicator: the measure
 - Trend axis: time field
 - Target goals: target measure
 - Auto color-codes: green if above target, red if below

Gauge — circular indicator with min/max/target
 - Useful for: progress toward goal
 - Caveat: takes lots of space for one number

When to use cards vs KPIs:
- Card: just the number ("Total sales: $1.2M")
- KPI: number + status + trend ("Sales: $1.2M ▲ vs target $1.0M")
- Gauge: progress percentages, fuel-gauge metaphors

Slicers and filtering visuals

Slicer — visual filter; user-friendly
 - Modes: List, Dropdown, Tile, Between (numeric), Date range
 - Single select vs multi-select
 - Sync slicers across pages

Date slicer — special types:
 - Between: range with two handles
 - Before / After
 - Relative date (last 7 days, etc.)
 - Relative time

Drillthrough page — special page where user can drill into details
 Right-click a value → Drillthrough → page name

Tooltip page — custom hover popup
 Format pane → Tooltip → Page name
 Shows a mini-report on hover

Custom and AI visuals

Marketplace visuals — from AppSource (Format → Get more visuals)
 Examples: Histogram, Box-and-whisker, Word cloud, Bullet chart

AI visuals:
 Q&A — natural language → visual (type questions)
 Key influencers — what drives a metric up/down (auto-analysis)
 Decomposition tree — interactive break-down with AI hints
 Smart narrative — auto-generated text description of charts
 Anomaly detection — built into line chart; flags unusual values

When to use AI:
- Q&A: end-user self-service (allow business users to "ask")
- Key influencers: when you want to know WHY a number moved
- Decomposition tree: exploring without a fixed path
- Smart narrative: accessibility / executive summaries

Choosing the right visual — decision tree

QuestionRecommended visual
"Which is biggest?"Bar chart (horizontal, sorted)
"How did this change over time?"Line chart
"How does X break down?"Treemap, donut, or decomposition tree
"What's the relationship between X and Y?"Scatter or bubble chart
"Where is this happening?"Filled map (choropleth) or Map (bubbles)
"How am I doing vs target?"KPI visual
"What's the single number?"Card
"Why did this change?"Waterfall or Key influencers
"Show drop-off through stages"Funnel
"Show rank changes over time"Ribbon chart

Common visual selection mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Pie chart with 10+ slices — use treemap or bar
  2. 3D charts — distorted; almost never appropriate
  3. Bar chart for time series — use line for continuity
  4. Line chart for categorical comparison — bar shows ranking better
  5. Map without geocoding categorization — slow + inaccurate
  6. Combo chart with confusing dual axes — labels and scales must be clear
  7. Scatter plot with 100k+ unaggregated points — slow; aggregate first
  8. Gauge for non-goal metrics — wastes space; use card
  9. Treemap for ranking — bar shows ranking; treemap shows proportions
  10. Funnel for non-sequential data — only use for ordered stages
★ ON THE EXAM

"Ranking categories?" → Bar chart, sorted by value.

"Trend over time?" → Line chart.

"Composition of a whole?" → Pie/donut (≤5), treemap (more).

"Correlation?" → Scatter or bubble.

"Geographic?" → Filled map (regions) or Map (points).

"Single KPI vs target?" → KPI visual.

"Variance analysis?" → Waterfall chart.

"Drop-off through stages?" → Funnel.

"Rank changes over time?" → Ribbon chart.

"Show breakdown interactively?" → Decomposition tree.

"Why did the metric move?" → Key influencers visual.

"Hierarchical data with sizing?" → Treemap.

"Filter on the report itself?" → Slicer.

"Pivot table-style view?" → Matrix visual.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power BI groups visuals into five categories: comparison, composition, distribution, relationship, geospatial
  • Bar charts for ranking; column for time; ribbon for rank changes over time
  • Pie/donut only for ≤ 5 categories; treemap for many
  • Waterfall explains variance between two totals — actuals vs budget
  • Funnel shows sequential drop-off (pipelines, signups)
  • Scatter for two numeric relationships; bubble adds size dimension
  • Maps require geocoding via Bing — categorize fields and use lat/long when available
  • Filled map for choropleth (color by value); Map for bubble at point
  • Table = flat list; Matrix = pivot-style with drill
  • Card for single metric; KPI for metric + target status; Gauge for progress
  • Slicers are user-facing filters; sync them across pages for consistency
  • Drillthrough pages let users navigate from summary to detail
  • AI visuals: Q&A, Key influencers, Decomposition tree, Smart narrative, anomaly detection
  • Marketplace visuals add specialized chart types (histogram, box plot, bullet)
  • Match the visual to the question being asked, not personal preference

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Choosing the right visual is half the work; making it readable is the other half. Power BI gives extensive formatting control through the Format pane, plus interaction settings that determine how visuals affect each other. The PL-300 exam tests format options, themes, conditional formatting, and visual interactions.

The Format pane

Select any visual → Format pane (paint roller icon)

Two tabs:
 Visual — settings specific to the chart (axes, legend, data labels)
 General — universal settings (size, position, background, border, header)

Common General settings:
 Properties → Size and position
 Effects → Background, Visual border, Shadow
 Header icons (filter icon, focus mode, etc.)
 Title (text, font, alignment, background)
 Tooltips → Page-based tooltips

Common Visual settings (varies by chart type):
 X-axis / Y-axis → titles, scale, gridlines
 Legend → position, font, title
 Data labels → display, units, decimals
 Data colors → custom colors per category
 Plot area → background, transparency

Themes

View tab → Themes
 - Built-in themes (Default, City Park, Classroom, etc.)
 - Browse from marketplace
 - Customize current theme
 - Import / Export theme as JSON

Theme JSON structure:
{
 "name": "MyTheme",
 "dataColors": ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", ...],
 "background": "#FFFFFF",
 "foreground": "#000000",
 "tableAccent": "#1f77b4",
 "visualStyles": { ... } // detailed per-visual defaults
}

Why use themes:
- Consistent colors across all visuals in a report
- Branding (use company colors)
- Apply to multiple reports at once
- Save time: don't format every visual individually

Conditional formatting

Available on: Card, KPI, Bar, Column, Table, Matrix, and more
 - Background color
 - Font color
 - Data bars
 - Icons (▲▼, traffic lights)
 - Web URL (turn text into hyperlinks)

Three formatting basis options:

1. Color scale (gradient)
 Min: white → Max: blue
 Common for heatmaps in matrix visuals

2. Rules
 IF value > 1000 THEN green
 ELSE IF value > 500 THEN yellow
 ELSE red
 Multiple if-then conditions

3. Field value
 Use a calculated column or measure to drive the color
 Most flexible — DAX measure returns hex color
 Example:
 ColorByStatus = SWITCH(MAX(Tbl[Status]),
 "Active", "#00FF00",
 "Pending", "#FFFF00",
 "Cancelled", "#FF0000")

To apply:
 Visual → Format → Cell elements (in matrix/table)
 Or: right-click value in field well → Conditional formatting → Background color

Data labels

Format → Data labels → On

Common settings:
 Display units: None / Thousands (K) / Millions (M) / Billions (B) / Auto
 Decimal places: 0, 1, 2, ...
 Font color, size
 Position: Inside end / Outside end / Center (depends on chart)
 Show background: helpful when labels overlap chart elements

Special:
 Show as percent (where applicable)
 Custom format (use # and , for digit grouping; % for percent)

Examples of format strings:
 "$#,0.00" → $1,234.56
 "0.0%" → 12.3%
 "#,0,K" → 1K (thousands)
 "#,0.0,,M" → 1.2M (millions)

Axes

X-axis / Y-axis formatting:
 Title: text, font, alignment
 Values: font size, color, units, decimals
 Scale type: Linear / Log
 Range: Auto / Min / Max (override default)
 Concatenate labels (for hierarchies on X-axis)
 Maximum size (truncate long category labels)

Continuous vs Categorical X-axis:
 Date field → Continuous by default (date scale, gaps for missing dates)
 Date with hierarchy → Categorical (one tick per visible level, e.g., one per month)
 Choose via: X-axis → Type
 Continuous: better for trends with even spacing
 Categorical: shows every value as discrete category (no date gaps)

Data colors and gradient

Set colors per category (without using Legend):
 Data colors → expand → custom color per value

Conditional color on data points:
 Click "fx" next to Default color
 Format style: Gradient / Rules / Field value

Highlighting one category among many:
 Color all gray except the focus category
 Use a measure with SWITCH or IF + DAX
 Example:
 ColorHighlight =
 IF(SELECTEDVALUE(Sales[Region]) = "North America", "#1f77b4", "#cccccc")

Why this matters:
 Highlights tell the reader which category the chart is "about"
 Reduces cognitive load — fewer colors to interpret

Visual interactions — how charts affect each other

Default behavior:
 Click a category in Chart A → Chart B updates to show only that category's data

Three interaction modes (per visual pair):
 Filter — Chart B shows ONLY rows matching the clicked category
 Highlight — Chart B shows all data but highlights the relevant portion (default for bar/column)
 None — Chart B doesn't react to clicks in Chart A

How to configure:
 Select Chart A (the source)
 Format tab → Edit interactions
 Now Chart A shows interaction icons on every OTHER visual
 Click each icon to switch between Filter / Highlight / None

Use cases:
 Cross-filter dashboards: default behavior, lets users explore
 Disable interactions on KPI cards: prevent confusing "total = clicked total"
 Mix: line chart highlights, table filters

Cross-highlight vs cross-filter:
 Same when applied to most non-aggregated visuals
 Different on bar / column: highlight darkens the filtered portion of each bar

Sync slicers

View tab → Sync slicers pane

Each slicer can:
 Sync — affects matching slicers on other pages
 Show — appears on other pages

Example: a "Year" slicer on Sales page
 Check Sync + Show on Customers page
 Now changing Year on Sales also changes it on Customers
 Same physical slicer; one filter persists across pages

Advanced:
 Group sync — multiple slicers in a named group
 Different visual fields can sync if their underlying data field matches

Page-level vs visual-level vs report-level filters

Filter scopeApplies toWhere to set
VisualOnly the selected visualFilters pane → Filters on this visual
PageAll visuals on the current pageFilters pane → Filters on this page
ReportEvery page in the reportFilters pane → Filters on all pages
DrillthroughA specific drillthrough pageFilters pane → Drillthrough
 
Filter precedence (most specific wins):
 1. Visual filter
 2. Page filter
 3. Report filter
 4. Drillthrough filter (when navigating in)

Hidden filter:
 Eye icon → hides filter from end-user; still applies
 Useful: enforce "Country = USA" without showing it

Filter modes:
 Basic — checkboxes
 Advanced — value comparisons (greater than, contains, etc.)
 Top N — top/bottom N by a measure

Drillthrough setup

Goal: let users right-click a value → jump to a detail page filtered to that value

Steps:
1. Create a new page (e.g., "Customer Detail")
2. Drag the drillthrough field (e.g., Customer Name) into Filters → Drillthrough
3. Power BI auto-adds a back button — keep it
4. On the source page, right-click a value → Drillthrough → Customer Detail

The detail page is filtered to the clicked customer
Back button returns to the source page

Keep drillthrough field hidden from page filter — it appears automatically
Add report-level filters from the source page via "Keep all filters" toggle

Tooltips — basic and page tooltips

Basic tooltip:
 Hover over a data point → see Category, Value, Legend automatically
 Drag additional fields to Tooltips well to enrich

Page-based tooltip (custom):
 Create new page (small, e.g., 320×240 px)
 Page → Format → Tooltip → On
 Page must have content (any visual)
 In the destination visual: Format → Tooltip → Page name → select the tooltip page

 Example: hover over a bar in main chart → mini-report with sparkline + KPI

Tooltip page can have:
 - Filtered visuals (auto-filtered to the hovered data point)
 - Static images / text
 - Multiple measures
 - Drillthrough filters

Use cases:
 - "Show YoY growth and trend on hover"
 - "Quick customer profile on hover"
 - Saves space by hiding details until requested

Common formatting and interaction mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Formatting every visual differently — use a theme
  2. Disabling interactions everywhere — kills the value of an interactive dashboard
  3. Forgetting unit display ($1,234,567 vs $1.2M)
  4. Categorical x-axis when continuous is needed — gaps appear in time series
  5. Too many decimal places — 0 or 1 decimal usually enough
  6. Bright/clashing custom colors — stick to theme or use grayscale + one accent
  7. Page filters without communicating — users wonder why numbers don't match
  8. Forgetting to hide drillthrough field — clutters the filter pane
  9. Conditional formatting on irrelevant cells — color the metric value, not the row label
  10. Tooltip pages too large — should be small (~320×240) and quick to render
★ ON THE EXAM

"Apply consistent colors?" → Use a Theme (View → Themes).

"Color cells by value in a matrix?" → Conditional formatting → Background color.

"Color by DAX expression?" → Conditional formatting → Field value (returning hex).

"Filter one visual but not another?" → Edit interactions → set to None.

"Bar chart cross-filter type?" → Highlight (default) vs Filter.

"Slicer on multiple pages?" → Sync slicers with Show enabled on each page.

"Filter all pages in a report?" → Filters on all pages (report-level filter).

"Right-click to navigate?" → Drillthrough.

"Custom tooltip on hover?" → Page-based tooltip; small dedicated page.

"Hide filter from users?" → Eye icon in Filters pane.

"Format millions as M?" → Display units = Millions or custom format "#,0.0,,M".

"Highlight one category?" → Conditional color: gray + one accent via SWITCH measure.

"Categorical x-axis?" → Discrete categories; no time gaps shown.

"Continuous x-axis?" → Date scale; honors gaps in dates.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Format pane (paint roller) has Visual-specific and General settings
  • Themes ensure consistent colors across all visuals; can be saved/shared as JSON
  • Conditional formatting works by gradient, rules, or field value (DAX measure)
  • Use Field value formatting to drive colors from DAX SWITCH expressions
  • Data labels: configure display units (K, M, B), decimal places, position
  • Format strings: "$#,0.00", "0.0%", "#,0.0,,M" for custom number formatting
  • X-axis can be Continuous (date scale, gaps) or Categorical (each value as discrete)
  • Visual interactions: Filter (only matching) vs Highlight (darken matching) vs None
  • Edit interactions: select source visual → Format tab → Edit interactions → set per target
  • Sync slicers across pages: View → Sync slicers → check Sync + Show per page
  • Filter scopes: visual (most specific) → page → report (most general) → drillthrough
  • Hide filters from end users with the eye icon; still applies but not visible
  • Drillthrough: filter pane → Drillthrough; right-click value → navigate to detail page
  • Page tooltips: small dedicated pages shown on hover; configurable per visual
  • Use highlighting (gray + accent) to draw attention to one category in many

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Static reports are limited; interactive reports let users navigate and drill into questions. Bookmarks, buttons, and navigation features turn a Power BI report into a small application. The PL-300 exam tests bookmarks, drillthrough, navigation buttons, and the selection pane.

Bookmarks — saved views

View tab → Bookmarks pane

A bookmark captures:
 - Current page
 - Slicer / filter selections
 - Visual visibility (Selection pane state)
 - Sort order
 - Drill state
 - Spotlight (Focus mode)
 - Cross-highlighting

Add bookmark:
 Bookmarks pane → Add → name it (e.g., "Q4 Sales View")

Bookmark options (right-click bookmark):
 ✓ Data — slicers and filters
 ✓ Display — visual visibility
 ✓ Current page — switches to bookmark's page
 Selected visuals — bookmark applies only to specified visuals

Use cases:
 - Save useful view combinations ("Top 10 Customers", "EU sales", "YoY view")
 - Create "story" navigation: Bookmark 1 → 2 → 3
 - Toggle between alternate visuals on the same canvas

Selection pane — show/hide visuals

View tab → Selection pane

Shows all visuals on the current page in layer order
For each visual:
 - Eye icon: show/hide
 - Drag to reorder z-index (top of list = on top)
 - Group visuals together (multi-select → Group)
 - Rename for clarity

Common workflow:
 1. Create two charts that occupy the same space
 2. Use Selection pane to hide one (eye off)
 3. Make a bookmark with the other visible
 4. Use a button to switch bookmarks
 → User toggles between two views

Buttons

Insert tab → Buttons → choose icon or blank

Built-in icons:
 Back, Information, Help, Q&A, Reset, Bookmark, Page navigator, ...

Button actions (set in Format pane → Action):
 Type:
 Back — return to previous page (great after drillthrough)
 Bookmark — apply a bookmark
 Drill through — go to a drillthrough page
 Page navigation — navigate to a specific page
 Q&A — open Q&A dialog
 Web URL — open external link
 Apply all slicers — apply Apply mode slicers
 Clear all slicers — reset filters

Format → Style:
 Default state, On hover state, Pressed state
 Each state can have its own text, icon, fill, border
 Common: change color on hover to signal interactivity

Tooltip: hover text explaining what the button does

Page navigator and bookmark navigator

Insert → Buttons → Navigator → Page navigator
 Auto-generates buttons for every page in the report
 Auto-updates when pages are added/renamed
 Tabs adapt to current page

Insert → Buttons → Navigator → Bookmark navigator
 Auto-generates buttons for bookmarks in a chosen Group
 Useful for: "View options" toggle within one page

Benefits over manual buttons:
 - No need to maintain links by hand
 - New pages / bookmarks appear automatically
 - Consistent styling
 - Saves time on multi-page reports

Drillthrough — right-click navigation

Setup (recap from s2):
 1. Create destination page
 2. Drag field to Filters pane → Drillthrough field section
 3. Power BI adds Back button automatically

User flow:
 Right-click a value on source page → Drillthrough → page name
 Destination page filters to that value
 Back button returns to source

Keep all filters option:
 Drillthrough fields pane → "Keep all filters"
 ON — current page filters carry over (default)
 OFF — only the drillthrough field applies

Cross-report drillthrough:
 PowerBI service only; not in Desktop
 Allows jumping between separate reports
 Source report must have "Allow visuals in this report to use drillthrough targets from other reports"

Drill down and drill up — hierarchical exploration

When a visual has multiple fields in the Axis well (hierarchy):
 e.g., Year → Quarter → Month

Drill toolbar (top-right of visual):
 ↓ Drill mode — single click drills down on clicked item
 ↑ Drill up
 ↓↓ Go to next level (all items at next level)
 ↓→ Expand all (all items + next level combined)

Right-click a data point → Drill down

When to use:
 - Hierarchical data with natural levels
 - Don't want to clutter with multiple visuals
 - Let user choose drill granularity

Drill through vs Drill down:
 Drill THROUGH: jump to a different page filtered by clicked value
 Drill DOWN: stay on same visual, go to a finer level of the hierarchy

Building a navigation system

Pattern: side navigation bar
 1. Insert shapes/buttons for each page (Home, Sales, Customers, Settings)
 2. Set each button's Action to Page navigation
 3. Group buttons (Selection pane → Group)
 4. Pin to the same spot on every page (or use Page navigator)

Pattern: tabs at top
 Same idea, horizontal layout

Pattern: bookmark-based view switcher
 Bookmarks for "Trend", "Geography", "Customer" views on same page
 Buttons trigger each bookmark
 Selection pane hides irrelevant visuals per bookmark
 User toggles without changing pages

Pattern: filter reset button
 Insert button → Action: Clear all slicers
 Or: bookmark with all slicers cleared, action = Apply bookmark

Drill-down example — sales by date

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Hierarchical drill
// Build a column chart of sales by date
// Axis well: Date hierarchy → Year, Quarter, Month, Day
// Values: Sum of Sales

// In the visual, click drill-down arrow (↓↓):
// Initial view: 2022, 2023, 2024 (3 columns)
// After ↓↓: Q1-2022, Q2-2022, ..., Q4-2024 (12 columns)
// After ↓↓: Jan-2022, Feb-2022, ... (36 columns)
// After ↓↓: Daily

// Or: click on a year (e.g., 2023)
// With drill mode on, drills into 2023 only → Q1-2023, ..., Q4-2023

// Drill up arrow (↑) returns to previous level

// Pro tip: enable "Expand all" (↓→) to combine current + next level
// Shows year totals AND quarter breakdown together

Spotlight and focus mode

Spotlight:
 Right-click a visual → Spotlight
 Dims all other visuals; highlights this one
 Captures in bookmark (great for storytelling)

Focus mode:
 Click visual's expand icon (top-right)
 Visual takes over full page; other visuals hidden
 Better for detailed inspection
 User clicks "Back to report" to exit
 Captured by bookmark? No — focus mode is per-session

Anchor: the report Q&A feature

Insert → Q&A visual

Lets the user type natural language questions:
 "Total sales by region"
 "Top 5 customers by revenue"
 "Sales last quarter compared to this quarter"

Configuration:
 Q&A setup (gear icon)
 - Field synonyms (alternate names for fields)
 - Suggested questions
 - Promoted searches
 - Train Q&A on common requests

Limitations:
 - Works best with well-named fields (avoid "tbl_dim_cust_001")
 - English-only fully supported
 - May not recognize custom DAX measures unless described

Common navigation mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Drillthrough without a Back button — users get stuck (Power BI usually adds one automatically; verify)
  2. Bookmarks that don't capture data state — uncheck "Data" if you don't want slicers saved
  3. Too many bookmarks — confusing; group related ones
  4. Inconsistent navigation buttons across pages — use Page navigator for auto-update
  5. Forgetting selected visuals option — bookmark unexpectedly hides/shows other visuals
  6. Multiple drillthrough pages without clear naming — users get lost
  7. Disabling cross-filtering on every visual — kills the value of interactive design
  8. Bookmark for layout AND filter changes mixed together — split into separate bookmarks
  9. Q&A enabled without field naming cleanup — embarrassing AI responses
  10. Drill down hierarchy mismatched with visual type — only certain visuals support drill
★ ON THE EXAM

"Save view state?" → Bookmark.

"Show/hide visuals?" → Selection pane (eye icon).

"Toggle two visuals?" → Bookmarks + Selection pane + Button.

"Auto-update nav buttons?" → Insert → Buttons → Navigator → Page navigator.

"Right-click filter to detail page?" → Drillthrough.

"Drill into hierarchy?" → Drill down arrow on visual.

"Drill through vs Drill down?" → Through = jump page; Down = next hierarchy level same visual.

"Back from drillthrough?" → Back button (auto-added) or device back.

"Reset all filters?" → Button with Action = Clear all slicers.

"Tab navigation?" → Manual page navigation buttons or Page navigator.

"Natural language Q&A?" → Insert Q&A visual; train with synonyms.

"Bookmark only captures data?" → Uncheck "Display" in bookmark properties.

"Bookmark only affects some visuals?" → Use "Selected visuals" option.

"Cross-report drillthrough?" → Service only; enable in source report.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Bookmarks capture page + filters + visibility + drill state for one-click navigation
  • Configure each bookmark to capture only what's needed: Data / Display / Selected visuals
  • Selection pane shows all visuals on the page; toggle visibility with the eye icon
  • Buttons trigger actions: navigate pages, apply bookmarks, drill, clear slicers, open URLs
  • Page navigator and Bookmark navigator auto-generate consistent navigation tabs
  • Drillthrough = jump to a different page filtered to the clicked value (right-click)
  • Drill down = move within the same visual along a hierarchy
  • "Keep all filters" controls whether source page filters carry to drillthrough page
  • Combine bookmarks + Selection pane + buttons for view-toggle UX without extra pages
  • Spotlight dims other visuals; Focus mode expands one visual full-page
  • Q&A visual lets users type natural-language questions; needs clean field naming
  • Reset filter button: Action = Clear all slicers
  • Page navigator scales automatically with the number of pages — preferred over manual buttons
  • Cross-report drillthrough works in Power BI service, not Desktop
  • Hide drillthrough fields from page filters to keep filter pane clean
