◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A Power BI report that loads slowly, displays inconsistently, or confuses users won't be used — regardless of how good the data is. Good design plus performance optimization is essential. The PL-300 exam tests responsive layout, mobile views, accessibility, and performance tuning.

Page layout fundamentals

Format pane (without selecting visual) → Canvas settings

Canvas settings:
 Page size:
 16:9 — standard widescreen (default 1280×720)
 4:3 — older displays
 Letter — print landscape (1100×850)
 Tooltip — small for tooltip pages
 Custom — for unusual ratios

 Type:
 Fit to page — visuals scale with browser window
 Fit to width — fills horizontally; vertical scroll allowed
 Actual size — fixed pixel layout

Page background:
 Color / Image
 Transparency

Wallpaper (outside canvas) — for letterbox-free embed views

Grid and snap

View tab:
 ☐ Show gridlines — visual reference grid
 ☐ Snap objects to grid — auto-align to grid
 ☐ Snap to other visuals — magnetic edges between visuals

Alignment toolbar (Format tab when visual selected):
 Align: Left, Center, Right, Top, Middle, Bottom
 Distribute: Horizontal, Vertical (even spacing across selected visuals)
 Group / Ungroup

Why this matters:
 - Misaligned visuals look amateur
 - Consistent spacing improves readability
 - Use snap + align for clean grids

Spacing and grouping

Design principles:

White space:
 Don't fill every pixel
 Leave breathing room between visuals (8-16 px)
 Use page margins (top: 60px, sides: 24px typical)

Grouping related content:
 Visual elements close together imply relationship
 Section headers with shapes / lines as dividers
 Background shapes group multiple visuals into "cards"

Visual hierarchy:
 Most important visual: largest, top-left
 KPIs: top row across the page
 Detail visuals: below or right

Consistency:
 Same fonts across the report
 Aligned grid (4-column or 12-column layout)
 Same color for the same concept (revenue always blue, etc.)

Mobile layout

View tab → Mobile layout

Power BI separates DESKTOP layout from MOBILE layout
 Desktop layout: default 16:9 canvas
 Mobile layout: 9:16 portrait canvas (320×640 typical)

Set up mobile:
 1. Click Mobile layout button
 2. Drag visuals from sidebar onto the mobile phone canvas
 3. Not every visual must appear on mobile
 4. Reorder vertically for portrait scrolling

Hidden visuals:
 Not added to mobile layout = invisible on phone
 Useful: large tables hidden on phone, KPIs shown

Both layouts are saved in the same .pbix
 Power BI app auto-detects device and shows correct layout

Common mobile design:
 Top: 1-3 KPI cards
 Middle: 1 chart at a time, full width
 Bottom: optional table
 Slicers in floating sidebar

Themes for branding

View → Themes → Customize current theme:
 Name and colors:
 Theme colors (8 swatches; rotate through visuals)
 Sentiment colors (positive/neutral/negative)
 Divergent colors (min/center/max)
 Structural colors (background, foreground, gridlines)

 Text:
 Default font, size
 Per-element overrides (titles, callouts, tooltips, KPI)

 Visuals:
 Default styling per visual type
 Custom padding, borders, shadow

Export theme: View → Themes → Save current theme
 Saves as .json — reuse across reports

Standard themes: City Park, Classroom, Bloom, Tidal, ...
Custom enterprise theme:
 Use brand colors (e.g., from style guide)
 Ensure accessibility contrast
 Distribute .json to team

Accessibility

★ ACCESSIBILITY CHECKLIST
  • Alt text on every visual (Format → General → Alt text) — for screen readers
  • Tab order sensible (View → Tab order; visual layer order matters)
  • Color contrast > 4.5:1 for text (WCAG AA standard)
  • Don't rely on color alone — also use labels, icons, shapes
  • Avoid red-green only for colorblind users (8% of men)
  • Keyboard navigable — verify Tab + Enter works
  • Title and labels with descriptive names (not "Chart1")
  • Avoid flashing/animated content (epilepsy)
Setting alt text:
 Select visual → Format → General → Alt text
 Static text or:
 Dynamic alt text via DAX (recommended):
 Format → General → Alt text → fx button
 Returns a string describing the visual contents
 Updates as data changes
 Example:
 "Total sales " & FORMAT([Total Sales], "$#,0") & " across " & DISTINCTCOUNT(Region[Region]) & " regions"

Tab order:
 View → Tab order
 Lists all visuals; drag to reorder
 Determines screen-reader navigation sequence
 Hidden visuals can be excluded

Performance — the basics

IssueCauseFix
Slow loadToo many visuals per pageLimit to ~15 visuals per page
Slow refreshLarge fact tablesStar schema, aggregations, incremental refresh
Slow filterBidirectional relationshipsUse single-direction; only bidirectional if needed
Slow measuresComplex DAX, FILTER in iteratorsUse CALCULATE with simpler filter expressions
Large file sizeHigh-cardinality columnsDrop unused columns, split datetime to date+time
Slow visualVisual querying millions of rowsAggregate first, use TopN filter

Performance Analyzer

View tab → Performance Analyzer

How to use:
 1. Click "Start recording"
 2. Click "Refresh visuals"
 3. Interact (apply slicer, click bar, etc.)
 4. Stop recording
 5. Expand each visual to see breakdown:
 - DAX query (data engine time)
 - Visual display (render time)
 - Other (network, other waits)

Diagnosis:
 DAX query > 1 second → optimize the measure
 Visual display > 500 ms → simplify visual or reduce points
 Total > 5 seconds → simplify the page

Copy DAX query for tuning in DAX Studio (free Microsoft tool)

Star schema and model optimization

Star schema (recommended):
 Fact table in middle (transactions, events)
 Dimension tables around (Customer, Product, Date, Region)
 Each dimension joins to fact via single foreign key

Why star beats snowflake for Power BI:
 - Fewer relationships → faster DAX
 - Simpler model for users to understand
 - Vertipaq engine optimized for this pattern

Optimization tips:
 - Single direction relationships (fact ← dimension)
 - Use Date table marked as date table (Modeling → Mark as date table)
 - Disable auto date/time (File → Options → Current file → Time intelligence)
 - Hide foreign-key columns from report view
 - Remove unused columns (cardinality reduction)
 - Use Integer keys; avoid GUID/string keys
 - Set Sort by column for fields with custom order (e.g., Month Name sorted by Month Number)

Reducing visual count

⚠ ONE BIG PAGE OR MANY SMALL PAGES?

15 visuals → page loads quickly, easy to navigate

30+ visuals → slow load, overwhelming, hard to maintain

Strategies for too many visuals:

  • Split into multiple pages with consistent navigation
  • Combine related visuals (e.g., 5 KPI cards → 1 multi-row card)
  • Use bookmarks + buttons to toggle views on the same page
  • Use drillthrough pages for detail
  • Replace 10 individual category visuals with 1 visual + slicer

Data reduction techniques

Page-level "default" filter:
 Page filter set to e.g., "Year = current year"
 Limits queries on every visual on the page

Top N filter:
 Visual filter → "Show items when value is Top 10 by [Sales]"
 Don't render rest of the data

Filter context limits:
 Visual settings → Properties → Data limit (default 30,000)
 Some visuals have higher caps (scatter)
 Adjust carefully — high limits slow rendering

Aggregations table:
 Pre-aggregate millions of rows to summary
 Power BI uses aggregations automatically when possible
 Model view → Manage aggregations

Incremental refresh:
 Refresh only new partition (last month) instead of full table
 Setup in Power Query Editor → Incremental refresh policy
 Requires Premium for some features

DirectQuery vs Import — performance trade-offs

ModeProsCons
ImportFast queries, full DAX, compressedRequires refresh; size limits
DirectQueryLive data, no size limit, no refreshSlow queries, limited DAX
CompositeCombines both modes per tableComplex; needs careful planning

Worked example — performance audit

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Audit a slow report
// Steps to audit a slow Power BI report:

// 1. Open Performance Analyzer
// View → Performance Analyzer → Start recording → Refresh visuals

// 2. Identify slow visuals
// Anything > 1000 ms in DAX query → investigate
// Anything > 500 ms in visual display → consider simplification

// 3. Common findings and fixes:

// FINDING: Total measure takes 5 seconds
// Original DAX:
Total Sales =
 SUMX(
 FILTER(Sales, Sales[Year] = SELECTEDVALUE(Date[Year])),
 Sales[Amount]
 )

// Fix: use CALCULATE with column filter (faster than FILTER on iterator)
Total Sales =
 CALCULATE(
 SUM(Sales[Amount]),
 Sales[Year] = SELECTEDVALUE(Date[Year])
 )

// FINDING: 25 visuals on home page
// Fix: split into 3 themed pages (Overview, Detail, Trends) with Page navigator

// FINDING: bidirectional relationship
// Fix: change to single direction unless RLS or many-to-many really needed

// FINDING: 100M-row fact table
// Fix:
// - Add Aggregations table (daily totals)
// - Use Incremental refresh
// - Drop unused columns
// - Replace string dimension keys with integers

// FINDING: Datetime column slows everything
// Fix: split into Date column and Time column; turn off auto date/time

Publish settings and gateway considerations

When publishing to Power BI service:

Refresh:
 Import mode requires scheduled refresh
 Set in service: Workspace → Dataset → Schedule refresh
 Free: 8 refreshes per day; Premium: 48 per day

Gateway:
 Required for on-premises data sources
 Personal gateway: single user
 Enterprise gateway: multi-user, more secure
 Install on a server, not a laptop

Row-Level Security (RLS):
 Modeling → Manage roles → DAX expression filter
 Example: User can only see their region
 Test in service: Workspace → Dataset → Security → Test as role

Sharing:
 Workspaces: collaborative editing
 Apps: published bundles for read-only users
 Direct sharing: per-report (use sparingly for governance)

Common design and performance mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. 30+ visuals on one page — slow load; split into pages
  2. Inconsistent visual sizes and spacing — use snap to grid
  3. No mobile layout — broken phone experience
  4. No alt text — fails accessibility audits
  5. Bidirectional relationships everywhere — kills performance
  6. Auto date/time on every date — bloats model with hidden date tables
  7. FILTER in CALCULATE when column filter would work
  8. Snowflake schema instead of star — slower DAX
  9. Importing 50M rows when 5M would suffice (aggregate first)
  10. String keys for joins — integer keys are much faster
  11. Custom fonts and complex backgrounds — slow render
  12. No incremental refresh on large fact tables — full refresh every time
★ ON THE EXAM

"Make report responsive?" → Mobile layout for phone-portrait view.

"Snap to grid?" → View → Snap objects to grid.

"Theme JSON?" → Custom branding; reusable; from View → Themes.

"Alt text dynamic?" → fx button in alt text field → DAX expression.

"Audit performance?" → View → Performance Analyzer → Start recording.

"Optimal model?" → Star schema (fact + dimensions).

"Limit data per visual?" → Page filter or Top N filter.

"Refresh new data only?" → Incremental refresh policy.

"DirectQuery use case?" → Live data, massive datasets, can't fit in memory.

"Single direction relationship preferred?" → Yes; bidirectional only when needed.

"Best for many-to-many?" → Bidirectional, but test performance.

"Reduce DAX time?" → CALCULATE with column filter beats FILTER in iterator.

"Mark as date table?" → Modeling → Mark as date table; enables time intelligence.

"Tab order for accessibility?" → View → Tab order; drag to reorder.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Set page size and type for the intended viewing context (desktop, mobile, print)
  • Use snap to grid and visual alignment tools for clean layouts
  • Mobile layout is separate from desktop; build it explicitly
  • Themes apply consistent colors/fonts across all visuals; save as JSON for reuse
  • Accessibility: alt text (dynamic via DAX), tab order, contrast, don't rely on color alone
  • Performance Analyzer (View → Performance Analyzer) identifies slow visuals
  • Star schema is the gold standard — fact + dimension tables with single-direction relationships
  • Mark date tables explicitly to enable time intelligence functions
  • Disable auto date/time to avoid hidden date table bloat
  • Limit to ~15 visuals per page; split larger reports into multiple pages
  • Use CALCULATE with column filters instead of FILTER in iterators
  • Incremental refresh for large fact tables — only new partitions reload
  • Import = fast queries + refresh required; DirectQuery = live + slower
  • Composite mode combines Import + DirectQuery per table
  • RLS via Manage roles in Modeling tab; test in service before deploying

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power BI Desktop builds reports; Power BI Service publishes, shares, and refreshes them. The Service runs in the cloud and is where collaboration happens. The PL-300 exam tests workspaces, sharing models, capacities, and the publishing workflow.

Desktop vs Service vs Mobile

ToolPurposeWhere
Power BI DesktopBuild reports, model data, write DAXWindows app (free)
Power BI ServicePublish, share, refresh, schedule, RLSCloud (app.powerbi.com)
Power BI MobileConsume reports on phone/tabletiOS, Android, Windows
Power BI Report ServerOn-premises hosting alternativeSelf-hosted Windows server

Workspaces — collaboration containers

A workspace is a collection of:
 - Reports (.pbix files published)
 - Datasets (the data models)
 - Dashboards (pinned tiles from reports)
 - Dataflows (reusable ETL queries)
 - Datamarts (self-service databases)
 - Paginated reports (.rdl files)

Two types:
 My Workspace — personal sandbox; not for production
 Workspaces — collaborative; shared with team

Workspace settings:
 Name, description
 Members (Admin / Member / Contributor / Viewer)
 License: Pro vs Premium per User vs Premium per Capacity
 Workspace OneDrive integration
 Workspace image / branding

Workspace roles

RoleCan do
AdminEverything; add/remove users; delete workspace
MemberPublish; share; update apps; add other Members/Contributors/Viewers
ContributorPublish reports; can't share / add users; can't publish apps
ViewerView only; no edit; no publish

Publishing a report from Desktop

In Power BI Desktop:
 Home tab → Publish
 Choose destination workspace
 Sign in if required

What gets uploaded:
 - Report (the .pbix file)
 - Dataset (the data model, including imported data)
 Both appear in Service under chosen workspace

Replacing a published report:
 Publish from Desktop → if same name, prompt to overwrite
 Or in service: Workspace → ... → Replace report

Datasets in Service

After publishing, the dataset is independent from the report
 Multiple reports can connect to the SAME dataset
 Different teams can build their own reports on shared data

Dataset settings (Workspace → Dataset → Settings):
 Refresh schedule
 Gateway connection
 Q&A and Featured questions
 Endorsement (Promoted / Certified)
 Data source credentials
 Parameters
 Row-Level Security (RLS) roles

Connect a new report to existing dataset:
 Desktop → Home → Get data → Power BI datasets → choose
 Build report; publish; uses same dataset
 Benefits: single source of truth; one refresh; consistent metrics

Refresh and gateways

Refresh types:
 Manual — click Refresh on dataset
 Scheduled — automatic at set times
 Incremental — only new/changed partitions

Limits (per dataset):
 Pro: up to 8 scheduled refreshes per day
 Premium: up to 48 scheduled refreshes per day
 Total refresh duration: typically < 2 hours

Gateway (for on-premises sources):
 Required for: SQL Server, Oracle, file shares, on-prem APIs
 Personal Gateway (single user, runs on one machine)
 On-premises data gateway (multi-user, runs on a server)

Setup:
 1. Install gateway on a server (admin)
 2. Configure data source connections in Power BI service
 3. Dataset → Settings → Gateway connection → choose

Without gateway:
 Cloud sources (Azure SQL, SharePoint Online) work without gateway
 Files in OneDrive for Business / SharePoint refresh natively

Apps — packaged reports for consumers

An App is a published "view" of a workspace
 - Read-only for consumers
 - Curated content (only chosen reports/dashboards visible)
 - Branded with app icon
 - Updates require explicit "Update app"

Publishing an app:
 Workspace → Create app
 - Setup: name, description, icon
 - Navigation: choose which content appears, group into sections
 - Permissions: who can access (specific people, security groups, entire org)
 - Update existing app: Update app button (consumers see changes after update)

Why apps:
 - Cleaner UI for consumers
 - Don't expose workspace internals
 - Easier to manage permissions
 - Versioned: consumers see stable view while contributors edit

Distinction:
 Workspace = building space
 App = publishing destination

Sharing options compared

MethodUse forLicense required
Workspace accessCo-authoring; small teamAll members need Pro (unless Premium)
AppWide read-only distributionConsumers need Pro (unless Premium)
Direct shareOne-off sharing of specific reportSharer + receiver need Pro
Embed in TeamsIn-context viewing during meetingsPro
Publish to webPublic reports (caution!)Pro; data is publicly visible

Licensing tiers

Power BI Free
 - Use Desktop, publish to My Workspace
 - Can't share with others
 - Can't access shared content from others

Power BI Pro (per user, monthly fee)
 - Share with other Pro users
 - Publish to workspaces
 - 1 GB dataset size limit
 - 8 scheduled refreshes / day
 - All standard features

Power BI Premium Per User (PPU)
 - Pro features + Premium capabilities at user level
 - 100 GB dataset size
 - 48 refreshes / day
 - Deployment pipelines, paginated reports
 - Both creator AND consumer need PPU

Power BI Premium Per Capacity
 - Dedicated capacity (P SKUs)
 - Pro license needed only for creators
 - Consumers can be FREE users
 - Best for: large orgs, many consumers
 - 400 GB dataset; AI features; XMLA endpoint

Microsoft Fabric:
 Premium capacity now part of Microsoft Fabric SKUs (F SKUs)
 Includes Power BI + Data Engineering + Data Science + Real-Time Analytics

Deployment pipelines (Premium)

Three environments per pipeline: Development → Test → Production
 Each is a separate workspace
 Pipeline manages promoting content from one to the next

Workflow:
 1. Build in Dev workspace
 2. Validate in Test (UAT users review)
 3. Promote to Production (consumers access via App)

Promotion includes:
 - Reports
 - Datasets
 - Dataflows
 - Datamarts

Configurable:
 Dataset rules (e.g., change connection string per environment)
 Deployment history audit

Premium-only feature
For non-Premium: manual export/import or third-party tools

Endorsement — Promoted vs Certified

Endorsement is a quality signal on shared datasets / reports

Levels:
 None — default
 Promoted — marked by content owner; "this is good for use"
 Certified — marked by data steward / admin; gold standard for the org

Setup:
 Dataset → Settings → Endorsement
 Admin tenant settings control who can certify

Why use:
 Many self-service users build redundant datasets
 Endorsement helps users find the AUTHORITATIVE source
 Certified datasets appear at the top of the data hub
 Promoted is informal; Certified requires governance approval

Power BI tenant admin features

Power BI Admin portal (app.powerbi.com/admin-portal):
 Tenant settings (global org policies)
 Usage metrics (who views what; how often)
 Audit logs (export to log analytics)
 Data sources gateway management
 Capacity settings (Premium / PPU)
 Custom branding (logo, colors for the tenant)

Common tenant settings:
 Export to Excel: allowed or restricted
 Publish to web: usually restricted
 External sharing: B2B guest access
 Workspace creation: who can create workspaces
 Custom visuals: marketplace allowed or curated only

Common service mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Publishing to My Workspace — not shareable; use a workspace instead
  2. Sharing reports individually — use apps for scale; sharing tab for ad-hoc only
  3. Forgetting to set the gateway for on-prem data — refresh fails
  4. Pro license for everyone when Premium-per-Capacity would be cheaper at scale
  5. Building 5 separate datasets for similar reports — use 1 shared dataset
  6. Manual report copies across workspaces — use deployment pipelines
  7. No endorsement on key datasets — users build duplicates
  8. Publishing to web with confidential data — major data leak risk
  9. RLS not tested after publishing — Service has separate "View as role" tool
  10. Forgetting incremental refresh on large datasets — refresh times explode
★ ON THE EXAM

"Publish from Desktop?" → Home → Publish → choose workspace.

"Where to collaborate?" → Workspace (not My Workspace).

"Wide read-only distribution?" → App.

"Workspace roles?" → Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer.

"On-prem data source refresh?" → On-premises data gateway.

"Pro vs Premium per Capacity?" → Pro per user; Premium capacity dedicates compute.

"Free users consume Premium reports?" → Yes, on Premium capacity (not PPU).

"Three-environment promotion?" → Deployment pipelines (Premium).

"Trusted dataset marker?" → Certified endorsement.

"Multiple reports on same data?" → Shared dataset (Get data → Power BI datasets).

"Scheduled refresh limit Pro?" → 8 per day.

"Scheduled refresh limit Premium?" → 48 per day.

"View as role?" → Service: Workspace → Dataset → Security → Test as role.

"Update app?" → Workspace → Update app button (republishes to consumers).

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Power BI Desktop builds reports; Service publishes, shares, and refreshes them
  • Workspaces are collaborative containers; My Workspace is personal sandbox
  • Workspace roles: Admin (full), Member (publish + share), Contributor (publish only), Viewer (read-only)
  • Publish reports via Home → Publish in Desktop
  • Datasets can be shared across multiple reports — single source of truth
  • Refresh: Pro = 8/day, Premium = 48/day; Import requires refresh, DirectQuery doesn't
  • On-premises data needs the On-Premises Data Gateway
  • Apps publish curated read-only content for consumers; preferred for wide distribution
  • Sharing methods: workspace access, app, direct share, embed in Teams, publish to web
  • Pro license per user; Premium per Capacity lets Free users consume
  • Premium Per User (PPU) gives Premium features at user level (both sides need PPU)
  • Deployment pipelines (Premium): Dev → Test → Prod environments
  • Endorsement: Promoted (informal) or Certified (governance-approved)
  • Test RLS in Service via "View as role" before going live
  • Tenant admin portal controls cross-org policies and capacity

Dashboard design rules: establish visual hierarchy — the most important metric is biggest and top-left, where eyes land first. Chart titles should state the takeaway ("Revenue grew 30% in Q3"), not just the label ("Revenue"). Order pages so the reader sees the summary first, then dives into detail. And pie charts work best with only 2–3 slices showing parts of a whole — beyond that, use a bar chart.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Row-Level Security (RLS) restricts which rows users can see based on their identity. One report, many users, each seeing only their own data. The PL-300 exam tests static vs dynamic RLS, USERPRINCIPALNAME, and testing roles in both Desktop and Service.

What RLS does

RLS = Row-Level Security
 - Applied at dataset level
 - Restricts which rows users see in their reports
 - Same report; different users see different data
 - Filters happen at query time (Service)

Example:
 Dataset: Sales (rows for all regions)
 User Alice (region=East) → sees only East rows
 User Bob (region=West) → sees only West rows
 User Carol (admin) → sees all rows

Without RLS:
 Every user sees every row regardless of identity
 Filter pane / slicer doesn't enforce security — users can clear filters

Static RLS — hardcoded role per region

Setup in Desktop:
 Modeling tab → Manage roles → Create
 Name: "East Region"
 Choose table to filter: Sales
 DAX filter: [Region] = "East"

 Create more roles: "West Region", "North Region", etc.

Assign users to roles in Service:
 Workspace → Dataset → Security
 For each role, add users / groups (Azure AD)
 Example:
 East Region role → alice@company.com, east-team@company.com
 West Region role → bob@company.com

When Alice opens the report:
 Power BI evaluates her role assignments
 Applies the role's DAX filter
 She only sees East rows

Pros:
 Simple to set up for < 10 roles
Cons:
 Manual user assignment per role
 Tedious with many regions / categories
 No flexibility for dynamic team membership

Dynamic RLS — single role, DAX-driven filter

DYNAMIC RLS PATTERN
Instead of one role per region, ONE role with a DAX filter that uses the LOGGED-IN USER'S identity.

USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the logged-in user's email (e.g., alice@company.com)
Use it to look up that user's permissions in a security table. 
Step 1: Add a security table
 Columns: UserEmail, AllowedRegion
 Examples:
 alice@company.com | East
 bob@company.com | West
 carol@company.com | East
 carol@company.com | West

Step 2: Build the relationship
 UserSecurity[AllowedRegion] → Sales[Region]
 Direction: depending on model — often bidirectional or unidirectional

Step 3: Single role with dynamic filter
 Modeling → Manage roles → "Region Access"
 Apply filter to UserSecurity table:
 [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

 When user logs in:
 USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns their email
 Filters UserSecurity to their row(s)
 Filter propagates via relationship to Sales
 They see only allowed regions

Step 4: Assign role to users in Service
 Workspace → Dataset → Security → Region Access role
 Add: "All Users" group (entire org)
 Each user gets filtered based on their email automatically

Pros:
 Single role; scales to thousands of users
 Update security table to change permissions; no role change
Cons:
 More complex setup
 Requires security table maintenance

USERPRINCIPALNAME vs USERNAME

FunctionReturns
USERPRINCIPALNAME()Email address (e.g., alice@company.com) — most common for RLS
USERNAME()Older: Desktop returns DOMAIN\user; Service returns email (varies)

Use USERPRINCIPALNAME() for consistent behavior across Desktop and Service.

Testing RLS

In Desktop:
 Modeling → View as
 - Other user: type any email to simulate
 - Other role: choose a role to apply
 - Combine: both at once

A banner appears showing the current "view as" state
Click "Stop viewing" to clear

In Service (after publishing):
 Workspace → Dataset → Security
 Click ... on a role → Test as role
 Opens the report applied with that role's filter
 Type "View as other user" to simulate dynamic RLS for a specific email

Why test BOTH:
 Desktop catches DAX errors
 Service catches issues that only appear in real environment (group memberships, etc.)

Static + Dynamic combined — flexible permissions

Pattern: dynamic regions + a hardcoded admin role

Role 1: "Regional User" (dynamic)
 Filter on UserSecurity: [UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
 All non-admin users go here

Role 2: "Admin" (no filter — sees everything)
 No filter expression at all (empty Filter DAX)
 Or use: TRUE()
 Sees all rows

In Service:
 Add user to BOTH roles → OR logic; sees both filters combined (effectively unrestricted)
 Just regional → sees their region only
 Just admin → sees everything

Role union behavior

★ MULTIPLE ROLES = UNION

When a user is assigned to multiple roles, Power BI takes the UNION of accessible rows (OR logic).

  • Role A: Region = East
  • Role B: Region = West
  • User in both → sees East OR West (not intersection)

This is the opposite of database row-level security in some systems. Plan for it.

Object-Level Security (OLS) — bonus

RLS restricts ROWS; OLS restricts COLUMNS / TABLES

Use case: HR data with Salary column
 All employees see employees table
 Only HR sees Salary column

Setup:
 Cannot be done in Desktop UI (as of writing)
 Use Tabular Editor (external tool):
 Connect to model
 Set [Salary].ObjectLevelSecurity = "None" for OLS roles
 Assign role in Service

Behavior:
 Users in restricted role: column is HIDDEN; queries error if referenced
 Other users: column visible as normal

Less common than RLS; included on PL-300 occasionally

Worked example — building dynamic RLS

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Region-level RLS
// Step 1: Source security table (in Excel, SQL, or Power Query)
// UserSecurity:
// UserEmail AllowedRegion
// alice@company.com East
// alice@company.com West (Alice covers two regions)
// bob@company.com West
// carol@company.com East
// manager@company.com East
// manager@company.com West
// manager@company.com North
// manager@company.com South

// Step 2: Load into Power BI; create relationship
// UserSecurity[AllowedRegion] → Sales[Region]
// Direction: Single (UserSecurity filters Sales)
// Cardinality: Many-to-Many or 1-Many depending on data

// Step 3: Create role
// Modeling → Manage roles → Create
// Name: "Regional Access"
// Table: UserSecurity
// DAX:
[UserEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

// Step 4: Test in Desktop
// Modeling → View as
// ☑ Other user → alice@company.com
// ☑ Other role → Regional Access
// Report now shows East and West (Alice's regions)

// Test as bob@company.com → only West
// Test as carol@company.com → only East
// Test as manager@company.com → all four regions

// Step 5: Publish and assign in Service
// Workspace → Dataset → Security → Regional Access role
// Add: "All Employees" Azure AD group
// Save

// Each user opening the report sees only their permitted regions
// Update the security table → permissions update on next refresh

Common RLS mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Forgetting USERPRINCIPALNAME() function — without it, dynamic filter doesn't know who's logged in
  2. Wrong relationship direction — security table doesn't filter fact table
  3. Testing only in Desktop — Service may behave differently with real groups
  4. Forgetting to add users to role in Service — RLS does nothing if role has no members
  5. Assuming roles intersect — they UNION; multiple roles widens access
  6. Admin role with weird filter instead of empty/TRUE → admins lose access
  7. RLS on imported data but not on DirectQuery — confused security model
  8. Hardcoded email in DAX instead of USERPRINCIPALNAME() — security breaks for everyone else
  9. Security table not refreshed — permissions stale
  10. RLS only applies to viewers in Service — workspace contributors and admins can still see everything
★ ON THE EXAM

"RLS scope?" → Restricts ROWS based on user identity.

"Static RLS?" → One role per access group; manual user assignment.

"Dynamic RLS?" → One role using USERPRINCIPALNAME() against a security table.

"Current user email?" → USERPRINCIPALNAME().

"USERNAME vs USERPRINCIPALNAME?" → USERPRINCIPALNAME for cross-environment consistency.

"Test in Desktop?" → Modeling → View as → choose role / user.

"Test in Service?" → Workspace → Dataset → Security → Test as role.

"Multiple roles for one user?" → UNION; user sees combined accessible rows.

"Admin role with no filter?" → Sees all rows; no DAX or TRUE().

"Where to assign users to roles?" → Power BI Service: Dataset → Security.

"Object-Level Security (OLS)?" → Restricts columns/tables; needs Tabular Editor.

"Workspace admin sees RLS-filtered data?" → No, RLS applies to Viewers; Admin/Member see all.

"Dynamic security table?" → User → Region mapping; relationship filters fact.

"Doesn't update permissions?" → Refresh the security table; check refresh schedule.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • RLS restricts which rows users see based on their identity
  • Set up in Desktop: Modeling → Manage roles → DAX filter expression
  • Assign users to roles in Service: Workspace → Dataset → Security
  • Static RLS: hardcode the filter per role (e.g., Region = "East")
  • Dynamic RLS: use USERPRINCIPALNAME() against a security table
  • USERPRINCIPALNAME returns the logged-in user's email — same in Desktop and Service
  • Test in Desktop: View as → role + other user
  • Test in Service: Workspace → Dataset → Security → Test as role
  • Multiple role assignments take UNION (OR logic) — user sees combined rows
  • Admin role: no filter or TRUE() → sees all rows
  • RLS applies to Viewers; workspace Members and Admins still see everything
  • Update the security table to change permissions — no role config needed
  • OLS (Object-Level Security) restricts columns / tables; requires Tabular Editor
  • Relationship direction matters — security table must filter the fact table
  • Refresh the security table regularly or permissions go stale

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Reports are interactive deep dives; dashboards are at-a-glance summaries from multiple sources. Subscriptions and alerts make Power BI proactive — pushing information to users without them logging in. The PL-300 exam tests pinning tiles, creating dashboards, subscriptions, and data alerts.

Reports vs dashboards

ReportsDashboards
Built in Power BI DesktopBuilt in Power BI Service only
Multiple pages; interactiveSingle page
One dataset per reportTiles from many reports/datasets
Filters, slicers, drillthroughNo interactive filters; tiles link back to reports
Bookmarks, buttons, themesLayout free-form
Detailed analysisAt-a-glance overview

Creating a dashboard

In Power BI Service:
 1. Open a report
 2. Hover a visual → click pin icon
 3. Choose existing dashboard or create new
 4. Visual becomes a "tile" on the dashboard

Pin from multiple reports:
 Same dashboard can have tiles from different reports / datasets
 Unifies content across data sources

Pin live page:
 Pin → Live page (instead of single visual)
 Whole page appears on dashboard
 Stays in sync with the report

Tile types on a dashboard:
 - Pinned visuals (from reports)
 - Web content (HTML iframe)
 - Image
 - Text box
 - Video (YouTube, Vimeo)
 - Custom streaming data (real-time tiles)

Dashboard layout and interaction

Tiles are draggable + resizable on a grid

Click a tile → opens the underlying report
 - Tile details (in three-dot menu): change link to a different report page
 - Or to a custom URL

Dashboard theme:
 Edit dashboard → Dashboard theme
 Built-in themes; or custom JSON
 Affects tile borders, title fonts, background

Dashboard view modes:
 Web — standard
 Phone — separate mobile layout (also configurable)

Featured dashboard:
 One per user; shown by default in home page
 Set: dashboard → ... → Set as featured dashboard

Favorites:
 Star any report / dashboard / app to add to Favorites tab

Q&A on dashboards

Dashboards have a built-in Q&A search box at top
 User types natural language → Power BI generates a visual
 Backed by the dashboard's tiled datasets

Q&A pinning:
 Ask Q&A → click pin → adds answer as a new tile

Q&A setup (per dataset):
 Power BI Service → Dataset → Q&A → Q&A setup
 - Field synonyms
 - Suggest questions
 - Promoted searches
 - Train Q&A on common requests
 - Review questions (logged queries)

Subscriptions — email automation

Email yourself (or others) regular snapshots of a report or dashboard

Setup:
 Report / Dashboard → Subscribe (envelope icon)
 - Subject (default: report name)
 - Frequency: Daily / Weekly / Hourly / Monthly / After data refresh
 - Time of day
 - Time zone
 - Subscribers: add recipients (org users only by default)
 - Optional: include a link to the report
 - Optional: attach as PDF (Pro), full report PDF (Premium)

Limits:
 Pro: 24 subscriptions per user
 Premium: unlimited

What gets sent:
 - Snapshot image of the report page or dashboard
 - Click-through link to live report
 - PDF attachment (if configured)

After-data-refresh trigger:
 Only available for Premium / PPU
 Sends only when dataset refreshes successfully
 Avoids stale snapshots when refresh fails

Data alerts on dashboards

Alert when a single value crosses a threshold

Only works on:
 Card, Gauge, KPI tiles on dashboards
 (Not on full reports; only the tile types listed)

Setup:
 Hover a tile → "..." → Manage alerts → Add alert rule
 - Condition: Above / Below
 - Threshold: numeric value
 - Frequency: at most once an hour / every 24 hours
 - ☑ Send email too

Trigger:
 Power BI checks the tile after every data refresh
 If condition met → push notification + optional email

Use cases:
 - "Alert when daily sales fall below $10,000"
 - "Alert when error count exceeds 50"
 - "Alert when inventory drops below safety stock"

Integration with Power Automate:
 Alert → "Use Microsoft Power Automate to trigger additional actions"
 Trigger workflow: send Teams message, create JIRA ticket, etc.

Sharing dashboards

Same options as sharing reports:
 Workspace access (collaborators)
 Apps (curated package; preferred for wide distribution)
 Direct share (one-off)
 Embed in Teams or SharePoint

Permissions:
 Viewers can interact with tiles, drillthrough, but not edit
 Contributors can edit the dashboard

Dashboard URL:
 Each dashboard has a unique URL
 Send directly (recipient needs access)

Mobile dashboards

Configure mobile layout separately from desktop view

Service → Dashboard → Edit (...) → Phone view
 Reorder tiles for portrait phone
 Hide tiles not relevant on mobile

Power BI Mobile app:
 - Phone-optimized view auto-shown
 - Pinch to zoom
 - Tap tile → opens underlying report
 - Offline cached view (some configurations)
 - Annotations and sharing from mobile

Real-time dashboards (streaming datasets)

For live updating dashboards (IoT, server health, social monitoring):

Streaming dataset types:
 Push — push data via REST API; data stored
 Streaming — push data; not stored (only displayed)
 PubNub — connect to PubNub real-time data network

Setup:
 Workspace → Create → Streaming dataset
 Define schema (columns, types)
 Get API endpoint or PubNub key
 Send data via Power Automate / custom script / Azure Stream Analytics

Create real-time tile:
 Dashboard → Add tile → Real-time data
 Pick streaming dataset; choose visual type

Tile updates with each push (no refresh needed)
Sub-second latency typical

Common pipeline:
 IoT device → Azure IoT Hub → Stream Analytics → Power BI streaming dataset → Dashboard

Common dashboard mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Creating a dashboard with 30+ tiles — defeats the purpose; use multiple dashboards
  2. Pinning every report visual — pin only the most important
  3. Forgetting that dashboards aren't interactive like reports
  4. Setting alert frequency too aggressive — every alert = email; spam
  5. Subscriptions to many recipients with PDF — Premium-only for full report PDF
  6. Mobile layout not configured — desktop tiles look bad on phone
  7. Q&A not trained — fields with technical names like "tbl_dim_cust" produce weird answers
  8. Mixing dashboards with reports in user expectations — explain the difference
  9. Streaming dashboards without data quality — anomalies trigger false alerts
  10. Privacy: dashboards via direct share bypass app permission structure
★ ON THE EXAM

"Dashboards built where?" → Power BI Service only.

"Reports built where?" → Power BI Desktop.

"Multiple datasets on one dashboard?" → Yes — pin tiles from many reports.

"Dashboard pages?" → Just one (no multi-page dashboards).

"Pin a visual?" → Hover visual → pin icon → choose dashboard.

"Pin a whole page?" → Pin Live page.

"Q&A on dashboard?" → Built-in search bar; pin answers as tiles.

"Subscription frequencies?" → Daily, Weekly, Hourly, Monthly, After data refresh.

"Alert tile types?" → Card, Gauge, KPI only.

"Alert frequency?" → At most once an hour / 24 hours.

"Trigger external actions on alert?" → Power Automate integration.

"Real-time data?" → Streaming dataset (Push / Streaming / PubNub).

"Mobile layout?" → Edit dashboard → Phone view.

"Subscription limit Pro?" → 24 per user.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Reports are built in Desktop and have multiple pages with interactivity
  • Dashboards are built in Service, single page, pinned tiles from many sources
  • Pin visuals to dashboards via the pin icon when hovering
  • Pin live page to mirror an entire report page
  • Q&A search bar at top of dashboard answers natural-language questions
  • Subscriptions email regular snapshots: daily, weekly, hourly, monthly, after refresh
  • Alerts trigger only on Card, Gauge, KPI tiles when a threshold is crossed
  • Alerts fire at most once an hour / 24 hours and can send email + push notification
  • Power Automate integrates alerts with external systems (Teams, ticketing, custom workflows)
  • Streaming datasets enable real-time tiles (IoT, monitoring) with sub-second updates
  • Mobile dashboards have a separate layout configured in Service
  • Dashboards share the same permission model as reports — workspace, app, or direct share
  • Tiles link back to the underlying report on click
  • Premium adds: After-refresh subscriptions, unlimited subscriptions, full-report PDF
  • Limit dashboards to ~10-15 key tiles for at-a-glance value

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When the same data prep logic appears in multiple reports, copying it everywhere creates a maintenance nightmare. Dataflows and datamarts let you build ETL ONCE and reuse it across the organization. The PL-300 exam tests dataflow creation, linked vs computed entities, and the difference between dataflows and datamarts.

The problem they solve

Without dataflows:
 Report A imports Sales CSV, cleans columns, joins to customers
 Report B does the SAME data prep + adds product info
 Report C copies all of that + handles new fields

Problems:
 - Logic duplicated 3 times
 - Bug fix in column rename → fix in 3 places (or forget one)
 - Each report re-runs prep on refresh (slow)
 - No single source of truth

With dataflows:
 Dataflow has the cleaning logic ONCE
 Reports A, B, C all consume the SAME dataflow output
 Refresh the dataflow → all reports see fresh, prepped data
 Fix a bug in dataflow → all reports update next refresh

What dataflows are

Dataflow = collection of entities (tables) built in Power Query Online
 - Lives in a workspace (not the .pbix file)
 - Built in the browser; no Desktop needed
 - Output stored in Azure Data Lake Gen2 (managed by Power BI)
 - Refresh on a schedule (independent of report refresh)

Tech under the hood:
 - Power Query (M language) for transformations
 - Same M as Power BI Desktop, with browser UI
 - Common Data Model (CDM) format for storage
 - Reusable from Power BI, Excel, Power Automate, Azure Synapse

Use cases:
 - Centralize ETL for many reports
 - Build a semantic layer for the organization
 - Pre-aggregate large data
 - Reusable date dimensions, security tables, master data

Creating a dataflow

Power BI Service:
 Workspace → New → Dataflow
 Options:
 Define new tables — start from scratch
 Linked tables from other dataflows — reuse another dataflow's tables
 Computed tables — build on existing dataflow tables (Premium)
 Import model — from another dataflow / .pq file

Build:
 Add new tables → choose source (similar to Power BI Desktop Get data)
 Power Query Online editor opens (familiar interface)
 Apply transformations (filter, rename, merge, etc.)
 Save and refresh

Each table = entity in the dataflow
Entity stored in CDM format

Consuming a dataflow in a report

Power BI Desktop:
 Get data → Power Platform → Dataflows
 Sign in to your workspace
 Choose dataflow → entity → Load

Benefits:
 - Skip all the data prep work (already done in dataflow)
 - Just build the model and visuals
 - Refresh: report refresh hits dataflow (fast), then dataflow refreshes from source (separately)

Two-level refresh:
 Dataflow refresh — pulls from source, applies transformations, writes to Data Lake
 Dataset refresh — pulls from dataflow output (fast)

Linked vs computed entities

TypeMeaningLicense
Linked entityReference to another dataflow's table (read-only)Pro / Premium
Computed entityNew entity built on top of linked entitiesPremium / PPU only
 
Example architecture:

Bronze dataflow (raw, just from source)
 - Customers_raw
 - Orders_raw

Silver dataflow (cleaned, deduped)
 - Customers_clean (linked entity from Bronze)
 - Orders_clean (linked entity from Bronze)

Gold dataflow (business-ready)
 - Customer360 (computed entity joining Silver tables; Premium)
 - Sales_Monthly (computed entity aggregating Orders)

Reports consume Gold layer
 - No raw cleaning logic in any report
 - Each layer can be refreshed independently
 - Common in medallion architecture (Microsoft Fabric)

Incremental refresh in dataflows

For large fact tables, don't refresh the entire entity every time

Setup (Premium / PPU):
 Dataflow → entity → Incremental refresh
 - Date/datetime column
 - Store data from past N years
 - Refresh data from past M days (typically much smaller than store)

Example:
 Store: 5 years of data
 Refresh: last 30 days

On each refresh:
 Only last 30 days re-queried from source
 Older data stays in dataflow storage
 Massive speed improvement for large fact tables

Limitations:
 Requires Premium / PPU
 Date column needed
 Source must support query folding (most databases do)

Datamarts — a step above dataflows

Datamart = dataflow + auto-generated SQL database + auto-generated dataset
 All in one Power BI Service workspace
 Premium / PPU only

Components (auto-managed):
 Dataflow — ETL layer
 Azure SQL Database — relational store (no SQL admin needed)
 Power BI dataset — analytical model

Capabilities:
 - SQL endpoint: query the underlying database from any SQL tool
 - Auto-generated dataset: Q&A and reports work out of the box
 - DirectQuery and Import both supported
 - Built-in measures and security

When to use a datamart vs dataflow:
 Dataflow: just ETL output for downstream Power BI use
 Datamart: ETL + SQL queryable + ready-to-use dataset — for self-service BI

Datamarts are positioned for departmental teams wanting a no-SQL relational backend

Dataflows vs datasets vs datamarts — comparison

ObjectPurposeBuilt with
DataflowReusable ETL output (tables)Power Query Online
DatasetSemantic model with relationships and DAX measuresPower BI Desktop (or Service modeling tools)
DatamartDataflow + SQL DB + Dataset, self-containedPower BI Service (browser-based)

Common dataflow architectures

PATTERN 1: simple shared source
 One dataflow with cleaned tables
 → Multiple reports consume it
 → Single source of truth for those reports

PATTERN 2: layered (Bronze/Silver/Gold; medallion)
 Bronze: raw extract
 Silver: cleaned, typed
 Gold: business-ready, aggregated
 → Reports consume Gold; auditors / advanced users can drop to Silver

PATTERN 3: standardized dimensions
 Date dimension dataflow
 Customer dimension dataflow
 Product dimension dataflow
 Each report combines these with its own fact data
 → Conformed dimensions across the organization

PATTERN 4: pre-aggregated for performance
 Dataflow with daily/monthly summaries
 Reports query small aggregate tables, not raw transactions
 → Sub-second query response on large datasets

Worked example — shared customer dataflow

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Build & consume a dataflow
// Step 1: Create dataflow in Power BI Service
// Workspace → New → Dataflow → Define new tables

// Source: Azure SQL Database
// Table: Customers
// Apply Power Query transformations:
// - Trim and uppercase email column
// - Filter out inactive accounts (status != 'cancelled')
// - Add full_name = FirstName & " " & LastName
// - Rename columns to BI-friendly names
// - Set data types explicitly

// Save dataflow as "Customers_Clean"
// Set refresh schedule: daily 6:00 AM

// Step 2: Consume in Power BI Desktop
// Open Power BI Desktop
// Get Data → Power Platform → Dataflows → sign in
// Select workspace → "Customers_Clean" dataflow → Customers entity
// Load (or Transform Data for further customization)

// Now Customers table is in the model — already cleaned, fast to refresh

// Step 3: Multiple reports
// Sales Report → also Get Data → Dataflows → same Customers_Clean
// Marketing Report → same
// Each report uses the same customer table
// Fix a bug in dataflow → all three reports get the fix on next refresh

// Step 4: Add a computed entity (Premium)
// Workspace → New → Dataflow → "Customer Summary"
// Link Customers_Clean as a linked entity
// Add computed entity:
// Customer_LTV = group by customer_id, sum(order_total)
// This computed entity is pre-aggregated, faster to query

// Reports can now use Customer_LTV directly instead of computing it themselves

Dataflow refresh and gateways

Refresh:
 Dataflow → Settings → Schedule refresh
 Configure frequency (8 daily for Pro, 48 for Premium per dataflow)

Gateway (for on-prem sources):
 Same gateway used by datasets also serves dataflows
 Configure gateway connection in dataflow settings

Common workflow:
 Source DB → On-prem gateway → Dataflow (cleansed) → Dataset (modeled) → Reports

Refresh dependencies:
 Best practice: schedule dataflow refresh BEFORE dataset refresh
 Otherwise dataset pulls yesterday's dataflow data
 Use Power Automate to chain refreshes if needed

Common dataflow mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Building a dataflow with just one downstream report — overkill; keep it in the report
  2. Forgetting to schedule dataflow refresh — datasets pull stale data
  3. Dataflow refresh after dataset refresh — dataset uses yesterday's prep
  4. Trying computed entities on Pro — Premium-only
  5. Mixing Bronze/Silver/Gold in one dataflow — layered architecture loses clarity
  6. Not using incremental refresh on large fact tables — full refresh = hours
  7. Forgetting that consumers need access to dataflow's workspace
  8. Confusing datamart with dataflow — datamart adds SQL DB + dataset; dataflow doesn't
  9. Building complex DAX in dataflows — dataflows are M (Power Query), not DAX
  10. Naming entities ambiguously — "Customers" vs "Customers_Clean" vs "CRM_Customers"
★ ON THE EXAM

"Dataflow built with?" → Power Query Online (browser).

"Dataset built with?" → Power BI Desktop (or web modeling).

"Reuse ETL across reports?" → Dataflow.

"Dataflow output stored where?" → Azure Data Lake Gen2 (managed).

"Linked entity?" → Reference to a dataflow table; read-only.

"Computed entity?" → Built on linked entity; Premium / PPU only.

"Datamart?" → Dataflow + SQL DB + dataset, all in one Service workspace; Premium.

"Dataflow + dataset refresh order?" → Dataflow first; dataset second.

"Incremental refresh in dataflow?" → Premium / PPU; date column required.

"Connect Desktop to a dataflow?" → Get data → Power Platform → Dataflows.

"Where do dataflows live?" → In a Power BI workspace.

"M vs DAX in dataflows?" → M (Power Query) for transformations; not DAX.

"Medallion architecture?" → Bronze (raw) → Silver (clean) → Gold (business-ready).

"Datamart SQL endpoint?" → Yes; can query with any SQL tool.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Dataflows are reusable ETL output entities; build once, consume in many reports
  • Built in Power Query Online (browser-based); same M language as Power BI Desktop
  • Live in a Power BI workspace; output stored in Azure Data Lake Gen2
  • Reports connect via Get data → Power Platform → Dataflows
  • Linked entities: reference another dataflow's tables (Pro / Premium)
  • Computed entities: build new entities on top of linked ones (Premium / PPU only)
  • Medallion architecture: Bronze (raw) → Silver (clean) → Gold (business-ready)
  • Incremental refresh in dataflows requires Premium and a date column
  • Schedule dataflow refresh BEFORE dataset refresh — otherwise datasets pull stale data
  • Power Automate can chain refresh dependencies
  • Datamarts add a SQL database and auto-generated dataset on top of a dataflow — Premium / PPU only
  • Datamart SQL endpoint lets non-Power-BI users query via standard SQL tools
  • Use dataflows when ≥ 2 reports share the same data prep logic
  • Dataflows use M for transformations; datasets use DAX for measures and calculations
  • Common patterns: shared dimensions, layered medallion, pre-aggregated for performance

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Power BI excels at interactive dashboards, but operational reports (invoices, contracts, perfectly-formatted PDFs) need pixel-precise layouts and exact pagination. That's paginated reports — built in Power BI Report Builder. The PL-300 exam tests when to use paginated reports vs interactive reports.

When to use paginated reports

Use casePower BI reportPaginated report
Interactive dashboard✓ BestLimited interactivity
Multi-page printableSingle page only✓ Best
Invoices, contracts, certificatesWrong tool✓ Best
Operational lists (e.g., 10K-row exports)Slow / impossible✓ Best
Email subscriptions (PDF)Snapshot only✓ Full report PDF
Exploratory analytics✓ BestNo

Power BI Report Builder

Power BI Report Builder = the authoring tool for paginated reports
 Free download from Microsoft
 Separate from Power BI Desktop
 Saves files as .rdl (Report Definition Language; XML)

Origin: Power BI inherited paginated reports from SQL Server Reporting Services (SSRS)
 Same .rdl file format works in SSRS, Power BI Service (Premium), Report Server

Interface:
 Report Data pane (left): data sources, datasets, parameters, fields
 Design surface (center): drag report items
 Properties pane (right): per-element configuration

Report items:
 - Table — tabular list, rows expand as data does
 - Matrix — pivot-style with row/column groups
 - List — free-form repeated layout (e.g., one card per customer)
 - Chart — column, line, pie, etc.
 - Gauge — progress indicators
 - Map — Bing maps integration
 - Image / Text — static elements
 - Rectangle — group containers

Page layout

Page is fixed size (e.g., Letter, A4)
Content flows from top to bottom, repeats across pages

Page parts:
 Page header — appears on every page (often with logo, title, page number)
 Page body — main content
 Page footer — appears on every page (often with timestamp, page X of Y)

Multiple body sections via:
 Rectangles → group related items
 Lists → repeat layout per record
 Subreports → embed another .rdl

Pagination:
 Tablix (table/matrix) breaks automatically across pages when content exceeds page
 Force page break: properties → PageBreak → Start / End / StartAndEnd

Print preview to verify layout

Data sources and datasets

Data source: connection to a database or service
 SQL Server, Azure SQL, Oracle, Power BI dataset (Premium feature)
 Connection string + credentials

Dataset: a query against a data source
 T-SQL, MDX, DAX (when connected to Power BI dataset)
 Returns a result set of fields

Multiple datasets per report common:
 - Main dataset for the report body
 - Lookup datasets for parameters
 - Subreport datasets

DAX as query language:
 Reports connected to Power BI dataset use DAX queries
 EVALUATE table_expression
 Or:
 EVALUATE
 SUMMARIZECOLUMNS(
 Date[Year],
 "Total Sales", [Total Sales]
 )

Parameters

Parameters let users customize the report at runtime

Examples:
 Start Date / End Date — filter date range
 Region — single-select or multi-select
 Customer Group — dropdown

Setup:
 Report Data pane → Parameters → Add Parameter
 - Name
 - Data type (Text, Integer, Date/Time, Boolean)
 - Allow multiple values
 - Allow blank / null
 - Default value
 - Available values (hardcoded or from a dataset query)

Reference in queries:
 WHERE OrderDate >= @StartDate AND OrderDate <= @EndDate
 (T-SQL uses @ParamName)

In DAX queries:
 FILTER(Sales, Sales[Date] >= @StartDate)

Cascading parameters:
 Region depends on Country (Region values filtered to Country's regions)
 Set up via "Get values from a query" + parameter reference

Subscriptions for paginated reports

Service feature: schedule paginated reports for email delivery

Output formats:
 PDF — most common
 Excel
 CSV
 PowerPoint
 Word
 XML

Schedule:
 Same options as regular subscriptions (daily, weekly, etc.)
 With parameter overrides: send different versions to different people

Premium / PPU required for paginated reports in service

Common pattern:
 Daily PDF of yesterday's sales sent to leadership
 Filtered by region; one email per regional manager
 Parameter binding to user's region (via email lookup)

Sample paginated report — sales by region

Layout:
 Page Header:
 [Company Logo] | "Sales Report" | "Generated: " & Globals!ExecutionTime

 Page Body:
 "Sales for region: " & Parameters!Region.Value (text box)

 Tablix (matrix):
 Row groups: Product Category, Product Name
 Column groups: Month
 Data: Sum(Sales)
 Subtotals at each level

 Chart:
 Bar chart of top 10 products

 Page Footer:
 "Page " & Globals!PageNumber & " of " & Globals!TotalPages

 Total: print-ready document, runs cleanly across many pages

Compared to interactive Power BI

AspectPower BI reportPaginated report
File extension.pbix.rdl
Built inPower BI DesktopPower BI Report Builder
PaginationSingle page (scrollable)Multi-page; precise page breaks
InteractivityHigh (slicers, drill, cross-filter)Low (parameters only)
Data modelIn-memory (Vertipaq)Query-based per render
ExportSnapshot PDFFull PDF, Excel, Word
Best forAnalytical dashboardsOperational documents
LicenseProPremium / PPU (for service)

Hybrid pattern — link from Power BI to paginated

Common workflow:
 Power BI dashboard for daily exploration
 → user spots an interesting customer
 → drills through to paginated report for printable detail

Setup:
 Insert button on Power BI report
 Action: Report page (paginated)
 Pass parameters: Customer ID, Date range
 Paginated report opens filtered to those values
 User prints / downloads PDF

Best of both worlds: interactive analytics + operational reporting

Common paginated report mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Building paginated reports in Desktop — wrong tool; use Report Builder
  2. Using paginated for interactive analytics — wrong direction; use Power BI
  3. Forgetting Premium / PPU requirement for service hosting
  4. Hardcoding parameter values instead of using cascade datasets
  5. Not testing pagination — content cut off across pages
  6. Mixing fonts and styles — paginated reports look unprofessional fast
  7. Forgetting page header/footer for multi-page docs — no context across pages
  8. Large datasets without server-side filtering — slow rendering
  9. Forgetting parameters in subscriptions — sending same content to all recipients
  10. Not using subreports when same content repeats
★ ON THE EXAM

"Built in?" → Power BI Report Builder (separate tool).

"File format?" → .rdl (XML).

"Use for what?" → Pixel-perfect, multi-page, operational reports.

"Pagination?" → Built-in; content flows across pages.

"Service hosting requires?" → Premium / PPU.

"Origin?" → Inherited from SSRS (SQL Server Reporting Services).

"Output formats?" → PDF, Excel, CSV, Word, PowerPoint, XML.

"Parameters?" → Runtime user input; T-SQL @ syntax in queries.

"Cascading parameter?" → One parameter filters values of another.

"Drill from Power BI to paginated?" → Button with Action = Report page (paginated).

"Data source?" → SQL DB, Azure SQL, Power BI dataset, or others.

"Query language for Power BI dataset?" → DAX (with EVALUATE).

"Interactivity vs Power BI?" → Limited (parameters only) — meant for static output.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Paginated reports are built in Power BI Report Builder (separate from Desktop)
  • File format is .rdl (Report Definition Language; XML)
  • Inherited from SSRS; same .rdl files run in SSRS, Power BI Service (Premium), Report Server
  • Best for pixel-perfect, multi-page documents: invoices, contracts, operational lists
  • Page parts: Header (each page), Body (content), Footer (each page)
  • Report items: Table, Matrix (Tablix), List, Chart, Gauge, Map, Image, Text
  • Data sources support SQL Server, Azure SQL, Oracle, Power BI dataset, and more
  • DAX queries when connecting to Power BI datasets: EVALUATE table_expression
  • Parameters allow runtime user input; can cascade (one filters another)
  • Subscriptions support multiple output formats (PDF, Excel, Word, CSV, PowerPoint, XML)
  • Premium / PPU required to host paginated reports in Power BI Service
  • Hybrid pattern: drill from Power BI interactive report to paginated detail
  • Use paginated reports for "I need a printable PDF" requirements
  • Use Power BI reports for interactive exploration
  • Cascading parameters: dropdown values filtered by another parameter's selection

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most Power Query transformations can be done through the UI, but complex scenarios require dropping into M code directly. Understanding M unlocks custom transformations, query folding, and parameterized queries. The PL-300 exam tests basic M syntax recognition.

What M is

M = "Mashup Query Language"
 Case-sensitive
 Functional language (like JavaScript or Haskell)
 Used in Power Query (Power BI, Excel, Dataflows, Power Automate)

Where you encounter M:
 - Auto-generated when you click ribbon buttons
 - Formula bar (visible in PQE)
 - Advanced Editor (View → Advanced Editor)
 - Custom Column dialog
 - Custom functions

When to write M directly:
 - Logic too complex for the UI
 - Parameterizing queries
 - Building reusable functions
 - Performance tuning (controlling query folding)

The let / in structure

Every M query has this skeleton:

let
 Source = Csv.Document(File.Contents("data.csv")),
 Promoted = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source),
 Filtered = Table.SelectRows(Promoted, each [Status] = "Active"),
 Renamed = Table.RenameColumns(Filtered, {"OldName", "NewName"})
in
 Renamed

Anatomy:
 let — open scope
 Source = ... — step name = expression
 Promoted = ... — next step (references previous)
 ...
 in
 Renamed — final output (returns this value)

Each step is a named variable
Steps are EAGER (evaluated in order, results stored)
The IN clause returns one value

The Applied Steps pane shows the named steps from let/in
Rename steps for clarity:
 let
 LoadCSV = Csv.Document(...),
 PromoteHeaders = ...,
 FilterActive = ...,
 RenameToFriendly = ...
 in
 RenameToFriendly

Common M functions by category

DATA SOURCE
 Csv.Document(File.Contents("path"))
 Excel.Workbook(File.Contents("path"))
 Json.Document(Web.Contents("url"))
 Sql.Database("server", "db")
 Folder.Files("path")

TABLE
 Table.PromoteHeaders(table)
 Table.RemoveColumns(table, {"col1", "col2"})
 Table.SelectColumns(table, {"keep1", "keep2"})
 Table.RenameColumns(table, {{"old", "new"}})
 Table.SelectRows(table, each [col] = "value")
 Table.RemoveDuplicates(table, {"col"})
 Table.Sort(table, {{"col", Order.Ascending}})
 Table.AddColumn(table, "NewCol", each [Existing] * 2)
 Table.Group(table, {"groupCol"}, {{"sum", each List.Sum([value])}})
 Table.Combine({t1, t2, t3})
 Table.Join(left, "key", right, "key", JoinKind.Inner)
 Table.NestedJoin(left, {"key"}, right, {"key"}, "newCol", JoinKind.LeftOuter)
 Table.ExpandRecordColumn(table, "col", {"sub1", "sub2"})

TEXT
 Text.Trim(s), Text.Upper(s), Text.Lower(s), Text.Proper(s)
 Text.Start(s, n), Text.End(s, n), Text.Middle(s, start, n)
 Text.Replace(s, old, new), Text.Remove(s, {chars})
 Text.Split(s, separator)
 Text.Contains(s, pattern)
 Text.Length(s)

NUMBER
 Number.Abs(n), Number.Round(n, digits)
 Number.From(value), Number.ToText(n, format)

DATE
 Date.Year(d), Date.Month(d), Date.Day(d)
 Date.DayOfWeek(d), Date.WeekOfYear(d)
 Date.AddDays(d, n), Date.AddMonths(d, n)
 DateTime.LocalNow(), DateTime.FixedLocalNow()

LIST
 List.Sum(list), List.Average(list), List.Min(list), List.Max(list)
 List.Count(list), List.Distinct(list), List.Sort(list)
 List.Generate, List.Transform

RECORD
 [field1 = value1, field2 = value2]
 Record.Field(rec, "fieldName")

The each keyword

"each" is shorthand for a lambda (single-argument function)

Verbose:
 Table.SelectRows(Source, (row) => row[Status] = "Active")

Shorthand:
 Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Status] = "Active")

Inside an each expression:
 [ColumnName] refers to the current row's value of that column
 _ refers to the entire current row (record)

Example:
 Table.AddColumn(Source, "Doubled", each [Amount] * 2)
 Table.AddColumn(Source, "FullName", each [First] & " " & [Last])
 Table.AddColumn(Source, "FullRecord", each _ )

Custom functions

Define reusable functions in M

Method 1: Blank Query → Advanced Editor → write function
 (input1 as text, input2 as number) => let
 result = input1 & Text.From(input2)
 in
 result

Save as "ConcatTextNumber"
Call from any other query:
 let
 Step1 = ConcatTextNumber("Item ", 42) // "Item 42"
 in
 Step1

Method 2: Convert query to function with parameters
 Right-click query in Queries pane → Create Function
 Power BI generates input parameters from the query's M code

Use cases:
 - Apply same transformation to many tables
 - Loop through files in folder, applying function to each
 - Parameterize URL or query string

Folder-with-function pattern

When using the Folder connector + "Combine":
 Power BI auto-generates:
 1. A function (Transform Sample File) that loads ONE file
 2. A wrapper query that maps the function over all files in the folder

 You can edit the Transform Sample File function to add transformations
 All files get them automatically

Manual version:

 let
 Source = Folder.Files("C:\Data\Monthly"),
 Filtered = Table.SelectRows(Source, each Text.EndsWith([Name], ".csv")),
 AddTable = Table.AddColumn(Filtered, "Table", each LoadAndTransform([Content])),
 Combined = Table.Combine(AddTable[Table])
 in
 Combined

Where LoadAndTransform is a custom function loading one file's content

Query folding

★ QUERY FOLDING

When connected to a database, Power Query translates M operations into SQL and pushes them to the source.

Benefits:

  • Database does the heavy lifting (faster)
  • Power BI only retrieves the result, not the full table
  • Critical for performance on large data

Folding breaks when:

  • Custom M functions used
  • Some operations not translatable to SQL
  • Mixing sources without compatible privacy levels

Check folding: right-click a step → View Native Query (grayed out = folding broken)

Folding-friendly operations:
 Filter rows
 Select columns
 Group by
 Sort
 Most numeric / text functions
 Joins to other database tables

Folding-breaking operations:
 Custom M functions
 Index columns
 Some advanced text operations
 Joining to a non-database query

Best practice:
 Push folding-friendly operations EARLY in the query
 Defer folding-breaking ones to later
 Get the database to do as much as possible

Parameters in M

Manage parameters: Home → Manage Parameters → New Parameter

Common parameters:
 Server name (for switching Dev / Test / Prod)
 File path
 Start / end date
 Filter values

Reference in M:
 let
 Source = Sql.Database(ServerNameParam, DatabaseNameParam),
 Filtered = Table.SelectRows(Source, each [Date] >= StartDateParam)
 in
 Filtered

Where ServerNameParam, DatabaseNameParam, StartDateParam are parameter names

Templates (.pbit files):
 Pack the parameters into a template
 Other users open template → enter their values → personalized report

Error handling

try / otherwise:
 let
 Result = try Number.From([Value]) otherwise null
 in
 Result

 Returns Number.From if successful; null if it errors

In Table.AddColumn:
 Table.AddColumn(Source, "AmountClean",
 each try Number.From([Amount]) otherwise null)

Replace errors UI:
 Transform → Replace Errors → choose value

Keep error rows:
 Home → Keep Rows → Keep Errors (for debugging)

Remove error rows:
 Home → Remove Rows → Remove Errors

Worked example — clean a JSON API response

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Custom M function for API data
// Custom function: fetch and clean one page of API data
// Save as: GetSalesPage
//
// Function definition (in Advanced Editor):

(pageNum as number) => let
 // Build URL with parameter
 Source = Json.Document(
 Web.Contents(
 "https://api.example.com/sales",
 [
 Query = [page = Text.From(pageNum), limit = "100"]
 ]
 )
 ),

 // Extract data array from response
 Records = Source[data],

 // Convert to table
 Table = Table.FromList(Records, Splitter.SplitByNothing()),

 // Expand record fields
 Expanded = Table.ExpandRecordColumn(Table, "Column1",
 {"id", "date", "amount", "customer_id"},
 {"id", "date", "amount", "customer_id"}),

 // Set types
 Typed = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Expanded, {
 {"id", Int64.Type},
 {"date", type date},
 {"amount", type number},
 {"customer_id", Int64.Type}
 }),

 // Add page info
 WithPage = Table.AddColumn(Typed, "page", each pageNum)
in
 WithPage

// Now call this function for each page 1-10:

let
 PageList = {1..10},
 PageTables = List.Transform(PageList, each GetSalesPage(_)),
 AllSales = Table.Combine(PageTables)
in
 AllSales

Common M mistakes

⚠ TYPICAL ERRORS
  1. Case sensitivity — Table.SelectRows is different from table.selectrows
  2. Mixing M and DAX — they're different languages used in different places
  3. Putting heavy transformations late — breaks query folding
  4. Hardcoded server names instead of parameters — breaks across environments
  5. No error handling on type conversions — single bad row fails the whole query
  6. Using "each" but referencing wrong scope — _ is row; [Col] is column on row
  7. Building tables with row-by-row appending — incredibly slow; use Table.FromRecords or List.Transform
  8. Web.Contents in functions without proper auth — refresh fails in service
  9. Not viewing the M code when debugging — formula bar shows it
  10. Forgetting that PQ is functional — no for loops; use List.Transform / Table.AddColumn instead
★ ON THE EXAM

"M language used in?" → Power Query (Power BI, Excel, Dataflows).

"M case sensitive?" → Yes.

"Query skeleton?" → let ... in.

"Step name = ?" → A variable assignment; previous steps available by name.

"each keyword?" → Shorthand for lambda; [Col] references current row's column.

"Apply function to all files in folder?" → Folder connector + Transform Sample File.

"View underlying SQL?" → Right-click step → View Native Query.

"Query folding?" → M operations pushed down to source DB.

"Folding broken by?" → Custom functions, some operations, index columns.

"try / otherwise?" → Error handling expression.

"Parameter in M?" → Manage Parameters; reference by name.

"Custom function?" → (arg) => let ... in ....

"Json.Document?" → Parse JSON response.

"Table.ExpandRecordColumn?" → Flatten nested records into columns.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • M is the case-sensitive functional language used in Power Query
  • Every query has a let ... in structure with named steps
  • Each step is a variable; later steps reference earlier ones
  • The IN clause specifies what value the query returns
  • each is shorthand for a lambda; [ColumnName] refers to current row's column
  • Common categories: Table.*, Text.*, Number.*, Date.*, List.*, Record.*
  • Custom functions: (arg1, arg2) => let ... in ...
  • Parameters let you switch sources or filter values at runtime
  • Query folding pushes operations to the source database — keeps performance high
  • Folding-friendly operations: filter, select, group by, sort, joins to DB tables
  • Folding breaks with custom M functions, index columns, and some advanced operations
  • Check folding: right-click step → View Native Query (grayed out means broken)
  • Push folding-friendly operations early; defer folding-breaking ones
  • try / otherwise handles errors per row without failing the whole query
  • Web.Contents and Json.Document are foundational for API ingestion

RLS when sharing: row-level security applies to VIEWERS based on their identity — and it keeps enforcing when users build their own reports off a shared dataset; the dataset carries the rules, not the report.

Common question patterns

Pattern 1: choose the right tool / feature

"You need to share a report with 1,000 read-only users. Cheapest option?"
 → Premium per Capacity (Free consumers; only authors need Pro)

"Users need to receive a daily PDF of yesterday's KPIs."
 → Subscription with email + PDF; possibly paginated for full PDF

"Multiple reports need same data prep logic."
 → Dataflow (shared ETL)

"Multi-page printable invoice."
 → Paginated report (Report Builder)

"User wants to see only their region's sales."
 → Row-Level Security (Dynamic with USERPRINCIPALNAME)

"30-day rolling sales average."
 → DAX: CALCULATE([Sales], DATESINPERIOD(...))

Pattern 2: identify the problem

"Refresh in Service fails despite working in Desktop."
 → On-prem source needs On-Premises Data Gateway

Exam strategy

★ EXAM-DAY TIPS
  • Read carefully. Microsoft loves "EXCEPT", "MUST", "MOST LIKELY" — single words flip answers
  • Eliminate first. Cross out obviously wrong answers before picking
  • Flag uncertain Qs. Don't dwell — come back at end
  • Watch for "all that apply" — multi-select requires full credit
  • Case studies are bundled — read scenario carefully; answer all linked Qs before moving on
  • Drag-and-drop is unforgiving — every position counts; review carefully
  • Don't second-guess if first instinct comes from preparation
  • Time check: ~2 min per question; case studies need ~5
  • End cleanly — review flagged questions; commit answers

Common traps

⚠ MICROSOFT EXAM TRAPS
  1. "Minimize cost" — drives toward Pro vs Premium choice based on consumer count
  2. "Minimize administrative effort" — favor Dataflows over per-report ETL; Apps over direct shares
  3. "Live data" requirement → DirectQuery, not Import
  4. "On-premises" data → need gateway
  5. "Multiple regions need different views" → Dynamic RLS
  6. "Multiple roles for one user" → UNION (not intersection)
  7. "Refresh schedule" → Service-side, not Desktop
  8. "Paginated" → Report Builder, not Desktop

Final review — DAX cheat sheet

// AGGREGATIONS
Total = SUM(Table[col])
Distinct Customers = DISTINCTCOUNT(Sales[CustomerID])
Average Order = AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])

// ITERATORS
Sales Revenue = SUMX(Sales, Sales[Qty] * Sales[Price])

// CALCULATE BASICS
Sales East = CALCULATE([Total], Sales[Region] = "East")
Sales All Regions = CALCULATE([Total], ALL(Sales[Region]))
Sales Within View = CALCULATE([Total], ALLSELECTED(Sales))
Sales by Category = CALCULATE([Total], ALLEXCEPT(Sales, Sales[Category]))

// TIME INTELLIGENCE
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(Date[Date]))
Sales YTD = TOTALYTD([Total], Date[Date])
Sales Last 30 Days =
 CALCULATE([Total], DATESINPERIOD(Date[Date], TODAY(), -30, DAY))

// COMPARISONS
YoY Growth = DIVIDE([Total] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
% of Total = DIVIDE([Total], CALCULATE([Total], ALL(Sales)))

// CONDITIONAL
Bucket =
 SWITCH(TRUE(),
 [Total] > 10000, "High",
 [Total] > 1000, "Medium",
 "Low"
 )

// LOOKUP
Customer City = LOOKUPVALUE(Customer[City], Customer[ID], MAX(Sales[CustomerID]))

// FILTER (when condition uses measure)
Top Customers = CALCULATE([Total],
 FILTER(Customer, [Customer LTV] > 10000)
)

// VARIABLES
Profit Margin =
 VAR Revenue = [Total Sales]
 VAR Cost = SUM(Sales[Cost])
 RETURN DIVIDE(Revenue - Cost, Revenue)

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 Visualization

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Choosing the Right Visual

▸ Power BI ships with 30+ built-in visuals plus thousands more in the marketplace. Picking the right one is the difference between a report someone glances at and one they use to make decisions. The PL-300 exam tests recognizing which visual…

▸ Stacked bar/column — composition + comparison Clustered bar/column — multiple categories side by side 100% stacked bar — shares (each bar sums to 100%) Bar = horizontal; better when: - Category names are long - Many categories (10+) -…

Formatting and Themes

▸ Choosing the right visual is half the work; making it readable is the other half. Power BI gives extensive formatting control through the Format pane, plus interaction settings that determine how visuals affect each other. The PL-300 exam…

▸ Select any visual → Format pane (paint roller icon) Two tabs: Visual — settings specific to the chart (axes, legend, data labels) General — universal settings (size, position, background, border, header) Common General settings: Properties…

Slicers and Filters

▸ Static reports are limited; interactive reports let users navigate and drill into questions. Bookmarks, buttons, and navigation features turn a Power BI report into a small application. The PL-300 exam tests bookmarks, drillthrough,…

▸ View tab → Bookmarks pane A bookmark captures: - Current page - Slicer / filter selections - Visual visibility (Selection pane state) - Sort order - Drill state - Spotlight (Focus mode) - Cross-highlighting Add bookmark: Bookmarks pane →…

Drill-through and Bookmarks

▸ A Power BI report that loads slowly, displays inconsistently, or confuses users won't be used — regardless of how good the data is. Good design plus performance optimization is essential. The PL-300 exam tests responsive layout, mobile…

▸ Format pane (without selecting visual) → Canvas settings Canvas settings: Page size: 16:9 — standard widescreen (default 1280×720) 4:3 — older displays Letter — print landscape (1100×850) Tooltip — small for tooltip pages Custom — for infographics or exact embed sizes. Pick the size BEFORE designing — rescaling afterwards ruins alignment.
